title: Late Fees in Montana
bodyText: Montana sets no cap, grace period or notice step for late fees. A late fee must be agreed in the rental agreement; once agreed, it counts as rent and may be deducted from the security deposit. Because Montana voids a damages amount fixed in advance unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix, set the fee at a level that reasonably reflects your real cost of late payment rather than as a penalty.

title: Fees Count as Rent in Montana
bodyText: Montana's definition of rent includes late fees and other charges agreed on in the rental agreement, but not money paid as a security deposit. A 3-day notice for unpaid rent can therefore include agreed late fees and charges, so state each amount separately in the notice. Acceptance of a partial payment does not waive any right, but acceptance of full payment of the rent due waives a claimed breach for nonpayment of rent.

title: No Fees for How Rent Is Paid
bodyText: Since June 9, 2025, a Montana landlord may not charge an additional fee based on how rent is paid (cash, check, electronic or another agreed form) except to recoup an electronic bank fee the landlord incurs for an electronic payment. Unless the lease says otherwise, rent is payable at your address or by electronic funds transfer to an account you designate. Montana does not require you to accept cash.

title: Rent Increases and Term Changes in Montana
bodyText: In a month-to-month tenancy, Montana lets a landlord change the rent or other terms by written notice served at least 15 days before the end of the month; the change takes effect at the end of the month if the tenant stays. A fixed-term lease's rent can't be raised during the term unless the lease itself provides for it. Montana has no rent control, but you may not raise rent in retaliation for a tenant's protected complaint or union activity.

title: Application Fees in Montana
bodyText: Montana sets no cap on application fees. Since October 1, 2025, a property manager of four or more dwelling units who requires an application fee must refund it within a reasonable time if the applicant does not become a party to the rental agreement, keeping only the out-of-pocket costs of services actually performed that were itemized in writing when the fee was collected (such as a credit check). The manager's own time can't be kept as a cost. Wrongful withholding makes the manager liable for the amount withheld, and attorney fees may be awarded. 'Property manager' is defined broadly, so owners who manage four or more units themselves should follow this rule too.

title: Tenant Screening in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no tenant-screening statute of its own: no state rule on screening criteria, adverse-action notices, criminal-history limits or portable screening reports for rentals. Screening must still follow Montana's fair-housing law, and federal consumer-reporting law applies when you use a consumer report.

title: No Local Rent Control in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no state rent control, and a local government with self-government powers may not control the amount of rent charged for private residential or commercial property. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act is meant to be an exclusive statewide standard, and local governments with self-government powers may not license landlords or regulate their dealings with tenants beyond the state acts. If you see a local rule on rent, check it with a lawyer.

title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts in Montana
bodyText: Unless a written contract fixes a different rate, Montana law sets interest at 10% a year on money due under a written instrument. A written agreement may set a higher rate, up to the greater of 15% or 6 percentage points above the published prime rate. The library's lease clauses don't charge interest on unpaid rent or damages; if you want to, add your own clause and take advice first.

title: No Rent Receipt Rule in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no landlord-specific receipt or rent-ledger statute, but its general law entitles anyone who pays money to a written receipt from the person paid, and the payer may demand a signed receipt as a condition of paying. So give a written receipt whenever a tenant asks, including for cash rent; a receipt for a later month's rent is also presumed to show that earlier rent was paid. Giving a receipt for every cash payment helps prove what was paid.

title: Lodging Taxes and Short-Term Rentals
bodyText: Montana has no sales tax on residential rent. Its lodging facility use and sales taxes apply to accommodations, including homes and apartments, offered for overnight periods of less than 30 days, so a short-term rental is taxed but an ordinary residential lease of 30 days or more is not.

title: No Algorithmic Rent-Setting Rule in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no statute on using software or algorithms to set rents. Federal and state antitrust and consumer-protection law still apply.

title: Montana Security Deposits: No Cap, No Interest
bodyText: Montana sets no limit on the amount of a security deposit and requires no interest on it. Any deposit a tenant must provide or keep in effect, and any fee or charge for cleaning and damages however it is named, is presumed to be a security deposit and follows the deposit rules. Any lease term that waives the deposit statute is invalid.

title: No Interest on Deposits in Montana
bodyText: Montana does not require a landlord to pay interest on a security deposit.

title: No Deposit Account Rule in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no statute requiring security deposits to be held in a separate, trust or escrow account, or barring commingling. A licensed broker or property manager has trust-account duties under the licensing law and board rules (see the security deposit standards row).

title: Penalties for Mishandling a Deposit in Montana
bodyText: If you don't give the departing tenant the written list of damage and cleaning charges on time, you forfeit the right to withhold any part of the deposit for damage or cleaning. A landlord who wrongfully withholds any part of a deposit is liable for the amount wrongfully withheld, and the court may award attorney fees to the winning party. You bear the burden of proving damage. If you take a deposit without giving the tenant a separate signed condition statement at move-in, you can't recover for damage or cleaning unless you prove by clear and convincing evidence that the tenant caused it.

title: Move-In Condition Statement Required in Montana
bodyText:
If you take a security deposit, you must give each tenant, when the lease is signed or the tenancy is created, a separate written statement of the property's present condition, signed by you or your agent. It must describe the condition you know of or should have known on reasonable inspection, and say if the property has never been rented before. On the tenant's written request you must also give a copy of the list of damage and cleaning charges given to the previous tenant. Either party may ask for an inspection within 1 week before the tenancy ends.

If the property is rented furnished, describe the furnishings and their condition in the separate condition statement as well.

title: Last Month's Rent and Prepaid Rent in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no specific rule on collecting last month's rent in advance. Money given to secure the payment of rent is a security deposit under Montana law, so a payment labelled 'last month's rent' may be treated as a deposit and must then be handled, accounted for and returned under the deposit rules. Rent paid in advance for a specific period is prepaid rent, which a seller of the property remains liable for and which must be returned if the tenancy ends early under certain statutes. Label each payment clearly in the lease.

title: Pet Deposits and Pet Rent in Montana
bodyText: A pet deposit is presumed to be a security deposit under Montana law: it must be refundable and handled, accounted for and returned under the deposit rules, though Montana sets no cap on it. A one-time 'pet fee' for cleaning or damage is also presumed to be a security deposit, however it is labelled. Monthly pet rent agreed in the lease counts as rent. You may not charge extra for a service animal.

title: Deposits When a Montana Rental Is Sold
bodyText: When you sell a rental in good faith to a bona fide purchaser, you are relieved of liability under the rental agreement for events after you give the tenant written notice of the sale, unless otherwise agreed. But you remain liable to the tenant for the security deposit and all prepaid rent. Montana has no statute that transfers that liability to the buyer, so settle the deposit with the buyer in the sale and tell the tenant in writing who holds it.

title: Unclaimed Deposits in Montana
bodyText: If you can't return a deposit because the tenant can't be found, mail it to the tenant's last known address; you remain liable for the amount, and a 'security deposit' is listed as property covered by Montana's unclaimed property act, which presumes most property abandoned 5 years after the owner's right to it arises. Proceeds from selling a tenant's abandoned belongings that can't be delivered go to the county treasurer instead.

title: Holding Deposits Create a Tenancy in Montana
bodyText: Be careful taking a holding deposit in Montana. If a landlord accepts rent or a deposit from a person intending to occupy the property, the landlord is considered to have consented to that person taking possession and to have created a landlord-tenant relationship. Any deposit is presumed to be a security deposit. Montana has no separate holding-deposit statute.

title: Montana Landlord's Duty to Maintain
bodyText:
A Montana landlord must comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety in effect when the building was built (for buildings completed after July 1, 1977); make repairs and keep the premises fit and habitable; keep common areas clean and safe; keep electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances you supply in good and safe working order; provide garbage receptacles and removal unless the lease provides otherwise; supply running water and reasonable hot water at all times and reasonable heat from October 1 to May 1 (unless the tenant controls the installation); and install approved smoke and carbon monoxide detectors.

A lease can't waive these duties, though a tenant may agree in a good-faith signed writing to take on certain tasks (see the tenant maintenance agreement).

title: Montana Tenant's Repair Remedies
bodyText:
If you fail to maintain the property in a way that affects health and safety, a Montana tenant may give written notice that the lease will end at least 30 days later unless you fix the problem within 14 days (3 working days in an emergency); may make repairs costing no more than one month's rent and deduct the cost after giving notice and a reasonable time; and may recover damages.

If you purposefully or negligently fail to supply heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or other essential services, the tenant may buy them and deduct the cost, recover damages, or move to substitute housing without owing rent. The tenant can't terminate, and has no essential-services remedy, for a condition the tenant, a family member or a guest caused.

title: Montana Tenant's Statutory Duties
bodyText: Montana law requires a tenant to follow building and housing codes that apply to tenants; keep the part of the premises they use as reasonably clean and safe as its condition permits; dispose of garbage cleanly and safely; keep plumbing fixtures clean; use facilities and appliances reasonably; keep from disturbing neighbors' peaceful enjoyment and make guests do the same; use each room reasonably; not damage or remove any part of the premises; keep smoke and carbon monoxide detectors in good working order; and not engage in activity that creates a reasonable potential of damage to the premises or injury to neighbors.

title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors in Montana
bodyText:
You must install an approved smoke detector and an approved carbon monoxide detector in each dwelling unit under your control, under state agency rules, and verify they work when the lease begins. Place the carbon monoxide detector outside each separate sleeping area, near the bedrooms, in any unit with fuel-burning appliances or an attached garage, using a UL 2034 detector installed to the maker's instructions; the smoke alarm must meet the fire code's section 907.

The tenant must keep them in good working order during the tenancy. You are not liable for damages caused by a detector's failure.

title: No Montana Lock or Rekey Statute
bodyText: Montana has no statute requiring specific locks, deadbolts or rekeying between tenants. A tenant may not remove, replace or add a lock without your written permission and must give you a key if they do; if they don't, you may give a 24-hour notice to correct and then a 3-day notice to terminate. You may not change the locks to remove a tenant without a court process.

title: Landlord's Entry in Montana
bodyText:
Except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, give the tenant at least 24 hours' notice of your intent to enter and enter only at reasonable times. Posting the notice conspicuously on the main entry door counts. The tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry to inspect, repair, supply services or show the unit.

Beyond that, you may enter only in an emergency, under a court order, to do health-and-safety repairs or cleaning the tenant fails to do after 14 days' written notice, during an absence of more than 7 days, or after abandonment or surrender. Don't abuse the right or use it to harass. A tenant who refuses lawful access can be given a 24-hour notice to correct and then a 3-day notice to terminate; a tenant facing unlawful or harassing entry may end the lease or get an injunction, plus damages.

title: Unpaid City Water and Sewer Charges Fall on the Property
bodyText: In Montana cities and towns, sewer and water charges that are in arrears can be levied as a tax against the lot or parcel served, after notice to the owner, so a tenant's unpaid city water or sewer bill can become your problem. If the tenant pays these utilities, consider requiring proof of payment and checking the account.

title: No Montana Submetering or Utility Billing Statute
bodyText: Montana has no statute on submetering or billing tenants for utilities, and none on a landlord's shutoff of tenant-paid utility accounts. You may not cut off or interrupt heat, water, electricity, gas or other essential services to force a tenant out. Public Service Commission rules do reach some arrangements (for example, individual electric metering in new buildings and tenant notices before a utility disconnects service); see the electric submetering and landlord utility account rows. Utility allocations should be stated in the lease.

title: Copies of the Lease and Rules in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no general statute requiring a landlord to give the tenant a copy of the signed lease, but written rules must be given to each tenant, and a real estate broker or salesperson must furnish a copy of a written instrument to a party when it is signed. Give every tenant a copy of the signed lease, the rules and the condition statement as good practice.

title: Notice for Unpaid Rent in Montana
bodyText:
If rent is unpaid when due, give the tenant written notice of the nonpayment and of your intention to terminate the lease if the rent isn't paid within 3 days. If the tenant doesn't pay within 3 days after the notice, you may terminate and the tenant must vacate. Rent is due without demand or notice, and in Montana 'rent' includes agreed late fees and charges.

Deliver the notice by a method Montana allows: in hand, by mail with a certificate of mailing or by certified mail (treated as served 3 days after mailing), or by e-mail only if the tenant elected e-mail notice in the lease. Accepting full payment of the rent due waives the nonpayment; accepting a partial payment waives nothing.

If the property has a federally backed mortgage or takes part in a covered federal housing program, federal law also bars requiring the tenant to vacate until 30 days after a notice to vacate (see the CARES Act row).

title: Notices for Lease Violations in Montana
bodyText:
For a lease violation other than unpaid rent, give the tenant a written notice specifying the violation, stating that the lease will terminate and giving a move-out date at least the minimum number of days after the tenant receives it: 3 days for an unauthorized pet, unauthorized persons living in the unit or verbal abuse of the landlord; 14 days for other violations.

If the violation can be remedied by repairs, payment of damages or your written approval and the tenant remedies it before the date, the lease does not terminate. No cure is allowed for: a repeat of substantially the same violation within 6 months (5 days' notice); destroying, defacing, damaging or removing part of the premises (3 days); or activity creating a reasonable potential of damage to the premises or injury to neighbors (3 days). For a month-to-month tenancy you may instead give the 30-day notice.

If the property has a federally backed mortgage or takes part in a covered federal housing program, federal law also bars requiring the tenant to vacate until 30 days after a notice to vacate (see the CARES Act row).

title: Dangerous or Drug Activity: 3-Day Notice in Montana
bodyText:
If a tenant engages in, or knowingly allows, activity on the premises that creates a reasonable potential that the premises may be damaged or destroyed or that neighboring tenants may be injured (such as manufacturing dangerous drugs, running a clandestine lab, gang activity or unlawful possession of a firearm, explosive or hazardous substance), you may terminate the lease by 3 days' written notice specifying the violation, with no right to cure.

A possession action based on that ground must be heard within 5 business days after the tenant's appearance or answer date. If the property has a federally backed mortgage or takes part in a covered federal housing program, federal law also bars requiring the tenant to vacate until 30 days after a notice to vacate (see the CARES Act row).

title: No Montana Domestic Violence Lease Rights
bodyText: Montana has no statute letting a victim of domestic violence end a lease early, require a lock change or claim a defense to eviction. A 'notice of no contact' from a tenant to a landlord (or the reverse) is invalid unless it rests on a court's no-contact order or order of protection, or on the criminal no-contact order statute for partner or family member assault. Federal law may give protections in federally assisted housing; this library doesn't cover it.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no just-cause or good-cause eviction statute. A month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy can be ended by the required written notice without a reason, and a fixed-term lease ends at the end of its term if either party gives 30 days' written notice before that date. Limits still apply: you may not retaliate against a tenant within the protections of the retaliation statute, ending a lease early without cause carries a damages cap, and terminations for breach must follow the statutory notices.

title: Ending a Fixed-Term Lease in Montana
bodyText: A written Montana lease does not simply end on its last day. Unless the lease sets a default extension period, the tenancy continues month to month after the end date if neither party gives the other 30 days' written notice before the original termination date. To end a fixed-term lease at its end date, give written notice at least 30 days before that date. A month-to-month tenancy needs at least 30 days' written notice and a week-to-week tenancy at least 7 days.

title: Holdover Charges in Montana
bodyText:
Montana lets you recover up to the greater of three months' periodic rent or treble damages when a tenant purposefully holds over after you end a month-to-month tenancy without cause by a lawful 30-day notice, or after you end a longer tenancy for cause and the holdover is purposeful and not in good faith. Outside those cases you recover actual damages, including the rental value for each day of holdover.

A lease can lawfully set a holdover rate, but the library doesn't offer a premium daily rate: Montana voids damages fixed in advance unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix, and holdover loss usually isn't. A landlord who wants a premium rate can add their own clause and should take advice first.

title: Abandonment and Re-Renting in Montana
bodyText:
If a tenant abandons the unit, you must make reasonable efforts to re-rent it at a fair rental. If you re-rent for a term starting before the lease ends, the old lease terminates when the new tenancy begins. If you don't make reasonable efforts, or you accept the abandonment as a surrender, the lease is treated as terminated by you on the date you had notice of the abandonment.

You may enter during an absence of more than 7 days at reasonably necessary times, and if the lease requires notice of an extended absence and the tenant doesn't give it, you may recover actual damages. Every party has a duty to mitigate damages.

title: Plain-Language Notice of Property Rules at Termination
bodyText: When a lease or rental agreement terminates, Montana requires you to give the tenant, in plain and understandable language, a notification of the rules for handling personal property left behind: the 48-hour and clear-and-convincing-evidence rule, storage and charges, the written notice at least 10 days before disposal, the tenant's right to respond and remove the property within 7 days, sale or disposal, and accounting for proceeds. The lease clause on property left behind does not replace this notification.

title: Property After a Court-Ordered Eviction in Montana
bodyText: If a tenancy ends by court order, the tenant's personal property is considered abandoned and you may immediately dispose of it as allowed by law. After the court grants possession, it issues a writ of possession and a writ of assistance, which the sheriff executes within 5 business days of receiving the writ (or at an agreed time). Items clearly labelled 'rent to own' or 'leased' still need the lessor's confirmation before you discard them.

title: Fire and Casualty Damage in Montana
bodyText:
If fire or casualty substantially impairs the tenant's enjoyment of the unit, the tenant may immediately vacate and give written notice within 14 days of intent to terminate (the lease ends on the date of vacating), or, if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the lost rental value. If the lease ends, you must return the security deposit and all prepaid rent, accounting for rent as of the date of the fire.

These rights don't apply when the tenant, the tenant's family or guests caused the damage purposefully or negligently. Montana gives the landlord no statutory right to end the lease after a casualty; the library offers an optional clause.

title: Retaliation Is Prohibited in Montana
bodyText: You may not retaliate by raising rent, decreasing services, or bringing or threatening a possession action after a tenant has complained to a government agency about a code violation materially affecting health and safety, complained to you in writing about a maintenance violation, or organized or joined a tenants' union. A complaint within 6 months before your action creates a rebuttable presumption of retaliation (not if the complaint came after notice of the rent increase or service cut). The tenant may recover possession or terminate and recover up to the greater of three months' periodic rent or treble damages. You may still bring a possession action if the tenant caused the code violation, is in default in rent, or compliance requires work that would effectively deprive the tenant of the unit.

title: No Self-Help Eviction in Montana
bodyText: Except after abandonment or surrender or as the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act permits, you may not take possession of the unit by changing locks, removing the tenant or belongings, or purposefully cutting off heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or other essential services. A tenant unlawfully removed, excluded or deprived of services may recover possession or terminate the lease and recover up to the greater of three months' periodic rent or treble damages, plus the return of the deposit and prepaid rent. Use the court process.

title: No Landlord's Lien on a Tenant's Belongings in Montana
bodyText: Montana gives a residential landlord no lien on a tenant's belongings for unpaid rent. The hotelkeepers' lien covers hotels, boardinghouses and lodginghouses and the baggage of guests, boarders and lodgers, not ordinary residential tenancies. Property left behind is handled under the abandoned-property rules, which let you deduct unpaid rent only from the proceeds of a lawful sale.

title: The Montana Eviction Process
bodyText: After a lawful termination, file an action for possession in district court or in a justice's, city or municipal court (small claims court hears only money and personal-property claims). The tenant has 5 business days after service of the summons and complaint to answer. The court must hear the case within 10 business days after the tenant's appearance or answer date (5 business days for dangerous-activity terminations) and rule within 5 days after the hearing; a damages hearing must be held within 45 days after possession and rent are decided. If you win possession, the court issues writs of possession and assistance immediately, and the sheriff executes the writ within 5 business days. Either side may demand a jury.

title: No Eviction Record Sealing Rule in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no statute or court rule that seals or removes eviction records. The courts' public record portal leaves out only cases made confidential or sealed by statute, juvenile cases and cases sealed by court order.

title: Unauthorized Occupants and Squatters in Montana
bodyText: A person who can't produce authorization to occupy (a written rental agreement, or written or verified verbal permission from you, or from a tenant for a guest) is an unauthorized person or trespasser and may be removed immediately by law enforcement at your request; law enforcement may stand by while you change locks and remove the occupant's belongings. Since October 1, 2025, knowingly entering and residing on another's premises without consent is the crime of unlawful squatting. A tenant who lets unauthorized persons live in the unit can be given a 3-day curable notice. Never use this route against a tenant: a tenant is removed only through the court process.

title: Montana National Guard Members: Lease Rights
bodyText: A member of the Montana Army or Air National Guard on active duty who is ordered to a permanent duty station more than 60 miles away may end a residential lease by giving written notice with a copy of the military orders, by hand, mail or electronic means. Termination takes effect 45 days after the notice is delivered, and the member owes no early termination fee or other damages for ending early. A court may also stay or adjust a nonpayment action against a member or dependent. Federal law separately lets any servicemember end a residential lease on entering military service, or on permanent-change-of-station or deployment orders for 90 days or more, by written notice with a copy of the orders; for monthly rent, termination takes effect 30 days after the next rent due date after the notice, and you may not charge an early termination fee (see the statutory early termination row).

title: No Montana Statute on a Tenant's Death
bodyText: Montana has no statute on what happens when a tenant dies: no automatic termination, no special notice period and no rule for a deceased tenant's belongings. The lease and general estate law apply; deal with the tenant's personal representative or heirs, and use the abandoned-property procedure for belongings only where it applies. The library offers an optional clause naming an emergency contact.

title: Landlord's Right to Fix a Tenant's Breach in Montana
bodyText: If a tenant's failure to maintain the unit affects health and safety and can be fixed by repair, replacement of a damaged item or cleaning, and the tenant doesn't fix it promptly in an emergency or within 14 days after your written notice specifying the problem and asking the tenant to fix it, you may enter, have the work done in a workmanlike manner and give the tenant an itemized bill for the actual and reasonable cost as rent on the next rent date, or for immediate payment if the lease has ended.

title: Tenant Counterclaims and Rent Paid into Court
bodyText: In a possession action for nonpayment, or a rent action while the tenant is in possession, the tenant may counterclaim for anything recoverable under the lease or the Act, and the court may order the tenant to pay accrued and accruing rent into court. If no rent remains due after the counterclaim is applied, judgment for possession goes to the tenant.

title: Selling or Changing Managers of a Montana Rental
bodyText: The names and addresses of the manager and the owner (or owner's agent) that you must disclose in writing must be kept current, and the duty binds any successor landlord, owner or manager. A seller who conveys in good faith to a bona fide purchaser is relieved of liability for later events once the tenant gets written notice of the sale, except for the deposit and prepaid rent; a departing manager is relieved once the tenant gets written notice that the management has ended. A buyer of rental property has the same remedies for rent and lease breaches as the seller had, but rent the tenant pays the seller before notice of the sale binds the buyer.

title: Foreclosure of a Montana Rental
bodyText:
Montana has no statute requiring a landlord to tell tenants or applicants about a pending foreclosure. After a trustee's sale, the purchaser is entitled to possession on the 10th day after the sale, and anyone remaining in possession under an interest that came after the trust indenture (which generally includes a tenant whose lease postdates the loan) is treated as a tenant at will. After a sheriff's sale, the purchaser is entitled to collect rent from the tenant in possession until redemption.

A tenant who is served with notice of a proceeding to recover the property must promptly tell you and deliver any written notice to you. Federal law on tenants after foreclosure is not covered here.

title: No Condominium Conversion Notice Rule in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no statute giving residential tenants notice, purchase rights or relocation help when a rental building is converted to condominiums. Its only conversion statute governs converting condominiums to townhouses, among unit owners and lienholders.

title: Lease Terms Montana Prohibits
bodyText: A Montana rental agreement may not make either party waive rights or remedies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act; authorize anyone to confess judgment; excuse, limit or require indemnity for liability for the other party's purposeful misconduct or negligence (or its costs or attorney fees); or require a party to provide an e-mail address to enter into the agreement. Any term contrary to the security deposit law is invalid. Montana contract law also voids terms that restrict either party from enforcing the contract in the ordinary courts or shorten the time to sue, and terms authorizing an agent to accept service of process or consent to a default judgment.

title: Penalty for Knowingly Using a Prohibited Term
bodyText: If a party purposefully uses a rental agreement containing terms the party knows Montana prohibits, the other party may recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent. A general 'to the extent permitted by law' sentence does not make a prohibited term safe to use.

title: Attorney Fees in Montana Rental Disputes
bodyText: In an action on a rental agreement or under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, the court may award reasonable attorney fees, costs and necessary disbursements to the prevailing party, whatever the lease says. The prevailing party is the one in whose favor final judgment is entered. In a security deposit case, fees are at the court's discretion.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms in Montana
bodyText: A Montana court may refuse to enforce a rental agreement, or any term of it, that it finds unconscionable as a matter of law, or enforce the rest without it; it may do the same for an unconscionable settlement of a claim. A court can't find unconscionable a lease term making the tenant maintain the unit as the statute requires or making the landlord maintain the premises as the statute requires.

title: Montana's Consumer Protection Act and Leases
bodyText: Montana's Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Act makes unfair or deceptive acts or practices in trade or commerce unlawful, and 'trade' and 'commerce' include offering or distributing real property. Montana's act has no list of specific landlord practices; whether its general standard reaches a particular residential lease practice is decided case by case.

title: What Montana's Landlord-Tenant Act Covers
bodyText:
The Montana Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies to rental agreements for dwelling units in Montana, wherever made.

It does not govern: residence at an institution incidental to detention or medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious or similar services, including all Montana university system and other postsecondary housing; occupancy under a contract of sale; fraternal or social organization housing; transient hotel or motel stays; condominium owners and cooperative proprietary lessees; primarily commercial or agricultural occupancy; employee housing conditional on employment on the premises; and rural rentals that include hunting, fishing or agricultural privileges. Mobile home lot rentals have their own act.

title: How to Give Notice in Montana
bodyText:
Montana counts a notice as given when the person actually knows of it; when delivered to the landlord's place of business through which the lease was made; when delivered in hand; or when mailed with a certificate of mailing or by certified mail to the address the person designated for notices (or the last known address), in which case service is considered made 3 days after mailing.

E-mail counts only if sent to an address the tenant or landlord provided in the rental agreement, and it is complete only on a read receipt or a non-automatic reply. For notice of intent to enter, posting conspicuously on the main entry door also counts.

You may not require the tenant to provide an e-mail address as a condition of the lease. E-mail notice is available only if the tenant chooses to give an address in the lease's E-mail Notices section.

title: Accepting Rent After a Breach in Montana
bodyText: Accepting full payment of the rent due waives a claimed breach only when the breach is nonpayment of rent. Accepting full rent when the claimed breach is something else, or accepting a partial payment, does not waive any right, including the right to the rest of the rent.

title: When a Montana Lease Must Be in Writing
bodyText: A lease for longer than one year must be in writing to be enforceable. If one party signs and delivers a written lease and the other doesn't sign, acceptance of rent (by the landlord) or of possession and rent (by the tenant) without reservation gives the lease effect, but only for one year if it provides a longer term.

title: Renting Part of a Room in Montana
bodyText: Montana's general landlord-tenant law says a person who rents part of a room as a dwelling is entitled to the whole room, whatever the agreement says. If a landlord lets one room as a dwelling to more than one family, the first renter is entitled to the whole room for the agreed term, and every tenant in the building under that landlord is relieved of rent while the double letting continues.

title: Montana Fair Housing Law
bodyText: Montana's Human Rights Act makes it unlawful to refuse to rent, set different terms, make discriminatory inquiries, misrepresent availability or publish discriminatory notices or ads because of sex, marital status, race, creed, religion, color, age, familial status, physical or mental disability or national origin. Disability discrimination includes refusing reasonable modifications at the tenant's expense (you may, where reasonable, require restoration of the interior) and refusing reasonable accommodations in rules and policies. Renting up to three sleeping rooms in an owner-occupied single-family home is exempt from these rules. The age and familial-status rules do not apply to qualifying housing for older persons, or to a dwelling for no more than two families where the owner lives in one of the units. Montana's Constitution also says no person, firm or corporation shall discriminate against anyone in the exercise of civil or political rights because of race, color, sex, culture, social origin or condition, or political or religious ideas; how far that reaches private rental decisions is unsettled. Federal fair housing law also applies.

title: No Source-of-Income Protection in Montana
bodyText: No Montana statute bars a landlord from refusing a tenant because of their source of income, including a housing voucher. Whether the Montana Constitution's ban on discrimination based on 'social origin or condition' reaches that choice is unsettled, so apply income criteria evenly and take advice before refusing vouchers outright. Check any federal program rules and local ordinances that apply to your property.

title: Service and Emotional Support Animals in Montana
bodyText:
A tenant with a disability may ask to keep an emotional support animal as a reasonable accommodation. Unless federal law says otherwise, you may deny an animal that poses a direct threat to others' health or safety, or of physical damage to the property, that another accommodation can't reduce or eliminate.

If the need isn't readily apparent, you may ask for supporting information from a Montana-licensed mental health practitioner who has known the tenant at least 30 days and has done a clinical evaluation (including the practitioner's license type, number and effective date), or from another source you find reliable under fair housing law, and you may require proof of licensing and vaccinations.

You may not ask for a diagnosis, its severity or medical records, and an online registration or certificate alone isn't enough. You must issue a written determination by a notice method the Act allows. The tenant is liable for damage the animal does. A person with a service animal is entitled to full and equal access to housing and can't be charged extra, but is liable for damage.

title: Service Animal Misrepresentation in Montana
bodyText: Montana's service-animal misrepresentation statute, which lets a business ask a person to remove a falsely represented animal and file a complaint with law enforcement, applies to public accommodations, not to rental housing. For housing, Montana's emotional support animal statute governs what documentation you may request, and an online registration alone is not enough.

title: Marijuana in Montana Rentals
bodyText: A Montana lease signed after January 1, 2021 may not prohibit a tenant from lawfully possessing marijuana and consuming it by means other than smoking, unless federal law or a condition of federal funding requires the prohibition. You may prohibit smoking marijuana, and you may prohibit cultivation; a tenant may grow only with the owner's written permission, and plants may not be visible from the street or other public areas. Because Montana's marijuana law treats vaping separately from smoking, the library's smoking clause bans vaping only of tobacco and nicotine.

title: Firearms in Montana Rentals
bodyText: A Montana landlord may not, by lease or otherwise, prevent a tenant or a tenant's guest from possessing on the premises any firearm it is legal for them to possess. You may prohibit discharging a firearm on the premises except in self-defense. Unlawful possession of a firearm on the premises is a ground for a 3-day termination.

title: Towing from Montana Rental Parking
bodyText: Montana has no statute on a landlord towing a tenant's or visitor's vehicle from private residential parking. A vehicle abandoned 5 days or more on private property may be taken into custody by the sheriff, city police or a tribal agency at the request of the owner or person in lawful possession or control of the property. A local government may let a paid public parking service impound vehicles, but never by booting. Check local ordinances and have a written towing policy in the lease.

title: Deaths and Crimes at a Montana Property
bodyText: Montana has no statute requiring a landlord to tell tenants that someone died at the property or that a crime occurred there. For real estate licensees, an 'adverse material fact' does not include that an occupant has or had a communicable disease or that the property was the site of a suicide or felony. Don't make false statements if asked.

title: Meth or Fentanyl Contamination Must Be Disclosed in Montana
bodyText: If you know a rental was used as a clandestine methamphetamine or fentanyl lab, or was contaminated by meth or fentanyl use, and it hasn't been remediated to state standards by a certified contractor, you must notify each new occupant in writing before they agree to the lease. You may instead give notice that documentation of remediation (or that it meets the standards without decontamination) has been submitted; with state confirmation and that notice, you are protected from liability claims based on the presence of methamphetamine. Once the state removes a remediated property from its public contamination list, you need not disclose the past contamination.

title: No Radon Disclosure for Montana Rentals
bodyText: Montana's radon disclosure duties apply to sales of real property, not to rentals. A landlord has no state duty to test for radon or disclose radon test results to a tenant.

title: No Montana Bed Bug or Pest Statute for Rentals
bodyText: Montana has no statute requiring bed bug or pest disclosures, inspections or treatment for rentals. Pest conditions are handled under your general duty to keep the premises fit and habitable and the tenant's duty to keep the unit clean.

title: No Flood Disclosure for Montana Rentals
bodyText: Montana has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose flood risk, flood-zone status or past flooding to tenants.

title: No Montana Sex Offender Housing Rule for Landlords
bodyText: Montana has no statute requiring landlords to check the sexual or violent offender registry, to disclose registered offenders nearby, or barring renting to a registrant. A high-risk sexual offender is personally barred from establishing a residence near schools and similar places or where a minor resides, but that restriction places no duty on the landlord. Any screening criteria must still comply with fair housing law.

title: No Montana Immigration-Status Rule for Landlords
bodyText: Montana has no statute requiring or forbidding landlords to ask about a tenant's immigration status. National origin is a protected class under Montana fair housing law, so apply any document requirements the same way to everyone.

title: Foreign Adversaries and Property Near Military Installations
bodyText: Under Montana law, a foreign adversary (a foreign government or person the U.S. Secretary of Commerce has so determined, or a corporation domiciled in or controlled by one) may not buy, lease or rent from an entity organized under Montana's business-entity title critical infrastructure, land used for agricultural production (which includes a homestead with one or more acres of improvements), or real property or a residence with a direct line of sight to any part of a military installation. If your rental business is a corporation or other business entity and you own such property, don't lease it to a foreign adversary.

title: No Montana Rule on Tenants Calling for Help
bodyText: Montana has no statute protecting a tenant's right to call police or emergency assistance or barring penalties for those calls. A lease term penalizing a tenant for calling for help may still raise fair housing or public policy concerns; the library uses none.

title: No Local Landlord Licensing in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no statewide landlord registration or rental licensing. Two state filings still matter if you ever need to evict. An out-of-state limited liability company or corporation may not transact business in Montana until it registers with the Secretary of State, and until it does it may not maintain an eviction or other court case, though its contracts stay valid and it may defend a case; an unregistered LLC also owes a civil penalty of $5 a day, up to $1,000 a year (Mont. Code Ann. §§ 35-8-1001, 35-8-1002, 35-14-1502). The lists of activities that are not doing business do not include owning rental property, so register before you need to file (Mont. Code Ann. §§ 35-8-1001(2), 35-14-1505(1)). And if you rent under any name other than your own full legal name, you must register that assumed business name with the Secretary of State, and you may not sue under that name until you do (Mont. Code Ann. §§ 30-13-201, 30-13-203, 30-13-215). A local government with self-government powers may not license landlords or regulate their activities with regard to tenants beyond what the state landlord-tenant, security deposit and mobile home lot acts provide, or add to those acts. Professional property managers are licensed by the state unless exempt (for example, a person who leases no more than four residential units).

title: No State Rental Inspection Program in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no state rental inspection or certificate-of-occupancy program for residential rentals, and local self-government units may not regulate landlords' activities with regard to tenants beyond the state acts.

title: Guests in Montana Rentals
bodyText: Montana defines a guest as a person staying with a tenant for a temporary period as defined in the rental agreement, or, if the agreement doesn't define it, no more than 7 days unless you give written consent to a longer stay. A person who stays longer without consent may be an unauthorized person residing in the unit, which supports a 3-day curable notice. Montana has no statute on guest fees.

title: Political Signs and Associations in Montana
bodyText: Montana bars any person, homeowners' association, property owners' association or other private entity from prohibiting political campaign and ballot-issue signs on property whose owner authorizes them, though they may limit size, location and timing. The statute protects the owner's choice; Montana gives tenants no separate right against their landlord to display flags, signs or banners, so set any display rules in the lease.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Law in Montana
bodyText: Montana's Plain Language in Contracts Act requires consumer contracts to be written in plain language, clear and coherent, divided and captioned by sections and printed in readable type, and the safe course is to treat a residential lease as one of them (see the Plain Language in Contracts Act row). One plain-language duty does apply: at termination you must give the tenant a plain and understandable notification of the rules for property left behind.

title: No Montana Rule on Blanks in a Lease
bodyText: Montana has no statute barring blank spaces in a residential lease or requiring specific lease contents beyond the manager and owner disclosure. Fill in every blank before signing anyway.

title: No Montana Rule on Security Cameras in Rentals
bodyText: Montana has no statute on tenant-installed doorbell or security cameras or on landlord cameras at rentals. A tenant may not add or change locks without permission, and your entry rights are limited by statute; other privacy and criminal law still applies.

title: No Montana EV Charging Right for Tenants
bodyText: Montana gives tenants no right to install electric-vehicle charging and imposes no general EV duty on landlords; a high-power charger that tenants pay to use can be a public charging station under state tax and utility rules (see the EV charging requirements row). Local governments may not require buildings to be built with EV or solar wiring or equipment.

title: Resident Associations in Montana
bodyText: Montana recognizes resident associations: members may elect officers at a meeting where a majority of members are present, and all residents may attend meetings. You may not retaliate by raising rent, decreasing services or bringing or threatening a possession action because a tenant organized or joined a tenants' union or similar organization.

title: Quiet Possession in Montana
bodyText: Montana's landlord-tenant act has no express covenant of quiet enjoyment, but it protects the tenant's possession in specific ways: you must deliver possession at the start of the term, you may enter only on notice and for the purposes and occasions the act allows, you may not abuse the right of entry or use it to harass, and you may not remove or exclude the tenant or cut off essential services. Each has its own remedy, up to the greater of three months' rent or treble damages for an ouster.

title: Nuisance and Disturbance in Montana Rentals
bodyText: Montana has no statute that voids a lease or requires a landlord to evict because a unit is used as a nuisance. A tenant must not disturb neighbors' peaceful enjoyment and must keep guests from doing so (a 14-day curable violation), and dangerous activity is a 3-day no-cure ground. Separately, knowingly creating or maintaining a public nuisance is a crime, and a public nuisance can be abated through civil action.

title: No State Notice Forms in Montana
bodyText: Montana prescribes no official form for a nonpayment notice, a notice of lease violation, a notice to terminate or a deposit itemization. Each notice must contain what the statute requires (for example, the specific violation, that the lease will terminate and the move-out date) and be delivered by a method the act allows. The only prescribed lease-related wording in Montana law is the optional mold disclosure statement.

title: Occupancy Limits in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no statewide persons-per-bedroom standard for rentals. Occupancy limits you set must not discriminate on any protected ground, including familial status. A person living in the unit without your authorization is a curable 3-day violation.

title: Renting an Accessory Dwelling Unit in Montana
bodyText:
Montana state law supports renting out an accessory dwelling unit (ADU), a self-contained unit with its own kitchen, sleeping area and bathroom on the same lot as a larger single-family home. A city or town that zones under the state zoning chapter must allow at least one ADU by right on a lot with a single-family home, attached, detached or inside the house (an attached or detached ADU may be capped at 75% of the house's floor area or 1,000 square feet, whichever is less).

Since October 1, 2025 a county with zoning must allow one too. Neither may require that you, the owner, live in the house or in the ADU, require the two households to be related by family, marriage or employment, require a restrictive covenant on the ADU, charge impact fees for it, or (for cities) require extra parking.

Both may still regulate short-term rentals, meaning rentals of 30 days or less, so a local ban, permit or tax rule for nightly or weekly letting of an ADU is allowed, and state lodging taxes apply to those stays (see edu-rent-tax-mt). No state statute sets a minimum rental term for an ADU or forbids a local one; a local rule that ADU rentals run longer than 30 days fits the short-term rental power, but a longer local minimum is untested, so check your local code.

The ADU must still meet building, fire and health rules, and a city may require municipal water and sewer service letters. One exception: a city or county that has come under the Montana Land Use Planning Act (cities of 5,000 or more in counties of 70,000 or more must; others may opt in) is, by that Act's words, not subject to the zoning chapter that holds these ADU protections.

That Act lets a city choose an ADU allowance from a menu of housing strategies, and we found no owner-occupancy bar in it, so in such a city follow the city's own ADU rules and take advice if they require owner occupancy. Once rented, an ADU is a dwelling unit under the landlord-tenant act like any other; local rent control is barred. An optional lease clause recording the lot layout and shared areas is in this library (accessory-dwelling-unit-term-co).

title: What counts as notice, and why texts are only a courtesy copy
bodyText:
What counts as notice in Montana.

Under the landlord-tenant act a person has notice of a fact if any one of these is true: the person actually knows it; for a landlord, it was delivered at the landlord's place of business through which the lease was made; it was e-mailed to an address the tenant or landlord gave in the rental agreement (complete only when a read receipt or a reply other than an automatic one comes back); or it was handed to the person, or mailed with a certificate of mailing or by certified mail to the address the person named for notices (or the last-known address), in which case it counts as served 3 days after mailing.

For a notice of intent to enter, posting it conspicuously on the main entry door also counts. Montana's general law defines actual notice as express information of a fact.

**Agreed extra methods.** No Montana statute lets the parties add their own notice method, such as a text message, an app or a portal. A text or portal message counts only if the recipient actually learns of it, and the sender must be able to prove that. E-mail is the one electronic method the act names, and only where the tenant chose to give an address under an election clause (the library's optional E-mail Notices clause); a lease may not require an e-mail address.

A clause adding texts as an extra copy is lawful, but the library does not offer one: a term making a text count as notice when the recipient never saw it would cut into the act's notice rules, which a lease may not waive, and knowingly using a prohibited term can cost up to 3 months' periodic rent on top of damages. Send texts as courtesy copies and use a listed method for every notice that starts a deadline; you can add your own clause after taking advice.

One statutory exception: if a tenant moves out without telling you, you may leave the move-out cleaning notice in a conspicuous place in the unit and tell the tenant by e-mail, phone or text, and the notice is then considered delivered. Notice to a company: notice received by an organization (an LLC owner or a management company) is effective once it reaches the person handling that tenancy, or when it would have with reasonable diligence.

No Montana rule makes a cure right turn on actual notice to the landlord's rent agent. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: Notice of proceedings against the property
bodyText:
Notice of proceedings against the property. Montana puts the duty on the tenant, not the landlord. A tenant who receives notice of a proceeding to recover the rental property or its possession (for example a foreclosure, a title suit or another claimant's eviction case) must immediately tell you and hand over the notice if it is written, and is liable to you for the damages you suffer if the tenant doesn't. The library's Notice of Proceedings Against the Property clause restates this duty in the lease.

A tenant's agreement to accept someone else as landlord (attornment) is void unless you consent or a court judgment requires it, so a stranger who claims the property can't take over your tenancy just by getting the tenant to agree.

Montana has no statute requiring a landlord to tell tenants about a foreclosure, condemnation, tax sale or other proceeding against the property. Tenants may still hear of it directly: a mortgage sale under a power of sale must be personally served on the occupant at least 30 days before the sale, and a trustee's sale notice must be posted on the property at least 20 days before. After a trustee's sale, a tenant whose lease came after the trust deed holds only as a tenant at will (see the foreclosure row).

This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: Detector tampering fees
bodyText:
Montana has no statute that lets a landlord charge a fee for removing or tampering with a smoke or carbon monoxide detector, and no statute that makes tampering an offence. We found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library.

What Montana does say: you must install approved detectors and check that they work when the lease begins, and the tenant must keep them in good working order during the tenancy. A tenant who removes, disables or damages a detector owes you the actual cost of repair or replacement as damages, and you may deduct that cost from the deposit as damage.

A set tampering fee is risky: Montana voids a damages amount fixed in advance unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix, and a detector's cost is easy to fix. The library's optional detector clause (detector-care-la) recovers the reasonable cost only.

title: No Alternate Housing Duty in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no statute or state rule requiring a landlord to provide, arrange or pay for alternate or temporary housing while a rental is repaired, after a fire or other casualty, or because a tenant asks for it. Substitute housing appears only as a tenant remedy: if, contrary to the lease or your statutory maintenance duties, you purposefully or negligently fail to supply heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, the tenant may give you written notice and, once you have had a reasonable opportunity to correct the problem, move to reasonable substitute housing for as long as your noncompliance lasts and owe no rent for that period. A tenant who uses that remedy can't also use the repair or termination remedies for the same breach, and has no such right if the tenant, a family member or a guest caused the condition. After a fire or casualty that substantially impairs the home, the tenant may move out at once and end the lease by telling you in writing within 14 days, or, if staying is lawful, stop using the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion; if the lease ends you return the recoverable deposit and all prepaid rent, but you owe no rehousing (see casualty-termination-mt and edu-casualty-mt). The relocation help and temporary disaster housing found in Montana law are government programs, for people displaced when an agency acquires property for a federally assisted project and for disaster victims, not landlord duties. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library.

title: No Animal-Care Entry Right in Montana
bodyText:
Montana gives a landlord no special right to enter a rental to feed, care for or remove a tenant's animal, and no statute on taking in a tenant's pet.

You may enter only as the access statute allows: with the tenant's consent, which the tenant may not unreasonably withhold, to supply necessary or agreed services, on at least 24 hours' notice and at reasonable times unless notice is impracticable; without consent only in an emergency, which Montana defines as an extraordinary occurrence beyond the tenant's control requiring immediate action to protect the premises or the tenant; under a court order; during a tenant's absence of more than 7 days at times reasonably necessary; or once the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the home.

An animal left alone isn't named as an emergency, so the library's optional Animal Care clause (animal-care-access-mt) makes care an agreed service, has the tenant name a person to collect the animal, and keeps the usual notice. If an animal seems to be in distress and you can't reach the tenant or the named person, call law enforcement or animal control rather than entering on your own.

Montana's cruelty law turns on custody, not on a set number of days of feeding: anyone who knowingly or negligently fails to give an animal in the person's custody enough food and water, minimum protection from the weather and, for an obvious serious illness or injury, veterinary care, or who abandons a helpless animal, commits cruelty to animals. So if you take a tenant's animal into your own care you take on those duties; handing it promptly to the named person or an animal agency is the safer course.

Don't sell, give away or destroy a tenant's animal yourself. Montana's rules for property left after a tenancy ends weren't written for animals, so after a move-out the cautious course is again to involve animal control. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library.

title: Asbestos in Montana Rentals
bodyText: Montana has no statute requiring you to tell an applicant or tenant about asbestos in a rental, to inspect for it, or to give tenants notice before asbestos work. What Montana regulates is the work itself. Under the Asbestos Control Act, encapsulating, enclosing, removing, repairing, renovating or demolishing asbestos in a building, or transporting or disposing of asbestos-containing waste, is an asbestos project (a project involving less than 10 square feet of surface area or 3 linear feet of pipe is excluded). An asbestos project needs a permit from the Department of Environmental Quality, the people doing it must be accredited, and you may not hire or employ anyone who is not. The department may fine a violator up to $10,000 a day administratively (up to $80,000 in all), a court may impose up to $25,000 a day, and a purposeful or knowing violation is a misdemeanor. The department may also order the owner of property where asbestos-containing material is located to clean it up when the material poses an immediate threat to public health, or is likely to soon. Your general duty to keep the premises fit and habitable still applies. If you give a tenant an option to buy a one-to-four-unit home or an individually owned unit, the seller disclosure statement applies and must say whether any part of the property has been tested or treated for asbestos. The cautious course: before work that may disturb older building materials, have them tested, use an accredited contractor with a permit, and tell the tenant in writing about the work and any precautions. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws, the Constitution and the Montana rules held for this pass.

title: Condominium and Association Disclosures in Montana Leases
bodyText:
A lease of a unit in a condominium created under Montana's Unit Ownership Act must contain the description of the land, the name of the property, the recording information and date of the declaration, the unit designation, the use the unit is intended for, and the unit's percentage of undivided interest in the common elements.

The rule applies to leases as well as deeds and states no penalty for leaving the items out, but include them; the library's Condominium Unit Particulars clause (condominium-unit-lease-contents-mt) does. Townhomes are covered only if a declaration submits them to the act.

Beyond that, Montana has no rule requiring a landlord to give a tenant the association's declaration, bylaws, rules or obligations, no required owner statement or tenant acknowledgment in the lease, and no condominium resale certificate, so a long lease or renewal options don't give a tenant a right to one.

Two related rules: a lease filed with the association's presiding officer can make the tenant count as the unit owner for the purposes it provides, including voting; and at the first conveyance or lease of each unit after the declaration is recorded, every mortgage and other lien on the unit must be paid off of record or the unit released by a recorded partial release, which matters to a developer leasing new units.

Giving the tenant the association documents is still wise, because the lease makes the tenant follow the association's rules (hoa-compliance); the clause's optional second paragraph records that you did. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library.

title: No Balcony Inspection Rule in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no statute or state rule requiring periodic inspection of balconies, decks, walkways, stairs or other exterior elevated elements of rental buildings, and no report or repair deadline tied to one (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state building and fire code rules held for this library). Balconies and decks are governed by the building code when built and by your general duties afterwards. The residential code as Montana adopted it requires guards along open-sided walking surfaces, including stairs, ramps and landings, more than 30 inches above the floor or grade below; for units completed after July 1, 1977 you must keep up the code requirements that applied when the unit was built, and you must keep the premises fit, habitable and safe and keep common areas safe. Cautious course: inspect balconies, decks, stairs and railings at least once a year and at each turnover, look for rot, rust, loose or missing railings and failing connections to the building, and repair them promptly; a tenant may end the lease or recover damages if a dangerous condition you fail to fix affects health and safety. The library's Use of Property clause already lets you set weight limits on balconies and porches.

title: Binding arbitration not offered
bodyText: The library doesn't offer an arbitration clause for Montana leases. Montana's Uniform Arbitration Act makes a written agreement to arbitrate future disputes valid and enforceable, but that rule doesn't reach claims arising out of personal injury, or a contract by an individual to acquire real or personal property, services, or money or credit where the individual's total consideration is $5,000 or less; whether a residential lease is such a contract isn't settled by the statute. Montana contract law voids terms that keep a party from enforcing the contract in the ordinary courts, except agreements enforceable under the arbitration act. Montana's landlord-tenant act also bars any lease term making a party waive rights or remedies under the act, and its remedies are court remedies: the action for possession with its fixed hearing deadlines, rent paid into court, injunctions, the court's power to refuse to enforce an unconscionable term, and attorney fees for the prevailing party whatever the lease says. Whether an agreement to arbitrate gives up those remedies, and how far federal arbitration law would override Montana's limits, turns on case law, and knowingly using a prohibited term lets the tenant recover actual damages plus up to 3 months' periodic rent. If you still want arbitration, take legal advice first, and know the act's fixed rules: each party may be represented by a lawyer at any hearing, and a waiver of that right before the hearing is ineffective; an agreement about venue involving a Montana resident is valid only if it requires arbitration in Montana, unless counsel signs to waive it; a neutral arbitrator must make written conflict disclosures; and the arbitrators' fees and expenses, not including counsel fees, are paid as the award provides unless the agreement says otherwise. Montana's 2025 code has no first-page, capital-letter or initialling notice requirement for an arbitration clause.

title: Carpet cleaning rules
bodyText:
Montana has no statute on carpet cleaning: nothing lets you require professional carpet cleaning at move-out on a condition such as pre-tenancy cleaning, and there is no age or useful-life test for carpet or paint deductions. We found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library. Montana's general cleaning rules decide what you can charge.

You may deduct only actual cleaning expenses, including a reasonable charge for your own labor, for cleaning needed to return the unit to its condition at the start of the tenancy beyond normal wear. Before deducting, you must give the tenant written notice of the cleaning not done and the amount and type of cleaning needed, and the tenant gets 24 hours to do it (unless the tenant left without notice, or the lease has already ended in a possession case and you have a claim pending in court).

You can't charge for routine maintenance you do on a regular cycle, such as carpet cleaning between tenants, if you noted it at move-in, unless the tenant's negligence made it necessary. A flat or automatic carpet-cleaning fee is presumed to be a security deposit, however it is labelled. Record the carpets' condition in the move-in condition statement. The library's optional carpet clause (carpet-cleaning-mt) follows these rules.

title: Casualty and mitigation rights cannot be waived
bodyText: A Montana lease can't take away the tenant's fire and casualty rights or your duty to try to re-rent a unit the tenant has abandoned. If fire or casualty substantially impairs the tenant's enjoyment of the unit, the tenant may move out at once and, within 14 days, tell you in writing that the lease is ended (it ends on the move-out date), or, if staying is lawful, stop using the part made unusable and pay rent reduced in proportion to the lost rental value. If the lease ends, you return the security deposit the tenant is owed and all prepaid rent, with rent accounted for as of the date of the fire or casualty. These rights don't apply when the tenant, the tenant's family or guests caused the damage purposefully or negligently. If a tenant abandons the unit, you must make reasonable efforts to re-rent it at a fair rental, and every party claiming damages must mitigate them. A rental agreement may not make either party waive rights or remedies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, so a term waiving either rule is unenforceable, and knowingly using one lets the tenant recover actual damages plus up to 3 months' periodic rent. Unlike some states, Montana has no general casualty statute that an express written agreement can override; we found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library. Mobile home lot rentals have their own casualty rule (move out and end the agreement) and the same bar on waivers. The library's optional landlord casualty-termination clause and tenant-caused-damage clause are drafted to leave these rights intact.

title: No Certificate-of-Occupancy Disclosure Duty in Montana
bodyText: Montana puts no certificate-of-occupancy duty on you as a landlord. No statute makes you tell a tenant whether the home has a certificate of occupancy or whether it is valid, or give the tenant a copy, and no statute voids a lease or bars rent because a certificate is missing. A certificate of occupancy in Montana is a building-code document: the state or a certified city, town or county building department issues it for a building built under the applicable code, certifying that the building conforms to the building regulations that apply to it. The state building code does not reach houses and other residential buildings of fewer than five units unless your city, town or county has adopted a building code that covers them, so many smaller rentals, especially older homes or homes outside a local code area, never had one. Where a local building code applies, building or converting a unit without the permits and certificate it requires is a code violation, and your duty to keep the unit habitable includes complying with the building and housing codes that applied when it was built (for units completed after July 1, 1977). Montana has no state rental certificate-of-occupancy or inspection program, and a local government with self-government powers may not license landlords or regulate their dealings with tenants beyond the state acts (see edu-no-rental-inspection-rule-mt). If a tenant asks, answer honestly.

title: Children and Occupancy Limits in Montana
bodyText:
Montana does not require a lease to say anything about children, and has no landlord-tenant rule of its own on a child born or joining the household during a tenancy and no statewide occupancy standard such as persons per bedroom (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library). Montana's Human Rights Act governs instead.

It is unlawful to refuse to rent, to set different terms, conditions or privileges, to ask about familial status in order to discriminate, to say a unit is unavailable when it is not, or to advertise a preference because of familial status, which means having a child or children who live or will live with a person, including any distinction based on a child's age. Montana also protects age itself, at any age.

So do not refuse a household with children, steer it to certain units, charge it more, set rules only for children, or end or refuse to renew a tenancy because a child has joined the household. Montana has no express carve-out for child-safety rules: write rules by conduct, apply them to every occupant, and keep any age-based safety rule (such as pool supervision) narrow and tied to a real safety need. Exemptions are narrow.

The Act does not apply to renting no more than three sleeping rooms in a single-family home the owner lives in. The age and familial-status rules do not apply to qualifying housing for older persons, or to a building with living quarters for no more than two families where the owner lives in one of them.

Federal law exempts some owners Montana does not (an owner-occupied building of up to four units, and some owners of three or fewer single-family houses), so a federal exemption does not excuse you under Montana law. Occupancy limits. Federal fair housing law does not limit reasonable local, state or federal restrictions on the maximum number of occupants; Montana's Act says nothing about occupancy limits, and Montana sets none statewide.

A cap you set yourself that is stricter than the local housing or building code can be challenged as familial-status discrimination, so peg any cap to the code that applies to the unit, apply it to every occupant whatever their age, and list children as occupants under the library's Permitted Occupants clause.

A complaint must be filed with the Department of Labor and Industry within 180 days, or a lawsuit brought within 2 years; penalties run up to $10,000 for a first violation, and a willful violation is a misdemeanor.

title: No winter eviction or cold-weather notice rule
bodyText:
No winter eviction rule: Montana has no statute or rule that stops or delays an eviction in winter or cold weather, and none that requires a special notice before a tenant moves out or leaves the unit in winter. The ordinary notices and the possession process apply all year.

Winter utility shutoffs: the Public Service Commission's rules limit when a regulated gas or electric utility may disconnect residential service: from November 1 to April 1, and on freezing or forecast-snowstorm days, no disconnection where the customer shows inability to pay, age 62 or over, or a disabled household member, and no disconnection at all from November 1 to April 1 without the Commission's prior approval; tenants get their own notice when a landlord's account is to be disconnected.

These rules bind utilities, not landlords, and they don't reach an eviction. You may never cut off or interrupt heat, water, gas, electricity or other essential services to make a tenant leave.

Heat and freezing: you must supply reasonable heat from October 1 to May 1 unless the building isn't required to have it or the heat comes from an installation in the tenant's exclusive control; the tenant must use heating and plumbing facilities reasonably. Your lease may require the tenant to tell you of an absence of more than 7 days no later than the first day of it, and you may enter during such an absence at reasonably necessary times, or without notice in an emergency.

The library offers an optional cold-weather precautions clause built on those rules. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the Administrative Rules of Montana subchapters in the library's research set (including the utility-disconnection rules).

title: Collection fees
bodyText: No Montana statute authorizes, caps or bans a fee for collecting a past-due rent debt from a tenant, and the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act doesn't mention one; we found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library. General rules decide what a collection-fee clause can do. A flat or percentage fee triggered by late payment or by referral to a collector is damages fixed in advance, which Montana voids unless the actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix, and collection costs usually can be fixed. In a court case, attorney fees, costs and necessary disbursements are for the court to award to the prevailing party, whatever the lease says, and a lease that gives one side a right to attorney fees gives the same right to the other. A clause that only reimburses collection costs you actually and reasonably incur is not barred by any Montana statute, but no statute or rule settles whether a court will enforce it. And any charge the lease makes payable to you counts as rent under the act, so a collection charge would be part of the rent due: it would belong in, and could be disputed in, a 3-day nonpayment notice, and accepting full payment of the rent due waives a nonpayment breach. For those reasons the library doesn't offer a collection-fee clause for Montana. A landlord who wants a clause limited to actual, reasonable costs can add their own after taking advice.

title: Common-Area Lighting in Montana
bodyText:
