Montana has no statute or state rule that sets a lighting standard for the hallways, stairways, entrances, parking areas or other common areas of rental housing, and none that governs putting common-area lights on a tenant's electric service (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state building, fire and utility rules held for this library). Your general duties cover it.

You must keep all common areas clean and safe, keep the electrical facilities you supply in good and safe working order, and, for buildings completed after July 1, 1977, keep up the building code requirements that applied when the building was built, which can include lighting for exits and stairways. Treat lighting of shared stairways, hallways and entrances as part of keeping them safe.

A lease may make the tenant pay for common-area lights wired to the tenant's own electric service; no Montana statute bars or regulates it. If you do this, disclose it before the lease is signed, keep every maintenance duty yourself, make sure the areas stay lit if the tenant's service is shut off, and consider a rent allowance where the lights serve other tenants too, since a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable term. The library's optional clause for this is common-area-lighting-mt.

title: No state approval rule for tribal or communal land leases
bodyText: Leases of tribal, communal or public land. Montana state law has no rule requiring a government officer to approve a residential lease of communal, tribal or native-owned land before it is valid, and no state statute says what happens to rent or possession before approval. Leases of Indian trust or restricted land on a reservation are governed by federal law and tribal law, which commonly require federal approval; those sources are outside this library's research set, so if your rental is on trust or restricted land, confirm the approval requirement and the applicable tribal law before signing. The related state rule is for state trust land: the Board of Land Commissioners prescribes the form of state land leases and must approve changes, and state trust land may be leased for up to 99 years for commercial purposes, which since 2025 include single-family or multifamily residential development under a master lease (including attainable workforce housing) and mobile home parks or manufactured housing for rent; if you rent homes built on such land, your tenancies sit under the master lease's terms. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No Express Rent Bar After Condemnation in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no statute that says in so many words that you may not collect rent once a dwelling is condemned, posted as unfit or ordered vacated, and no statutory penalty for doing so. Do not read that as permission. If fire or another casualty damages the unit so that the tenant's enjoyment is substantially impaired, the tenant may move out at once and end the lease by written notice within 14 days, with rent accounted for as of the date of the fire and all recoverable deposit and prepaid rent returned to the tenant; the tenant may stay in the usable part at a reduced rent only if continued occupancy is lawful, so once officials bar occupancy that option is gone. If the condition is a failure to keep the unit fit and habitable, the tenant may end the lease after notice, recover damages, and, where essential services such as heat or water fail, move to substitute housing and pay no rent while you are in breach. None of this applies to damage the tenant or the tenant's household or guests caused. Whether rent is owed at all for a period in which the law forbids occupancy is a question for case law, which this library did not research; the cautious course is to stop charging rent from the date occupancy became unlawful, return prepaid rent for that period, and take advice before suing for it. A fire-hazard repair or demolition order must also be served on an occupying tenant, who may contest it. A property on the state's meth or fentanyl contamination list carries a notice duty to new occupants, not a rent bar (see edu-meth-disclosure-mt).

title: No confession of judgment
bodyText:
Default rule: Montana still allows a judgment by confession, but only one the debtor makes personally: a written statement signed by the debtor and verified under oath, authorizing judgment for a specified sum and stating the facts showing the money is due. It is a step the tenant can choose to take once a debt exists, not something a lease can arrange in advance.

The bar: a Montana lease may not authorize anyone to confess judgment against the tenant on a claim arising out of the lease, and Montana contract law makes illegal and void any term in a written contract to pay money that lets someone confess judgment, accept service of process or consent to a default judgment on a party's behalf. That reaches separate papers signed as part of the same transaction. Such a clause can't be enforced in Montana courts, and knowingly using it in a lease can cost you the tenant's actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent. No Montana statute or court rule authorizes a confessed judgment for possession: to recover the unit you must terminate by the required notice and bring an action for possession. If a tenant appeals a possession judgment from a justice's or city court, execution is stayed only if the tenant files a written undertaking with sureties (waived if the court finds the tenant indigent). This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: Habitability: present and absent rules
bodyText: How Montana compares on habitability rules found elsewhere. Present: a duty to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety (for buildings completed after July 1, 1977), to keep the premises fit and habitable, to keep facilities and appliances you supply in good working order, and to supply running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat from October 1 to May 1, which a lease can't waive and which can't be separated from your right to rent; a tenant may take on specified tasks only by a separate signed, good-faith agreement for adequate consideration; termination on written notice (14 days to remedy, ending no sooner than 30 days after the notice; 3 working days in an emergency); repair-and-deduct up to 1 month's rent; essential-services remedies including substitute housing; approved smoke and carbon monoxide detectors; casualty termination or reduced rent; rent paid into court in a possession case; protection from retaliation for complaints; and disclosure of known mold and of mold testing. Absent (no provision found in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library): (1) a lock, deadbolt or rekeying duty (a tenant may not change locks without your written permission); (2) a bed bug or pest disclosure, inspection or treatment rule for rentals (pest infestations appear only in the seller's disclosure on a sale); (3) radon testing or disclosure for rentals (the radon statement applies to sales, and the radon-resistant construction appendix of the residential building code applies only where a certified local jurisdiction adopts it); (4) a duty to supply air conditioning or a maximum indoor temperature (you must only keep in good working order any air conditioning you supply); (5) a minimum heat temperature in degrees (the standard is reasonable heat); (6) a general right to withhold rent or pay it into escrow for repairs, outside a possession case; (7) a right to end a lease because repairs cost too much; and (8) a required repair-notice address or portal in the lease. Each point has its own row in this library.

title: Other rules Montana does not have
bodyText: Rules found in some other places for which we found no Montana statute or rule in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library, each explained in its own row of this library: no rule on using algorithms or software to set rents (antitrust and consumer law still apply); no rule on tenant or landlord security cameras or video doorbells at rentals (your entry rights and the lock rule still apply); no tenant right to install electric-vehicle charging and no landlord EV duty (local governments may not require buildings to be built with EV or solar wiring or equipment); no protection of a tenant's right to call police or emergency help, and no ban on penalizing those calls; no right for either party to end a lease because repairs cost too much; no statute authorizing or barring a collection fee or a notice-service or eviction fee (general contract and fee rules decide them, and the library offers neither); and no landlord-tenant arbitration statute and no arbitration-clause notice or type-size rule (the library offers no arbitration clause); the general Plain Language in Contracts Act readable-type and caption rule can still apply to the whole lease of a landlord who regularly rents (see edu-plain-language-contracts-act-mt).

title: Checked across all of Montana law
bodyText: Three points checked across all Montana law in the corpus, not only the landlord-tenant chapters. (1) Squatters: present. A person who can't produce authorization to occupy (a written rental agreement, or verified permission from you or, for a guest, from a tenant) may be removed immediately by law enforcement at your request, and law enforcement may stand by while you change locks and remove the occupant's belongings. Since October 1, 2025, knowingly entering and residing on another's premises without consent is the crime of unlawful squatting, with restitution of fair market rent. Never use this route against a tenant, who can be removed only through the court process. (2) Rent receipts: Montana has no landlord-specific receipt or rent-ledger rule, but its general law entitles anyone who pays money to a written receipt from the person paid, and lets the payer demand a properly signed receipt as a condition of paying. A receipt for later rent is presumed, until disproved, to show that earlier rent was paid. Give a signed written receipt whenever a tenant asks, and for every cash payment. (3) Registration before eviction: there is no landlord registration or rental licensing, and local governments may not license landlords. But an out-of-state corporation or limited liability company doing business in Montana without registering can't maintain any court case, eviction included, until it registers (it can still defend one), an out-of-state limited partnership needs its certificate of authority, and a landlord renting under an assumed business name can't sue under that name until the name is registered. Also checked across all titles: no landlord duty tied to the sexual or violent offender registry (high-risk offenders' own residence limits bind only them); no rule requiring or forbidding questions about immigration status; and no duty to disclose flood risk to tenants (floodplain rules govern building and subdivision). Each point has its own row in this library.

title: Tenant's contractors and liens on your property
bodyText:
Construction liens for work a tenant orders. In Montana, a contractor or supplier the tenant hires can lien the improvement and the tenant's leasehold, but not your ownership interest unless you contracted for the improvement or agreed to it before it was begun.

A lien reaches only the interest of the "contracting owner", the person who contracts for the work personally or through an agent, and Montana presumes agency only between employer and employee, spouses, joint tenants and tenants in common, not between landlord and tenant. If the tenant's lease is forfeited, the lienholder can still have work that can be removed without harm valued, sold and taken out.

What this means for your lease. Montana has no notice of nonresponsibility and no statute letting a lease keep your interest lien-free; a lease can't bind a contractor who isn't a party to it. The risk point is your own consent: because the test is whether you agreed to the improvement, a written approval of a tenant's alteration (which the library's No Alterations clause requires) could be argued to be that agreement.

The cautious course is to approve only what you are willing to see liened, say in the approval that the tenant alone is contracting and paying, and require proof of payment or lien releases. The library's optional No Liens for Tenant Work clause makes the tenant pay everyone it hires, clear any lien, tell each contractor that the tenant (not you) is responsible, and confirms the tenant is not your agent.

This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No Defective Drywall Disclosure in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose defective, corrosive or imported drywall, and no statute on testing or remediating it. The general rules apply instead. You must keep the premises fit and habitable and keep the electrical, plumbing, heating and other systems you supply in good and safe working order, which corrosion damage can affect. If you give a tenant an option to buy a one-to-four-unit home or an individually owned unit, the seller disclosure statement must cover known problems with the structure and its systems and any other adverse material fact. The cautious course: if you know the property has problem drywall, tell applicants in writing before they sign and never answer a direct question misleadingly. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws, the Constitution and the Montana rules held for this pass.

title: No preset cleaning or damage charges
bodyText:
Montana's deposit law allows cleaning and damage deductions only at actual cost, so a preset cleaning or damage charge should not be taken from the deposit. The deduction list also names penalties due under the lease and other money owing; no statute says whether a preset cleaning charge can come in that way, and the cautious course is to deduct actual cost only.

A cleaning deduction may only be the actual cost of cleaning needed, beyond normal wear, to bring the unit back to its move-in condition, including a reasonable charge for your own labor, and only after you give the tenant written notice of the cleaning still needed and 24 hours to do it (unless the tenant left without notice). You may not charge for cyclical maintenance you noted at move-in, such as periodic carpet cleaning or repainting, unless the tenant's negligence forced it.

A damage deduction must equal the damage the tenant actually caused, which you must prove. Nothing else may be deducted except unpaid rent, late charges, utilities, penalties due under the lease and other money the tenant owes. So a lease term fixing a carpet-cleaning, cleaning, move-out or damage charge should not be deducted as written, a lease term contrary to the deposit law is invalid, and a fee for cleaning or damage collected up front is presumed to be a security deposit however it is labelled.

Montana contract law also voids a damages figure agreed in advance unless the actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix.

What you can do: state at move-in the cyclical maintenance you perform; and set in the lease charges that are owed on their own terms, such as rent, the late fee, or the actual cost of rekeying when keys aren't returned, which you may then deduct as money owed.

title: No deposit installment right
bodyText: Montana gives a tenant no right to pay a security deposit in installments, and does not stop you from agreeing to it. You may require the whole deposit before the tenant moves in, or agree to a schedule. If you agree, list each installment and its due date in the lease's due-at-signing clause, which the library already offers for this; the library doesn't offer a separate installment clause because that clause holds the schedule. Every amount paid is part of the security deposit and is accounted for and returned under the deposit rules. A missed installment is not rent, because Montana's definition of rent leaves out money paid as a security deposit, so use the 14-day notice for a lease violation, not the 3-day notice for unpaid rent. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: Deposit clock and surrender
bodyText:
Your deposit deadline does not wait for any notice of surrender or forwarding address from the tenant. The 30-day and 10-day rules do not apply if the lease was ended in a court action for possession and you have a claim pending in court; you must still account for the deposit, and the cautious course is to raise it in that case or give the list anyway.

The 30 days to give the written list of rent due and damage and cleaning charges, with the balance, run from the end of the tenancy, or from the tenant's surrender of the unit and your acceptance of it, whichever comes first. If there is no damage, no cleaning needed and no unpaid rent, and the tenant shows no utilities are unpaid, the deposit must be returned within 10 days. A tenant who does not give you a new address in writing can still recover the deposit.

You may ask for a forwarding address in the lease (the library's deposit-return clause does), refund by electronic transfer, cash, check or another method, or mail it to the address the tenant gave or, if none, to the last-known address. Mailing to the last-known address is not a wrongful withholding if it never arrives, but you still owe the money. The written list must be delivered by a method the landlord-tenant act allows for notices.

A tenant who moves out without telling you also gives up the 24-hour cleaning notice: you may deduct actual cleaning costs without it, or leave the notice in a conspicuous place in the unit and tell the tenant by e-mail, phone or text. Montana does not define "surrender and acceptance"; count the days from when you know the tenant has gone and you take the unit back, even if keys come back later.

title: No Designated-Repairer Rule in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no statute or state rule requiring a landlord to name a repair contact or approved repairer, setting how fast you must answer a repair request, or letting you choose who does the repairs a tenant is entitled to make. What Montana does have limits a designated-repairer clause. You must give the tenant, in writing, the name and address of the person managing the property and of the owner or the owner's agent for notices (landlord-disclosure-mt), and the lease can say where to report repairs. But if a failure to maintain affects health and safety and you don't make the repair within a reasonable time after the tenant's notice, the tenant may make repairs costing no more than one month's rent and deduct the cost from the rent; in an emergency the tenant may have repairs made only by a person qualified to make them. A lease can't make the tenant waive or give up that remedy, so a clause requiring your written consent before any tenant repair, or requiring the tenant to use only your repairer, would be unenforceable, and knowingly using one can cost you the tenant's actual damages plus up to 3 months' periodic rent. A clause that only lists your preferred repairers as a request is lawful, but because the tenant could ignore it the library doesn't offer one for Montana; you can add your own after taking advice. If you want a tenant to take on specified repairs, that needs a separate writing signed by both of you and supported by adequate consideration (maintenance-allocation-mt). Whether particular electrical, plumbing or gas work needs a licensed tradesperson is a licensing question this library hasn't read. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library.

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications in Montana
bodyText:
Montana's Human Rights Act makes two refusals disability discrimination in housing: refusing to let a person with a disability make, at that person's expense, reasonable modifications of the premises that may be necessary for full enjoyment of them; and refusing reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices or services that may be necessary to give the person an equal opportunity to use and enjoy the housing.

An accommodation that would impose an undue hardship or endanger anyone's health or safety is not a reasonable accommodation. The protection covers the tenant, anyone living or intending to live in the unit, and anyone associated with them.

**Modifications.** Where it is reasonable, you may make permission conditional on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior to its condition before the modification, except reasonable wear and tear. Federal rules also let you ask for a reasonable description of the work and reasonable assurances that it will be done in a workmanlike manner with any required building permits.

Montana does not require the restoration condition to appear in the lease (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library); it is your option, and the library's optional clause is disability-modification-restoration-mn.

**Restoration money.** Montana has no rule on a restoration deposit or account. Federal rules bar increasing your customary security deposit for a person with a disability, but where it is necessary to ensure with reasonable certainty that the restoration can be paid for, they let you negotiate, as part of the restoration agreement, payments into an interest-bearing escrow account over a reasonable period, not more than the cost of the restoration, with the interest accruing to the tenant.

Because Montana presumes any deposit the tenant must keep with you during the tenancy to be a security deposit, also handle that account under Montana's deposit-return rules (itemized list and refund after the tenancy).

**New construction.** Covered multifamily buildings (four or more units with an elevator, and ground-floor units in buildings of four or more units) must be designed with the accessibility features the Act lists. Assistance and service animals are covered in edu-assistance-animals-mt. A complaint must be filed within 180 days, or a lawsuit brought within 2 years; penalties run up to $10,000 for a first violation, and a willful violation is a misdemeanor. If the property is federally assisted, separate federal rules may require you to pay for some modifications.

title: Disaster-Displaced Guests in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no rule about a tenant taking in people displaced by a wildfire, flood or other disaster. No statute lets a tenant house them despite the lease's guest or occupancy limits, suspends those limits during an emergency, or bars you from enforcing them, and none requires you to allow it. We found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library. So the ordinary guest rules apply: a guest is someone staying with the tenant for the temporary period the lease defines, or, if the lease is silent, no more than 7 days unless you consent in writing to a longer stay (Guests in Montana Rentals, edu-guest-definition-mt; the library's guest clauses set the lease's period). A person living in the unit beyond that without your consent can support a 3-day notice to cure for unauthorized persons. After a disaster, the practical course is to agree in writing with the tenant how long displaced friends or family may stay, rather than to rely on the default. The emergency rules that exist run through government: during a declared emergency the Governor may order evacuations and control the occupancy of premises within the emergency area, and the state and local governments may arrange temporary housing for disaster victims. Hotels and motels may voluntarily give free emergency lodging to displaced people referred by a designated charitable organization, with the guest (or, if the guest cannot pay, the referring organization) liable for damage; a transient hotel or motel stay is not a tenancy under Montana's landlord-tenant act.

title: Disasters and Montana Tenancies
bodyText: A declared disaster does not by itself end a Montana tenancy, stop the rent or bar evictions, and Montana has no price-gouging law capping rents during an emergency. We found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library. Damage is handled by the fire-or-casualty rule: if fire or casualty substantially impairs the tenant's enjoyment of the unit, the tenant may move out and give written notice within 14 days to end the lease as of the move-out date, or, if staying is lawful, stop using the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the lost rental value; if the lease ends you must return the deposit and all prepaid rent, accounted as of the date of the fire or casualty. These rights don't apply if the tenant, the tenant's family or guests caused the damage purposefully or negligently (Fire and Casualty Damage in Montana, edu-casualty-mt; the library's optional landlord termination clause, casualty-termination-mt). The tenant's essential-services remedies apply only when you purposefully or negligently fail to supply heat, water, power or other essential services, and your ordinary duty to keep the premises fit and habitable continues; there is no separate disaster cleanup or testing duty. Emergency powers: during a declared emergency the Governor may order evacuations and control occupancy of premises in the emergency area, but no state or local official may, except in an evacuated or controlled area, interfere with rent collection or with eviction actions for more than 60 days without legislative approval. Check for a current emergency order before collecting rent or filing for possession in a declared area.

title: Drug-Free Housing Addenda in Montana
bodyText: Montana law neither requires nor prescribes a drug-free or crime-free housing addendum for a private rental, and no Montana statute bars one; we found no such rule in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library. A drug term is therefore lawful within Montana's limits, but the library does not offer a separate addendum, because its optional No Dangerous or Criminal Activity clause (criminal-activity-mt) already covers the ground: it bars manufacturing dangerous drugs, running a clandestine lab and similar activity that endangers the premises or neighbors, which you may end the lease for on 3 days' written notice without a chance to cure, and treats other criminal activity on the premises as a lease violation handled on the ordinary notices (Dangerous or Drug Activity: 3-Day Notice in Montana, edu-dangerous-activity-eviction-mt). If you draft your own drug clause after taking advice, keep one Montana limit in mind: a lease signed after January 1, 2021 may not prohibit a tenant from lawfully possessing marijuana and consuming it by means other than smoking, unless federal law or a condition of federal funding requires the prohibition, so a clause banning all "controlled substances" or all marijuana use is unenforceable to that extent and may expose you to a penalty. You may ban smoking marijuana (smoking-policy-mt) and growing it (cannabis-cultivation-mt). Federally assisted housing has its own federal lease and drug-activity rules; if you rent under a federal program, use the program's required lease terms and addendum (Federal Rules for a Housing Choice Voucher Lease, edu-voucher-tenancy-addendum).

title: No landlord confidentiality duty for victims
bodyText:
Montana has no statute requiring a landlord to keep confidential a tenant's status as a victim of partner or family member assault, sexual assault or stalking, or to accept a substitute address. Montana's address confidentiality program, run by the Department of Justice, gives an approved victim a substitute address and forwards their mail, and the department may not reveal the participant's name or addresses except to law enforcement or under a court order. The law requires state and local government agencies to accept the substitute address card; it does not bind private landlords. A court issuing an order of protection must also withhold a petitioner's new residence if the petitioner fled the shared home.

In housing assisted under a covered federal housing program (including Section 8 and the low-income housing tax credit program), federal law requires the owner or manager to keep in confidence any information a tenant gives about being a victim, including that fact itself, and not to put it in a shared database or disclose it, except with the tenant's written request or consent, for an eviction proceeding under that law, or where other law requires it. As good practice in any rental, keep what a tenant tells you about abuse private, share it only with staff who need it, and accept a mailing address the tenant asks you to use for notices if it does not conflict with the lease's notice terms. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No special deposit rule for abuse victims
bodyText:
Montana has no deposit rule for a tenant who leaves because of partner or family member assault, sexual assault or stalking. The ordinary deposit rules apply (unless the lease was ended in a possession action and you have a claim pending in court): within 30 days after the tenancy terminates, or after the tenant surrenders the unit and you accept the surrender, whichever comes first, give the written list of rent due and damage and cleaning charges with the balance, or return the whole deposit within 10 days if nothing is owed and the tenant shows no utilities are unpaid.

Montana's deposit law does not say whether the clock starts when one co-tenant leaves while others stay, or how one deposit is divided among co-tenants. The cautious course when a victim moves out and a co-tenant stays: get a written agreement signed by all the tenants on whether the deposit stays in place or what share is released, and if there is no agreement, keep holding the deposit for the continuing tenancy and account for it to all the tenants when it ends. If the lease is ended for everyone, the ordinary clock runs from that date. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No eviction protection for abuse victims
bodyText:
Montana has no statute that protects a tenant from eviction because the tenant is a victim of partner or family member assault, sexual assault or stalking, or because of the abuser's conduct, and no special eviction defense for a victim. The ordinary grounds and notices apply, for example 3 days for unpaid rent, 14 days for most lease violations and 30 days' written notice to end a month-to-month tenancy. A court can remove and exclude an abuser from the victim's home under an order of protection, whoever owns it, but the order does not change the lease. A "no contact" demand between you and a tenant is valid only if it rests on a court order.

Federal law adds protections only in housing assisted under a covered federal housing program, which includes Section 8 and the low-income housing tax credit program. There a tenant may not be evicted because the tenant is a victim of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault or stalking; an incident of that violence is not a serious or repeated lease violation by the victim or good cause to end the victim's tenancy; and the owner may split the lease to evict the abuser and keep the victim. Before acting against a tenant who is a victim, take advice, especially in assisted housing. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No victim lock-change statute
bodyText:
Montana has no statute giving a victim of partner or family member assault, sexual assault or stalking a right to have the locks changed, and none saying who pays. The general lock rule applies: a tenant may not remove, replace or add a lock without your written permission, and must give you a key to any lock they add. If they don't, you may give a 24-hour notice to correct and then a 3-day notice to end the lease. So when a tenant asks for a lock change for safety, give written permission promptly or change the lock yourself, keep a key, and agree in writing who pays.

If the person to be kept out is a co-tenant, be careful. A court can remove and exclude an abuser from the victim's home under an order of protection, whoever owns it, and in a divorce a court can exclude a spouse from the family home. But no statute says a landlord may lock out a co-tenant on the strength of such an order, and you may not take possession from a tenant except through the court process. Change or rekey the locks only at the protected tenant's request, keep a copy of the order, leave enforcement of the order to law enforcement, and don't remove the excluded tenant's belongings or end that tenant's lease without the court process. Federal housing-program rules for victims, as read for this library, give no lock-change right. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: Where protection-order law sits
bodyText:
Montana's protection-order law has not moved. Orders of protection for victims of partner or family member assault, sexual assault, stalking and related offenses are in Title 40, chapter 15 of the Montana Code Annotated: part 1 (purpose, who may petition, and the address confidentiality program), part 2 (temporary orders and orders of protection), part 3 (which courts, appeals and registration) and part 4 (enforcing other states' protection orders). No 2025 law amended or renumbered any section of that chapter; several 2025 laws refer to it under its current number. Related orders sit elsewhere: criminal no contact orders in partner or family member assault cases are in the criminal code (Title 45), and restraining orders in divorce cases are in Title 40, chapter 4.

For your lease, one rule depends on these orders: a "no contact" notice between you and a tenant is valid only if it rests on a court's order of no contact, a criminal no contact order or an order of protection. That rule describes the orders rather than citing a chapter, so a renumbering would not affect it. No other Montana lease, lock, deposit or eviction rule depends on a protection order (see the library's rows on domestic-violence termination, lock changes and eviction protection).

title: No victim document list for tenancies
bodyText:
Montana has no tenancy statute listing the documents a tenant must give to show partner or family member assault, sexual assault or stalking, because no Montana lease right turns on it. The one document rule that touches you is about "no contact" demands: a notice of no contact between you and a tenant is valid only if it rests on a court's order of no contact, a criminal no contact order issued in a partner or family member assault case, or an order of protection. If a tenant or someone acting for them tells you not to contact a person, or tells you a person must not come to the unit, ask for a copy of the court order and follow its terms; you need not act on a notice without one, but use judgment where safety is at stake.

In housing assisted under a covered federal housing program (including Section 8 and the low-income housing tax credit program), the owner may ask in writing for documentation of the violence, the tenant has 14 business days to provide it, and the tenant chooses among an approved certification form, a statement signed by a victim service provider, attorney, or medical or mental health professional and the tenant under penalty of perjury, or a law enforcement, court or administrative record (or, at the owner's discretion, other evidence). Whatever is provided must be kept confidential. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: Submetering and Reselling Electricity or Gas in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no statute, and no Public Service Commission rule among those searched, that sets terms for a landlord who submeters or resells electricity or natural gas to tenants, or that requires a lease disclosure about it. Two rules matter. First, a regulated electric utility must sell electricity to a new building through an individual meter for each unit, and may not serve a new building that doesn't comply. A new building is one whose construction began after early 1981, or a multi-unit building whose electrical system was replaced after then where each occupant controls part of the electricity used. The exceptions are transient lodging such as hotels and dormitories, and an owner who showed the utility in writing, before construction, that separate metering costs more than its long-run benefits. So landlord submetering of electricity is mostly limited to older buildings and buildings granted that exception. Second, Montana defines a regulated public utility broadly: any individual or company that owns, operates or controls equipment for furnishing heat, light or power to other persons. There is no exception for landlords (privately owned water and sewer systems that do not serve the public are excluded). Whether a landlord who bills tenants for metered electricity or gas becomes a utility the Commission regulates is not settled by the statutes or rules searched. Cautious course: let the utility meter and bill each unit for electricity and gas. If you must bill tenants yourself, charge no more than the utility's actual charge, with no markup or billing fee, state the method in the lease, and ask the Public Service Commission or a lawyer before you start. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws, the Constitution, and the Commission's rules on billing errors, rates, deposits, termination, master meters, line standards, water utilities and service reliability; other Commission rules, Commission orders and court decisions were not.

title: No Emergency Contact Rule in Montana
bodyText:
Montana has no statute or state rule requiring a tenant to name an emergency contact, requiring you to collect one, requiring you to give tenants an emergency telephone number, or requiring the lease to show a management website or a social-services hotline.

What Montana does require is the written name and address of the person managing the property and of the owner or the owner's agent for notices and service, kept current (landlord-disclosure-mt); a telephone number isn't required, though giving one for urgent repairs is sensible.

For the tenant's side, the library's optional Emergency and Death Contact clause (tenant-death-contact-mt) lets the tenant name a person to contact in an emergency or on the tenant's death; the library doesn't add a second contact clause for Montana.

Two limits apply to any contact term: a lease can't make giving an e-mail address a condition of renting (a party may volunteer one where the lease lets a party choose e-mail notice), so ask for a contact's telephone number and address rather than requiring e-mail; and naming a contact gives that person no right to enter, since entry follows the access statute. In a real emergency you may enter without the tenant's consent.

Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library.

title: If the rental is taken by eminent domain
bodyText:
If the rental is taken by eminent domain. Montana's landlord-tenant act and condemnation law say nothing about what happens to a residential lease or the rent when the property is taken for public use: no statute ends the lease, stops or reduces the rent, lets the court cancel the lease, or says how the award is split between you and the tenant.

The lease decides, which is why the library offers an optional Condemnation clause (lease ends on a total or near-total taking with rent prorated, rent reduced on a partial taking, award to the landlord except the tenant's own relocation or moving payments).

**How compensation works.** The state constitution requires just compensation to the full extent of the loss. In a condemnation case the commissioners must value the property and each separate estate and interest in it separately, so a tenant's leasehold can be valued apart from your interest; the money is paid or deposited in court and distributed according to the assessment or judgment, and it can be withdrawn early only if there is no dispute about ownership.

The complaint must name owners, contract-for-deed buyers, mortgagees, lienholders and other claimants of record; a tenant under an unrecorded lease may not be named, so tell your tenant if you are served. A tenant's share of the award is a question between you and the tenant that the lease can settle, but how a court treats a lease term assigning the tenant's share to you is a matter of case law; the clause keeps the tenant's relocation payments, which is the cautious course.

On a project with federal money, the acquiring agency must, as far as practicable, give a lawful occupant at least 90 days' written notice before a move is required and may offer relocation assistance under federal law. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: Screening Property Staff in Montana
bodyText: Montana does not require a landlord or property manager to run background checks on employees, such as maintenance staff or managers who hold keys or enter units, and sets no screening standard for them; we found no such rule in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library. Montana's employee background-check mandates are for other fields, such as assisted living facilities, schools and child care. Screening is still prudent, because an employer can face a claim for negligent hiring. Montana gives a private employer who acts reasonably and in good faith a limited shield: no liability for negligent hiring for an employee's acts outside the scope of employment where, before hiring, the record showed only an arrest without a disposition or ending in acquittal or dismissal, or the conviction was for a misdemeanor or an offense unrelated to the job, or the employee is under supervised probation or parole and the supervising officer approved the job. If you screen, the usual employment rules apply: a consumer reporting agency may furnish a report for employment purposes; it generally may not report an arrest, indictment or conviction more than 7 years old (counted from disposition, release or parole); and if you refuse employment because of a consumer report you must tell the applicant and give the name and address of the agency. You may not refuse to hire because of race, creed, religion, color, national origin, age, disability, marital status or sex unless the job's reasonable demands require it. Federal rules on employment background reports also apply and are not covered here. Key handling and entry rules: edu-no-key-control-mandate-mt and landlords-access-mt. An employee whose housing depends on working at the property is outside Montana's landlord-tenant act (edu-scope-mt).

title: Tenant Energy Usage Data in Montana
bodyText:
Montana treats a utility customer's energy use data as private. A utility the Public Service Commission regulates may not disclose it except as the law provides. It may disclose aggregated, anonymous data, and it must make data from an advanced (smart) meter available to the customer or the customer's designee when the customer asks.

Separately, a regulated electric or gas utility must provide a property's average annual energy use, as a 12-month dollar average, to the owner or the owner's representative and to someone involved in selling or leasing the property, without the tenant's consent. No Montana statute requires building energy benchmarking or lets a lease clause by itself authorize a utility to release a tenant's usage. If you want a tenant's own monthly usage, have the tenant name you as the designee with the utility.

The library's optional Energy Usage Data Authorization clause asks the tenant to sign the utility's release, limits how you use the data, and lets the tenant withdraw without breaching the lease. Electric cooperatives and city utilities follow their own policies, and the statute does not cover water usage. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws, the Constitution and the held Commission rules; utility privacy policies were not.

title: Who can appear in court for an LLC or corporation landlord
bodyText:
Who can go to court for a company landlord. In a Montana justice's or city court case for possession (eviction) or for rent, a corporation must appear through a lawyer licensed in Montana. The Montana Supreme Court's rules for those courts let a party represent itself or be represented by a licensed attorney and no one else, with one exception: unless its articles of organization say otherwise, a member who holds a majority interest in an LLC may represent the LLC in justice's court. The civil rules for justice and city courts add that anyone other than an individual (including an owner's agent) must file the complaint through an attorney. That filing rule names limited liability companies, and the rules do not say whether the majority-member exception reaches filing, so the cautious course is to have a licensed attorney sign and file an LLC's complaint even where the majority member will then appear for it in justice's court. So a non-lawyer officer, any LLC member (majority or not), an employee or a property manager should not sign or file the complaint, and none of them except an LLC's majority member in justice's court should argue the case for an entity owner, or for an individual owner as that owner's agent; a manager can still testify as a witness. The justice's court statute is broader on its face (any person except the constable who served the papers may act as attorney for a party), but the court rules are stricter and later, and the cautious course is to follow them. In city court the LLC exception is written for justice's court only, so the cautious course there is a licensed attorney even for an LLC. District court requires a licensed attorney.

Small claims (money claims up to $7,000 only, never possession): by statute a corporation may be represented by a director, officer or employee and an LLC by a majority member; no party may use an attorney unless every party has one; only a party to the transaction may file, and no party may file more than 10 claims a year. Attorney fees: a court may not award attorney fees to a party represented by anyone other than a licensed attorney, so an LLC that appears through its majority member gives up the prevailing-party fee award the landlord-tenant act otherwise allows.

Before you file. An out-of-state LLC or corporation that does business in Montana must register with the Secretary of State. Until it does, it may not maintain any case in a Montana court, eviction included; its leases stay valid and it may defend a case a tenant brings, and for an LLC the court may pause the case until it registers. Owning and renting out income-producing property is not on the lists of activities that are not doing business, so register before you need to file. An unregistered foreign LLC also owes a civil penalty of $5 a day, up to $1,000 a year. If you rent under any name other than your full legal name, register that assumed business name: no one doing business under an unregistered assumed name may sue in a Montana court under that name. The statute bars suing under the name; the safe course is to register, or to sue in the owner's true legal name. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the court rules printed in it, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: Ending a lease after fire, flood or other disaster
bodyText:
Fire or casualty is the only event rule: Montana's only statute on ending a lease because of a damaging event is the fire-or-casualty rule. If the unit or premises are damaged or destroyed by fire or casualty so that enjoyment of the unit is substantially impaired, the tenant may move out at once and give written notice within 14 days to end the lease, or, if staying is lawful, vacate the unusable part and pay reduced rent; you must return the deposit and prepaid rent, accounted from the date of the event. The rule does not apply if the tenant's household or guests caused the damage purposefully or negligently. A flood, wildfire, windstorm or similar event that damages the unit would ordinarily be treated as a casualty; there is no separate statute for disasters, environmental contamination, evacuation orders or condemnation.

Landlord's option: the statute gives the landlord no termination right after an event, and none bars one, so the library offers an optional clause letting you end the lease by written notice after a fire or casualty that substantially impairs the unit (see the Landlord's Option to End the Lease After a Fire or Casualty clause). Other routes: a condition that makes the unit unfit is also a habitability breach the tenant can act on after notice; for a methamphetamine or fentanyl contamination you must give written notice before leasing a contaminated, unremediated property. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: EV Chargers at the End of a Montana Tenancy
bodyText:
Montana has no statute specific to electric-vehicle chargers at the end of a tenancy (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library). Montana's general fixture law governs instead, and the lease can change it. A charger hard-wired or bolted to the building is a fixture.

If it was installed without an agreement allowing the tenant to remove it, it belongs to the owner of the property, unless the owner chooses to require the tenant to remove it. A tenant may remove a fixture installed for domestic use at any time during the tenant's term if removal can be done without injury to the premises and the charger has not, by the way it is attached, become an integral part of the premises; that right ends with the term.

A plug-in charger that is not attached is the tenant's personal property: if the tenant leaves it behind after the tenancy ends, follow Montana's abandoned-property procedure (inventory and store anything of value, give written notice by certificate of mailing or certified mail at least 10 days before disposing of it). You owe the tenant nothing for a charger the tenant leaves unless the lease says so.

Damage the tenant causes in installing or removing a charger (beyond ordinary wear and tear) may be deducted from the security deposit with the itemized list Montana requires. Decide the outcome in the lease: the library's optional clause ev-charger-installation-mt lets you choose removal and repair or that the charger stays and becomes yours, and gives you the choice if the tenant fails to remove it when required.

title: Electric Vehicle Charging Rules in Montana
bodyText:
Montana has no statute or state rule giving a tenant (or a condominium or homeowners' association member) a right to install an electric-vehicle charger, requiring a landlord to provide charging, or limiting the terms on which a landlord may allow it (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library). A tenant may install a charger only with your written consent, on the terms you set. Three state laws can still reach charging you allow or provide.

**Public charging stations.** Montana taxes electricity delivered to a "public charging station" at 3 cents a kilowatt hour; the utility adds the tax to its bill to the station owner, so a landlord does not collect or remit it from tenants. A "charging station" is equipment rated above 25 kilowatts that is not installed at a residence or owned by a homeowners' or condominium association, and it is a public charging station if it charges the customer for the electricity or for charging time.

A public charging station must have its own meter installed or approved by the utility (the owner pays for it), must be registered with the Montana Department of Transportation within 30 days after it starts operating, and must post its rate at the site. An ordinary home or garage charger (typically well under 25 kilowatts) is outside these rules.

The law does not say whether an apartment building is "a residence", so if you install a high-power charger that tenants pay to use, treat it as a public charging station or ask the Department of Transportation first.

**Utility law.** A business that operates electric vehicle charging stations is not a public utility, and a utility serves a commercial charging station under a rate approved by the Public Service Commission.

**Weights and measures.** Montana's weights and measures law excludes electricity meters only when they are part of a public utility system, and it reaches measures used commercially to compute a charge. Whether a meter you own, or a charger's own kilowatt-hour readout, used to bill a tenant for charging must be inspected and tested under that law is not settled, and the department's rules and the national device standards it adopts were not read for this library.

Cautious course: have the charger connected to electric service in the tenant's own name, or include charging in the rent; if you bill by your own meter, ask the Department of Labor and Industry's weights and measures program whether the device must be tested, and charge no more than the actual cost on your utility bill.

**Buildings and associations.** Neither local governments nor the state building code may require new buildings to include charging wiring or equipment. If the rental is in a condominium or homeowners' association, its declaration, bylaws and rules bind you as the owner, and a unit owner may not make an alteration that would jeopardize the soundness or safety of the property without the consent of the other affected owners.

Ownership at the end of the tenancy is covered in edu-ev-charging-end-of-tenancy-mt; the library's optional installation clause is ev-charger-installation-mt.

title: No Montana Rule on EV Chargers in Shared Parking
bodyText:
Montana has no statute or state rule on electric-vehicle charging in shared parking: nothing gives a tenant a right to put a charger in a common lot or garage, sets or limits a fee to reserve the space, or allocates damage or upkeep of a charger in a shared area (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library). Whether to allow it, and on what terms, is your choice. Three general rules still apply.

You must keep all common areas, including shared parking, in a clean and safe condition, so a cord or cable across a walkway or drive aisle is your problem as well as the tenant's.

If a lease or your rules already hold shared parking out for all tenants, giving one tenant an exclusive charging space is a change to the others' bargain: a rule adopted mid-lease that substantially modifies a tenant's bargain is not valid until 7 days' written notice (week-to-week) or 30 days' written notice (month-to-month), and it binds a fixed-term tenant only as the lease allows.

In a condominium, the parking may be a common element that you as a unit owner may use only as intended and without encroaching on the other owners' rights, so get the association's consent first. A space charge agreed in the lease is rent under Montana's definition, and money held to secure the charger is a security deposit. The library's optional clause is ev-charging-shared-area-mt, used with ev-charger-installation-mt.

title: No hardship stay of eviction
bodyText:
No hardship stay: Montana law gives a court no general power to delay or stay an eviction because of the tenant's hardship, and there is no statewide eviction moratorium. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act instead sets fast deadlines: the hearing within 10 business days after the tenant's appearance or answer date (5 for dangerous-activity cases), a ruling within 5 days, writs of possession and assistance issued immediately, and the sheriff executing the writ within 5 business days. The hearing can go past the deadline only if you and the tenant agree.

What can delay possession: (1) for a Montana National Guard member on active duty, or a dependent, a court may stay a nonpayment action about their primary residence for up to 3 months, or adjust the payments; (2) a tenant who appeals a justice's or city court judgment for possession stays the writ only by filing the undertaking (or cash deposit) the court sets to cover use and occupancy, and the district court must waive it for a tenant found indigent; (3) the tenant's counterclaim in a nonpayment case, with rent paid into court. The older forcible-entry and unlawful-detainer chapter, which does let a court relieve a tenant against forfeiture for hardship, does not apply to tenancies under the Act; it reaches only occupancies the Act excludes.

Local moratoria: cities and counties with self-government powers may not regulate landlords' dealings with tenants beyond the state landlord-tenant and deposit acts or add to them, so a local eviction moratorium would very likely be preempted. Federal law (the CARES Act notice) can add a 30-day notice to vacate on covered properties. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No set eviction fee or penalty
bodyText:
Default rule: if you win an eviction case, the court may award you reasonable attorney fees, court costs and necessary disbursements, along with possession, unpaid rent and your actual damages; if the tenant wins, the tenant can get the same fee award against you. The court decides this whatever the lease says, and a lease clause giving only you a right to fees is treated as giving the tenant the same right.

Eviction fees and penalties: no Montana statute bans by name a lease clause charging the tenant a set fee or penalty when you serve a notice or file for possession, but none supports one either. Montana voids any contract term fixing damages for a breach in advance unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix. Eviction costs (filing and service fees, attorney time, lost rent) can be documented, so a flat "eviction fee" or "notice fee" in the lease is very likely void and worth nothing beyond the actual costs you could recover anyway. The library therefore offers no such clause: recover your actual, documented costs and fees through the court, and deduct from the deposit only the amounts the deposit law allows. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: A lease can't name someone to accept court papers
bodyText:
The bar: a Montana lease can't name a person to accept court papers for the tenant. Montana contract law makes void any provision in a written contract containing a promise to pay money (a lease with rent qualifies) that empowers someone, as a party's agent, to accept service of process, confess judgment or consent to a default in a court case on the contract. So a clause naming a friend, relative or the landlord's agent to receive the tenant's eviction summons is unenforceable, and service on that person would not be good service.

How to serve instead: in a justice's or city court possession case, serve the summons and complaint on the tenant personally (or by the mail-and-acknowledgment route the court rules allow), or on an agent the tenant has appointed outside the lease or one authorized by law. Each defendant must be served separately. A minor tenant is served by delivering the papers to the minor and to the minor's guardian or guardian ad litem. A lease can, however, name the address where the tenant wants to receive the landlord's written notices (as opposed to court papers).

Address confidentiality program: a victim of partner or family member assault, sexual assault or stalking can enroll in the Department of Justice's program, which gives a substitute address and makes the department the participant's agent to receive service of process and forward it. The statute does not say an eviction summons must go to the department, and personal service on the tenant at the rental still meets the court rules; if a tenant gives you a program card, the cautious course is to serve the tenant personally and also send a copy to the department. Your own side: you must give the tenant, in writing, the name and address of the owner or of a person authorized to receive service of process and notices for the owner. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws, the court rules printed in the Code and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No lease release from your own negligence
bodyText:
Default rule: you and the tenant are each responsible under ordinary law for harm caused by your own negligence or purposeful misconduct.

The bar: a Montana rental agreement may not make either party excuse or limit the other party's liability for that party's purposeful misconduct or negligence, or make either party indemnify the other for that liability or its costs or attorney fees. A "Landlord is not liable for any loss" sentence that reaches your own negligence is unenforceable, and knowingly using one can cost you the tenant's actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent. Montana contract law separately treats any contract exempting a person from responsibility for fraud, willful injury or violation of law as against public policy. A lease may still put on the tenant losses that aren't your fault, such as damage the tenant causes or the tenant's own belongings (with renters insurance), so long as it doesn't excuse your negligence.

What the law itself gives you, without a lease clause: you aren't liable for damages from the failure of the required smoke or carbon monoxide detector; you aren't responsible for loss to a tenant's stored abandoned property unless you caused it purposefully or negligently; you aren't liable for mold if you give the statutory mold statement and disclose known mold and testing; you aren't liable for methamphetamine contamination after state-confirmed cleanup and notice; until January 1, 2031, a premises owner isn't liable for covid-19 exposure absent gross negligence, willful and wanton misconduct or an intentional tort; and after a good-faith sale and written notice to the tenant you are released for later events (but not for the deposit and prepaid rent). Montana has no statute giving you immunity for removing a tenant's belongings when a possession judgment is carried out, or for acting on a police notice of drug activity. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: 10-day refund when nothing is owed
bodyText:
Montana's faster track is the 10-day refund: if, after inspection, there is no damage, no cleaning is needed and no rent is unpaid, and the tenant shows that no utilities are unpaid, you must return the whole deposit within 10 days. Otherwise you have 30 days from the end of the tenancy, or from surrender and acceptance if sooner, to give the written list and the balance. Either side may ask for an inspection within the week before the tenancy ends, which lets you settle the deposit quickly.

A tenant may sue over the deposit only after a written denial, after the 30 days, or 10 days after you indicated nothing was owed.

Montana has no other expedited procedure: no rule letting a tenant demand the money sooner, no separate track for abandonment, and no fee for faster processing (you may not deduct anything the deposit law doesn't list). The deadlines are outer limits, so you may always return the deposit sooner. They don't apply if the lease has been terminated and you have a pending claim filed in court under the act's section on a landlord's remedies after termination.

This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: Family Child Care in Montana Rentals
bodyText: Montana has no landlord-tenant statute giving a tenant a right to run a family or group day-care home over your objection, or setting conditions you may impose such as parent liability waivers, insurance or advance payment for changes. Paid care for other families' children is a business, so the cautious course is to treat it as the limited business Montana lets a tenant run with your written consent, which you may not unreasonably withhold if the day care follows your reasonable rules (residential-use-only-mt). Other Montana law protects home child care against everyone but you. Under a covenant, providing child care in a family day-care home (3 to 8 children) or a group day-care home (9 to 15 children) is a residential use and a residential purpose. Zoning must treat those homes as a residential use permitted in all residential zones, may not require a conditional use permit for them, and may not apply to them safety or sanitary rules that don't apply to homes generally (for 15 or fewer children under the older zoning statute, 12 or fewer under the newer Land Use Planning Act); since October 1, 2026 local zoning may not set a minimum parking requirement for a licensed or registered child-care facility. The provider must hold a state registration certificate (unless caring for six or fewer children without state child-care payments), and the licensing law bars the state from waiving its requirement that a day-care facility have current and adequate public liability and fire insurance. Reasonable rules you might set include proof of registration and insurance, the number of children the registration allows, parking and drop-off, use of outdoor areas, and the tenant paying for changes needed for registration. The state's registration standards for day-care homes are in rules this library hasn't read. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library.

title: Hunting rights on rented rural land
bodyText:
Hunting and fishing on rented rural land. Montana has no statute giving or denying a tenant hunting or fishing rights on rented land. A hunter or trapper on private land needs permission of the landowner, the lessee, or their agents, so a tenant in possession can lawfully let people hunt unless the lease reserves those rights; a tenant of the land may also get the landowner's $1 trapping license.

Recreational-use protection covers you: a person who hunts or fishes on the land without paying for it does so without any assurance that the property is safe, and the landowner (a term that includes a tenant or lessee) is liable only for willful or wanton misconduct.

The landlord-tenant act link: Montana's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act does not govern an occupancy outside a city or town under a rental agreement that includes hunting, fishing or agricultural privileges along with the use of the dwelling (unless the arrangement was created to avoid the act). So giving a rural tenant hunting, fishing or farming rights in the lease can take the tenancy out of the act, and general landlord-tenant law then governs; reserving those rights keeps a house-only rental under the act.

Reserving the rights does not let you or your hunters enter land leased to the tenant to hunt, fish or trap: that is not one of the act's grounds for entry. The library's optional Hunting, Fishing and Trapping Reserved clause therefore reserves those rights only on your land outside the leased area, bars the tenant from hunting or giving permission, and allows hunting on the leased land only with the tenant's written consent.

This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set; Fish, Wildlife and Parks rules outside that set, block management agreements and case law were not searched.

title: No fee-in-lieu-of-deposit statute
bodyText:
Montana has no statute on fees, bonds or insurance a tenant pays instead of a security deposit: no rules on offering the option to all applicants, on the tenant's right to switch to a deposit, or on notice before reporting a damage claim to a credit bureau or collector. The deposit law decides how such a fee is treated. Any fee or charge for cleaning and damage, however it is labelled, is presumed to be a security deposit, and so is any deposit the lease requires the tenant to give you. A monthly or one-time "deposit waiver" or "damage protection" fee paid to you is therefore likely to be treated as a security deposit: refundable, usable only for the listed deductions, and accounted for in the written list at move-out. A lease term saying it is nonrefundable would be invalid.

The cautious course is not to charge a fee in lieu of a deposit unless you are prepared to hold and refund it as a deposit. A bond or insurance policy the tenant buys from a third party is not a payment to you, but whether it is lawful and how claims against the tenant work are questions of Montana insurance law the library did not research, so take advice before requiring or offering one. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: Fee transparency
bodyText: Montana has no fee-transparency or all-in pricing law for rentals. Nothing requires you to show rent as one figure that includes mandatory fees, to list fees on the lease's first page or next to the rent, or to itemize fees in a set format; no statute lists fees a landlord may not charge, beyond the ban on fees based on how rent is paid; and no auto-renewal rule reaches leases. We found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library. Two rules do the work instead. First, rent under Montana's landlord-tenant act includes late fees and other charges only "as agreed on in the rental agreement", so a charge that isn't in the lease isn't rent and can't be the basis of a 3-day notice for nonpayment. Second, Montana's consumer protection act bars unfair or deceptive practices and covers people who lease real property for household use, so surprise fees carry risk. List every recurring and one-time fee in the lease, with its amount and when it's due. A lease that doesn't set its own extension period continues month to month unless either side gives 30 days' written notice before the end of the term.

title: Fees for services not provided
bodyText: Montana has no general rule barring a fee for a service you don't provide, such as an amenity, trash pickup or a utility the tenant doesn't get. We found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library. One narrow rule exists: a property manager of four or more units who keeps part of an application fee may keep only the itemized costs of services actually performed, never the cost of a service that wasn't performed (edu-application-fee-mt). For a tenancy, a service charge you agree in the lease is part of the rent, and failing to provide what the lease promises is your breach: if you fail, purposefully or negligently, to supply heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service the lease or the law requires, the tenant may, after notice and a reasonable chance for you to fix it, buy the service and deduct its reasonable cost from rent, recover damages, or move to substitute housing and stop paying rent for that period; for any other unkept lease promise the tenant may recover actual damages. Montana's consumer protection act also bars unfair or deceptive practices. Charge a service fee only for a service the tenant actually receives, describe it in the lease, and stop or credit the fee while the service isn't available.

title: Building and Fire Codes for Montana Rentals
bodyText: Two state codes reach a Montana rental building. The state building code, adopted by the Department of Labor and Industry (now the 2024 International Building, Residential and Existing Building Codes, with Montana changes), governs how a building is built, altered or changed in use. It does not apply to residential buildings with fewer than five units unless your city, town or county has made it apply, and a local building code may not be stricter than the state's. The state fire code, adopted by the state fire marshal (now the 2024 International Fire Code, with Montana changes), applies to existing buildings, but an existing building is to be maintained under the building code in effect when it was built; the fire marshal may still act where an existing condition is an imminent hazard. Your lease duty follows the same pattern: for units completed after July 1, 1977 you must comply with the building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety that were in effect when the unit was built (see edu-frozen-standard-incorporation-mt and edu-habitability-mt). The state fire safety law covers apartment houses, dwellings, lodging houses and other residential occupancies, except a building used only for private residential purposes for a family. Whether a rented single-family house falls in that exception is not settled; the fire marshal's rules treat a house as a private house only if no part of it is rented, so assume the law reaches a rented house. Fire officials may inspect, serve a written notice of violations with a deadline on the person responsible for the building's safety, and ask a court to stop occupancy until the building complies; each day of noncompliance after the deadline is a separate misdemeanor. It is unlawful to obstruct a fire exit or a hallway, corridor or entranceway leading to one. A city or town council may require an owner to put in fire escapes and proper exits where needed for safety, and a tenant who is required under the fire safety law to put in fire escapes may take the cost out of the rent without breaching the lease. No statewide statute or rule requires existing residential buildings to be brought up to the current code or to add fire escapes (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws and the state building and fire code rules). Elevators, escalators, platform lifts and stair chairlifts in buildings other than private residences must be registered with the Department of Labor and Industry and inspected every year, and the owner or lessee is responsible for the inspection. A lease may also require the tenant to keep exits, hallways and stairways clear and not to tamper with fire safety equipment. The library does not offer a separate clause for this: its grilling and flammables clause, its rules clause and the tenant's statutory duties cover the usual ground, and you may add your own rule after taking advice. Ask your local building or fire official which edition applied when your building was built.

title: Fire Sprinklers in Montana Rentals
bodyText: Montana requires automatic fire sprinklers only through its building code, and only when a building is built, altered or changed in use. The state building code may not require a sprinkler system in a single-family home or in a residential building with no more than two units, and Montana deletes the sprinkler sections of the residential code for one- and two-family homes and townhouses. For apartment buildings and other buildings under the commercial building code, Montana's version requires a sprinkler system throughout any residential building with 5 or more dwelling units, and in some lodging and group living buildings, unless, in a building no more than three stories above the lowest exit level, each unit has a door leading directly to an exterior exit access. An apartment building of up to six stories built with a single stairway must be sprinklered. The state code does not reach residential buildings with fewer than five units unless your city, town or county applies it, and a local code may not be stricter than the state's. No statute or rule requires you to add sprinklers to an existing building: the state fire code as Montana adopted it leaves out the model code's sprinkler requirements for existing buildings and says that retroactive fire alarm or sprinkler systems are not approved, and an existing building is maintained under the building code in effect when it was built (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws and the state building and fire code rules). If your building has a sprinkler system, keep it in good and safe working order as part of the facilities you supply, and have it serviced by a licensed fire protection company; a service tag on fire protection equipment may be removed only when new service is performed. Ask your local building or fire official what applied when your building was built.

title: No duty to disclose a foreclosure, but silence is risky
bodyText:
**Telling tenants about a foreclosure.** Montana has no statute requiring a landlord to tell a prospective or current tenant that the property is in foreclosure, that a notice of default or trustee's sale has been filed, that a contract for deed is being cancelled, or that a tax proceeding is pending.

Silence can still cost you: Montana contract law treats suppressing a true fact you know about, with intent to induce someone to sign, as fraud, and deceit includes giving other information that is misleading without the missing fact; the consumer protection act also bars deceptive practices in trade, which includes renting real property. A tenant who later loses the home to a foreclosure buyer may bring those claims.
