Why it matters to the tenant: after a trustee's sale the buyer is entitled to possession on the 10th day, and anyone holding under an interest that came after the trust deed (which usually includes a tenant whose lease is newer than the loan) is treated as a tenant at will; after a sheriff's sale the buyer collects the rent until redemption. The library offers an optional Foreclosure Disclosure clause that records, in the lease, what you told the tenant before signing.

See also the Foreclosure of a Montana Rental row. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No relief from forfeiture after the notice date
bodyText:
Cure before the notice date: for a lease violation that can be remedied by repairs, payment of damages or your written approval, the tenant keeps the tenancy by fixing it before the move-out date in your notice (14 days for most violations; 3 days for an unauthorized pet, unauthorized occupants or verbal abuse). For unpaid rent the tenant keeps the tenancy by paying within the 3-day notice period. No cure is allowed for a repeat of the same violation within 6 months, for damaging the premises, or for dangerous activity.

No relief after forfeiture: once the notice date passes and the tenancy ends, Montana gives a residential tenant no right to ask a court to undo the termination and restore the lease for hardship or on late payment or performance. The older unlawful-detainer chapter does let a court relieve a tenant against forfeiture for hardship, on a petition within 30 days after the judgment and only on full payment or performance, but that chapter applies only to occupancies the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act excludes (and also lets those tenants save the lease by performing within 3 days of the notice). A tenant can still defend the possession case (for example by counterclaim in a nonpayment case, or by showing retaliation or a defective notice), and a judgment can be reopened for mistake or excusable neglect on a motion within 30 days. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: Building Codes Frozen at Original Construction
bodyText: Montana fixes your building-code duty as a landlord at the code that applied when the unit was built. For a dwelling unit whose construction was completed after July 1, 1977, you must comply with the requirements of the applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety that were in effect at the time of original construction. A newer code edition does not reach the unit just because the state or your local government has since adopted it. Where that code duty asks more of you than your other maintenance duties, the code duty controls. The duty reaches only codes that actually applied to the building. The state building code has never applied to residential buildings with fewer than five units unless the city, town or county made it apply, so a small rental built outside a local code area may have had no applicable building code at all. For units completed on or before July 1, 1977 the code duty does not apply, but your other duties do, including keeping the premises fit and habitable. The state fire code takes the same approach: existing buildings are to be maintained under the building code in effect when they were built, although the fire marshal may act on an existing condition that is an imminent hazard. Adoption of the existing building code is not to be read as requiring upgrades, and the residential code as Montana adopted it lets the legal occupancy of an existing structure continue unchanged except where that code or the fire code specifically says otherwise. Work you do now, such as a remodel, repair, addition or change of use, follows the code in force when you do it (now the 2024 editions). A tenant can't agree to do work needed to bring the unit up to the code that applied when it was built, and a lease can't waive the duty. See edu-habitability-mt for the full list of your maintenance duties. Your local building department can tell you which edition applied when your building was permitted.

title: No Good-Cause Notice Rule in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no good-cause notice rule. When you end a week-to-week or month-to-month tenancy with the required written notice (7 days or 30 days), or let a fixed-term lease end, the notice does not have to give a reason, and no statute requires you to prove a reason. The notice must state a cause only when you end the tenancy for the tenant's breach: then it must specify the acts and omissions that make up the breach, say that the rental agreement will terminate and give the move-out date, or for unpaid rent say that the tenancy will end if rent is not paid within 3 days. Two limits apply to a no-reason notice: it may not be retaliation for a protected complaint or for joining a tenants' union, and if the tenant claims retaliation you may have to show your real reason. A local government with self-government powers may not add a good-cause or just-cause requirement, because it may not regulate landlords' dealings with tenants beyond the state landlord-tenant act. See also edu-for-cause-eviction-mt.

title: Passing government fines to tenants
bodyText:
Montana has no statute on passing government fines to tenants: nothing bars it, nothing limits it to conditions the tenant caused, and nothing makes a tenant liable to you for a fine as such. We found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library.

A fine you pay because the tenant broke the lease or the tenant's own statutory duties (including the duty to follow building and housing codes) can be recovered as actual damages; the lease clause makes that recovery clear.

The library's optional clause (tenant-caused-fines-oh) treats a tenant-caused violation as a breach and recovers the amount you actually paid as your damages, which Montana allows for a tenant's noncompliance with the lease or the tenant's statutory duties, including the duty to follow building and housing codes. It is framed as damages rather than reimbursement so that it stays clear of Montana's bar on lease terms making a party indemnify the other for that party's own misconduct or negligence. Never pass on a fine for a condition you are responsible for, and keep the citation and proof of payment.

title: Lease Guaranties and Renewals in Montana
bodyText:
Montana has no statute written for lease guaranties; Montana's general guaranty law applies, and it answers most renewal questions. A guaranty must be in writing and signed by the guarantor. Signed together with the lease it needs no separate consideration; a guaranty added later needs consideration of its own. A guarantor can never owe more than the tenant.

A guarantor of payment is liable as soon as the tenant defaults, without demand or notice, and your mere delay in pursuing the tenant doesn't release the guarantor. The key renewal rule: a guarantor is released if, by an act of yours not authorized in the original guaranty or without the guarantor's separate consent, the tenant's obligation is altered in any respect, or your rights against the tenant are impaired or suspended; undoing the change doesn't restore the guaranty.

So a renewal at a new rent, an extension or another lease change can release a guarantor unless the guaranty authorized it in advance, and whether a month-to-month continuation of the same lease counts as an alteration isn't settled by the statute. The cautious course is to have the guaranty say exactly which future changes it covers, as the library's optional Guaranty clause (guaranty-mt) does, and to get the guarantor's signed consent to anything else.

A guaranty of future, successive obligations can be revoked by the guarantor as to future transactions unless there is continuing consideration the guarantor doesn't renounce; whether a lease guaranty that covers renewals is such a guaranty is for the courts, so the clause lets the guarantor end it for renewal periods that begin after written notice. Montana doesn't require a guaranty to state a maximum or an end date.

A surety may require you to proceed against the tenant and is released to the extent prejudiced if you neglect to; whether a lease guarantor can use that rule is also for the courts, so if a guarantor asks you in writing to pursue the tenant, do so promptly. Montana has no cap on deposits, but any deposit a guarantor or tenant gives you to secure rent or damage is a security deposit under Montana's deposit law.

Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library.

title: When a repair problem is serious enough
bodyText:
Montana ties the tenant's strongest remedies to seriousness. A tenant may give the 14-day notice to cure (with termination at least 30 days later) or make repairs and deduct the cost only for a failure to maintain the premises that affects health and safety. Your code duty is likewise limited to building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety. The tenant can buy essential services and deduct their cost, recover reduced rental value, or move to substitute housing only if you purposefully or negligently fail to supply heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service.

Below that line the tenant still has a remedy: for any failure to comply with the lease or your maintenance duties, the tenant may sue for actual damages or an injunction, and Montana expressly allows damages for minor violations costing less than one month's rent to fix. So a cosmetic problem won't support a termination notice or repair-and-deduct, but it isn't outside the law. The statute doesn't define "affecting health and safety" further; that is for the court on the facts. Cautious course: treat any defect that could plausibly affect health or safety (heat, water, sewage, electrical, structural, pests, mold, locks on exterior doors) as qualifying, and repair it as promptly as conditions require after any notice, written or not: restore heat, water, hot water, electricity or gas at once, fix an emergency within 3 working days, and fix anything else within 14 days. A tenant's complaint to a code agency about a violation materially affecting health and safety is protected from retaliation.

title: What habitability duties can be shifted
bodyText:
Default rule: you must keep a Montana rental fit and habitable, keep supplied systems and appliances working, provide garbage receptacles and removal, and supply running water, reasonable hot water and, from October 1 to May 1, reasonable heat.

What can be modified, and how:
- Garbage: the lease itself may make the tenant responsible for garbage receptacles and removal.
- Water, hot water and heat: you and the tenant may agree in writing, in good faith and not to evade your duties, that the tenant supplies them (for example, the tenant pays for and keeps the propane or fuel that heats the unit).
- Specified repairs and maintenance tasks: only by a separate writing signed by both of you, made in good faith, supported by adequate consideration (such as a rent reduction), not covering work needed to bring the building up to code, and not reducing what you owe other tenants. The library's tenant maintenance agreement is drafted to meet these conditions.

Montana has no rule letting a lease waive the water or hot-water duty because the property has no well or utility water. The heat and hot-water duties don't apply where the building isn't required by law to be equipped for that purpose or the tenant controls the equipment that produces the heat or hot water, but whether a building is "not required by law to be equipped" depends on building codes outside the library's research set, so assume the duty applies unless your own adviser confirms otherwise. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No habitability presumption
bodyText:
Montana creates no statutory presumption about habitability. No statute presumes that you breached your maintenance duty because a code violation went uncorrected after notice, that a repair took unreasonably long after a set number of days, or that a code citation proves a condition affects health and safety, and none presumes a unit habitable. A tenant who relies on the repair remedies has to prove the failure and that it affects health and safety.

Don't confuse this with the presumption Montana does use: if a tenant complained to a code agency about a violation materially affecting health and safety, or complained to you in writing about a maintenance violation, within 6 months before you raise the rent, cut services or bring or threaten an eviction, the law presumes retaliation unless you produce evidence that it wasn't (with exceptions, including a violation the tenant caused and rent in default). The other tenancy presumptions concern abandoned property and security deposits. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No lease habitability statement required
bodyText:
No Montana statute requires your lease to state that you will deliver the unit fit for habitation, or to state the unit's agreed condition instead. You don't need the sentence: Montana law already requires you to deliver possession at the start of the term in compliance with the lease and your maintenance duties, and to keep the premises fit and habitable, whatever the lease says.

What Montana does require is different. If you take a security deposit, you must give the tenant a separate signed written statement of the unit's present condition when the lease is signed or the tenancy begins (see the condition statement rules). That is a separate document, not a habitability promise in the lease, and the lease can't replace it. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: Habitability can’t be waived
bodyText:
Default rule: a Montana landlord must comply with the building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety in effect when the building was built (for buildings completed after July 1, 1977); make repairs and keep the premises fit and habitable; keep common areas clean and safe; keep the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning facilities and appliances you supply in good and safe working order; provide garbage receptacles and removal; supply running water and reasonable hot water at all times and reasonable heat from October 1 to May 1; and install approved smoke and carbon monoxide detectors.

Waiver: a lease can't remove any of these requirements. Montana bars a rental agreement term in which a party agrees to waive or forgo rights or remedies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and separately bars any lease or related document that lets you collect rent free of the duty to maintain the premises. Such a term is unenforceable, and knowingly using it exposes you to the tenant's actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent.

What the law allows is moving the work, not lowering the standard. The lease itself may make the tenant responsible for garbage removal. A good-faith written agreement may have the tenant supply water, hot water or heat, and specified repairs or maintenance tasks belong in a separate signed agreement with real consideration that never covers work needed to bring the building up to code (see the tenant maintenance agreement). The heat and hot-water duties also don't apply where the building isn't required by law to be equipped for them or the tenant controls the equipment that produces them; that is a limit on the duty, not a waiver. Montana has no rule letting a tenant accept named defects in exchange for lower rent: a rent reduction can pay for work the tenant agrees to do, but it can't buy a unit below the standard. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: Contamination Disclosure for Montana Rentals
bodyText:
Montana has one contamination disclosure that reaches ordinary leases. If you know the rental was used as a clandestine methamphetamine or fentanyl lab, or was contaminated by meth or fentanyl use, and it has not been cleaned to state standards by a certified contractor, you must tell each new occupant in writing before they agree to the lease (see edu-meth-disclosure-mt).

The duty turns on what you know, not on whether the property appears on the Department of Environmental Quality's public list; once the department removes a cleaned property from the list, you need not disclose the past contamination.

Neither the statute nor the department's cleanup rules bars renting or occupying a contaminated property; the cleanup program is voluntary, though a local health officer may inspect and order a condition of public health importance corrected, and your duty to keep the premises fit and habitable applies. Known mold has its own disclosure (mold-disclosure-mt).

Montana has no statute requiring a landlord to tell a tenant about other contamination, a hazardous-substance release, a state or federal cleanup site, or a recorded institutional control (a deed restriction, covenant or similar limit filed under the state cleanup law), or to put one into a lease.

An institutional control does run with the land and binds everyone who later takes an interest in the property, and an owner who rents for residential use keeps a defense to state cleanup liability only while it complies with and carries out every required institutional control, so a lease term making the tenant follow it protects you (institutional-control-notice-mt).

If you give a tenant an option to buy a one-to-four-unit home or an individually owned unit, the seller disclosure statement applies and must cover hazardous materials on the property or in the immediate area and any testing or treatment for contaminated soil or water, fuel or chemical tanks, meth and similar hazards.

Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws, the Constitution and the Montana rules held for this pass, including the meth cleanup rules.

title: No Duty to Hand Over Local Health Rules in Montana
bodyText: Montana puts no duty on you to give a tenant a copy of a local health board's or health department's rules, on request or otherwise, and no duty to refer a tenant to the health department. Local health still reaches rentals in three ways. First, the county or city board of health and its health officer may inspect for conditions of public health importance in private buildings, order filth, contamination or other nuisances corrected, do the work themselves and recover the cost if you ignore an order, and adopt sanitation regulations, which generally may be no stricter than comparable state rules unless the board makes findings after a hearing. Second, if you rent sleeping rooms without kitchens to three or more people by the week or month (a roominghouse), or rent a whole non-owner-occupied home to travelers by the day or week (a tourist home), you need an annual state license validated by the local health officer and you are subject to inspections. Third, your duty to keep the unit fit and habitable includes complying with applicable housing and health codes, and you may not retaliate against a tenant who complains to a government agency that enforces a building or housing code. A local government with self-government powers may not use other powers to add landlord-tenant duties beyond the state acts.

title: Heat in Montana Rentals
bodyText:
You must supply reasonable heat between October 1 and May 1, along with running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times, and keep the heating system and other heating facilities you supply in good and safe working order. The heat duty does not apply if the building is not required by law to be equipped for heat, or if the unit is built so that heat is generated by an installation within the tenant's exclusive control, such as a furnace the tenant runs and fuels. You and the tenant may also agree in writing, in good faith and not to evade your duties, that the tenant will supply the heat, for example by paying for the gas or propane; that agreement does not shift your duty to keep the heating system in working order. Montana sets no indoor temperature; the standard is simply reasonable heat (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library). If you purposefully or negligently fail to supply heat, the tenant may give you written notice and, after you have had a reasonable chance to fix it, buy reasonable heat and deduct the cost from rent, recover damages for the reduced rental value, or move to reasonable substitute housing without owing rent for that period; these rights don't arise if the tenant, a family member or a guest caused the problem. Loss of heat can be an emergency, which shortens the time the tenant must give you before ending the lease. Never cut off or reduce heat to pressure a tenant to leave: that is unlawful and can cost you up to 3 months' rent or treble damages, whichever is greater. Where the tenant controls the heat, the library's optional Cold-Weather Precautions clause (cold-weather-precautions-mt) asks the tenant to keep the heat on so pipes don't freeze.

Boilers: Montana's boiler law requires a steam or hot water boiler to be inspected by a state or special boiler inspector before use and then on a schedule (each year for manually fired boilers and boilers of 400,000 Btu an hour or more, every 2 years for smaller automatically fired boilers), with the certificate of inspection displayed in the boiler room, and requires a licensed engineer to operate it. These inspection, certificate and license rules do not apply to a low-pressure steam heating boiler (15 psi or less), or a hot water heating or supply boiler (50 psi or less and 250 degrees F or less), in a private residence or an apartment building of six or fewer families. So a typical house or small apartment building is exempt, but a building of seven or more families with a central boiler needs inspections and a licensed operator, and the owner, renter or user of the boiler is liable for operating it without a licensed engineer. An inspector who finds a boiler unsafe will tell you what repairs are needed, and failing to comply with the department's order is a misdemeanor. Your lease duty to keep heating facilities in good and safe working order applies to every boiler you supply, exempt or not.

title: Homeowner and Condominium Associations and Rentals in Montana
bodyText:
How Montana law treats rentals in a homeowners or condominium association. Rental restrictions bind only owners who bought subject to them or agreed: an association may not adopt, amend or enforce a covenant, condition or restriction that makes the restrictions on a member's types of use more onerous than when the member acquired the property, unless the member agreed in writing when it was adopted or amended.

The protected types of use include the ability to rent the property for any amount of time, and residential, agricultural or commercial use unless the recorded restrictions already barred it. A later buyer takes the restrictions in force when the buyer bought. The rule covers condominium associations too.

If your association adopts a rental ban, rental cap, minimum lease term or tenant-approval rule after you bought, ask the association to record your exception (you give the date you acquired the property and pay the recording fee).

Montana has no statute on association approval of leases or tenants, caps on approval or application fees, association-held tenant deposits, limits on the tenant information an association may demand, or an association collecting rent directly from your tenant when you fall behind on dues; the governing documents control those. (In a foreclosure suit against a condominium unit, the unit owner must pay a reasonable rental if the bylaws so provide, and the plaintiff may have a receiver appointed to collect the rent.)

If the documents require approval, the library's optional Association Approval clause (association-approval-la) makes the lease depend on it; a cleaning or damage deposit you collect yourself is presumed a security deposit under Montana's deposit law.

Condominium unit owners must comply with the bylaws, rules and recorded covenants, and the association or another owner can sue over a violation; your tenant is bound through the lease (hoa-compliance), and a lease filed with the association's presiding officer can make the tenant count as the unit owner for the purposes it provides, including voting. A condominium lease must also carry certain particulars of the unit (condominium-unit-lease-contents-mt).

Other limits on associations: a homeowners association must get the owner's permission before its agent enters the owner's property, must try to set a convenient time and say what part it wants to reach, and the owner may insist on being present (this doesn't apply to condominium common elements reached through a unit under the documents, or to recorded easements for the association).

An association can't prohibit political signs on the owner's property, though it may limit their size, location and timing (edu-political-signs-mt). Under a covenant, a family or group day-care home is a residential use; that protects home child care against covenants and the association, not against you, because the lease and Montana's limited-business rule govern between you and your tenant (edu-family-child-care-mt).

Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library.

title: Home Businesses in Montana Rentals
bodyText:
Montana gives a tenant a qualified right to run a home business. A tenant may operate a limited business or cottage industry at the rental, subject to state and local laws, if you consent in writing, and you may not unreasonably withhold consent if the business is run within your reasonable rules. Otherwise the tenant must use the unit only as a dwelling unless you agree to something else.

A lease can't take that right away, so the library's Montana Residential Use Only clause (residential-use-only-mt) states the consent standard and has a space for your reasonable home-business rules; reasonable rules can address customer and delivery traffic, parking, signs, noise, hours, required licences and permits, liability insurance, and repairing damage the business causes. The library doesn't add a separate permission clause for Montana.

Montana has no statute making home businesses a permitted use under zoning generally; local zoning and home-occupation rules apply and weren't read. Two specific state rules exist: local governments may not prevent home digital asset mining at a private residence, except under existing noise ordinances, and a family or group day-care home is a residential use that zoning must allow (edu-family-child-care-mt).

Home food businesses (cottage food operations) may run from a rented home under the food laws' own registration rules. Associations: an association can't make restrictions on residential or commercial use more onerous than when the owner acquired the property unless the owner agreed in writing (edu-hoa-mt), but restrictions already in place bind your tenant through the lease (hoa-compliance).

Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library.

title: Homestead and exemption waivers
bodyText:
Default rule: Montana protects a debtor's homestead and certain personal property from collection. The homestead is the house or mobile home the claimant owns and lives in, with its land, claimed by an acknowledged declaration recorded with the county; it is exempt from execution up to a value limit (set by state rule, $350,000 in 2021 and rising 4% a year) except for judgments on construction or vendors' liens and certain mortgages. Personal property is protected too: health aids, public benefits, support payments and certain retirement accounts without limit; household goods, clothing, firearms and similar items up to $7,000 in total ($1,250 per item); one vehicle up to $4,000; tools of the trade up to $4,500; and most wages beyond the garnishment limit.

Waiver: Montana has no statutory words or procedure for waiving these exemptions in a lease. A tenant has no homestead in the home you rent to them, because a homestead must be the claimant's own property, so a lease waiver of homestead in the rental is empty. A waiver aimed at a tenant's own home elsewhere has no basis in the homestead law, which allows execution only for the listed liens and mortgages and requires a formal acknowledged instrument to encumber a married person's homestead. The one statute on exemption waivers makes them unenforceable in an unsecured promissory note; it doesn't name leases, but it points the same way. The library doesn't offer an exemption waiver: it would be worth nothing against the homestead and doubtful against personal property. Montana also gives a residential landlord no lien on a tenant's belongings. This covers the Montana Code Annotated (including the court rules it prints), the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No early termination for health, age or death
bodyText:
No statutory right: Montana gives a tenant no statutory right to end a lease early because of illness, age, disability, moving into a nursing home, assisted living or senior housing, or incapacity, and no rule ends a lease when a tenant dies. A month-to-month tenancy can be ended by the usual 30 days' written notice (7 days for week-to-week); a fixed-term lease ended early without cause leaves the tenant (or the estate) owing damages capped at 1 month's rent or an agreed lower or equal amount, plus rent until you re-let under the mitigation rules. You may agree to an early release, and the library's early-termination option lets the tenant leave on 30 days' notice and a fee of no more than one month's rent.

Two cautions: Montana's fair housing law treats refusing a reasonable accommodation in rules, policies or practices that a tenant with a disability needs as discrimination, so a request to end a lease early because of a disability should be considered as an accommodation request rather than refused out of hand; and federal servicemember law lets a servicemember end a lease after a catastrophic injury or illness, and a spouse or dependent end it within a year after the servicemember's death in service. When a tenant dies, deal with the personal representative or heirs. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No Duty to Disclose Code or Condemnation Orders in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no statute requiring you to tell an applicant or tenant about an outstanding building inspection order, code-violation notice, repair order or condemnation order on the property. Three Montana rules come close and you must follow them. First, if the property was used as a meth or fentanyl lab or contaminated by their use and has not been cleaned to state standards by a certified contractor, you must notify each new occupant in writing before they agree to the lease (see edu-meth-disclosure-mt). Second, if you take a security deposit, the separate move-in condition statement must describe the present condition of the premises that you know or should know from a reasonable inspection, so a known defect that is the subject of an order belongs in it (see edu-condition-statement-mt). Third, a fire-hazard order to repair or demolish a building must be served on any tenant occupying it, and the tenant may contest it in court, so the tenant will learn of it anyway. The cautious course is to tell an applicant in writing about any open order affecting the unit before signing and never to answer a direct question misleadingly. A local government with self-government powers may not add a disclosure duty for landlords beyond the state acts.

title: No Inspection-Notice Penalty in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no penalty tied to an inspection notice. You do not have to tell a tenant that a move-in or move-out inspection is available, there is no required walk-through, and there is no rule, like some states have, that a missed inspection notice costs you the right to keep any of the deposit or a multiple of it. Either you or the tenant may ask to inspect the premises within one week before the tenancy ends, but nothing turns on whether the other side is told of that option. Three related Montana rules do carry consequences. If you take a security deposit and do not give the tenant a separate written move-in condition statement (and, if the tenant asks in writing, the prior tenant's list of damage and cleaning charges), you may not recover anything for damage or cleaning unless you prove by clear and convincing evidence that this tenant caused it. You may not deduct cleaning charges until you give written notice of the cleaning still needed and the tenant has 24 hours to do it, unless the tenant left without notice or the tenancy has already ended for the tenant's breach and you have a claim pending in court. And entering to inspect requires at least 24 hours' notice and reasonable times except in an emergency; an unlawful or unreasonable entry lets the tenant get an injunction or end the lease and recover actual damages (see edu-landlord-entry-mt). A local government with self-government powers may not add inspection-notice rules beyond the state acts.

title: No lease jury waiver offered
bodyText:
Default rule: Montana's constitution secures the right to a jury trial, and allows a case to be tried without one only on default of appearance or by the parties' consent given in the way the law provides. An action for possession follows the Justice and City Court Rules of Civil Procedure: either side may demand a jury in writing no later than 5 days after the last pleading, and the jury is waived if no one demands it, if the parties consent on the court's docket, or if a party fails to appear for trial. In practice, then, an eviction is decided by the judge unless the tenant or you ask for a jury.

Waiver: no Montana statute or court rule either authorizes or bars a jury waiver signed in a residential lease, and Montana has no rule presuming one unconscionable. But the only ways the law provides for giving up a jury are steps taken in the case itself, and the act bars any lease term waiving the tenant's rights under it; whether a court would enforce a waiver signed before any dispute, or treat it as a prohibited waiver carrying a penalty of up to three months' periodic rent, would be decided under case law the library didn't review. Because the clause adds little (a jury happens only if someone demands one) and carries that risk, the library doesn't offer a jury waiver. A landlord who still wants one should take advice before adding it. This covers the Montana Code Annotated (including the court rules it prints), the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No Key-Control Mandate in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no statute requiring a landlord to keep a written key-control policy, to limit which employees hold master keys, or to run background checks on employees or contractors who have access to tenants' units. The lock and key rules Montana does have run the other way. A tenant may not remove a lock, or replace or add a lock you did not supply, without your written permission, and a tenant who does must give you a key so you keep your right of access; if the tenant does not, you may give a 24-hour notice to correct and, if it is not corrected, a 3-day notice to terminate. You, in turn, may enter only as the access statute allows, with at least 24 hours' notice except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable, and you may not change the locks to keep a tenant out without a court process. Those rules are already in the library's Montana entry clause (landlords-access-mt) and the shared Keys clause (keys). Montana also has no statute requiring rekeying between tenants (see edu-no-security-device-rule-mt). A written key-control practice, logging who holds each master key and rekeying after a key is lost or a tenant leaves, remains good practice and helps answer a negligence claim if an unauthorized entry occurs. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws, the Constitution and the Montana rules held for this pass.

title: Tenant's remedies for landlord breach
bodyText:
Montana sets a tenant's remedies for a landlord's breach in the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and a lease can't waive them.

If you fail to maintain the premises in a way that affects health and safety, the tenant may give written notice that the lease will end at least 30 days later unless you fix the problem within 14 days (3 working days after written notice in an emergency); may make repairs costing no more than 1 month's rent and deduct the cost after giving notice and a reasonable time; and may recover actual damages or get an injunction for any breach of the lease or of your maintenance duties.

If you purposefully or negligently fail to supply heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or other essential services, the tenant may, after written notice, buy them and deduct the cost, recover damages for the lost rental value, or move to substitute housing and owe no rent meanwhile. If you don't deliver possession, rent abates until you do.

An unlawful or harassing entry lets the tenant get an injunction or end the lease, with actual damages; an unlawful lockout or a purposeful cut-off of essential services lets the tenant recover possession or end the lease and recover up to the greater of 3 months' periodic rent or treble damages. In a possession case for unpaid rent, the tenant may counterclaim and the court may order rent paid into court. You may not retaliate against a tenant who complains.

Montana has no statute, health or lead law included, that lets a tenant simply withhold rent until repairs are made or that bars an eviction while a health or lead order is outstanding; we found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library.

title: No Landlord Insurance Mandate in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no statute or state rule requiring a residential landlord to carry liability or property insurance, to register or file proof of insurance with a government office, or to tell tenants whether you are insured. State law also bars cities and other self-governing local governments from licensing landlords or regulating their dealings with tenants beyond Montana's landlord-tenant, security deposit and mobile home lot acts, so a local insurance-and-registration mandate of the kind some states allow would face that bar (edu-local-regulation-mt). Insurance duties that touch rentals fall on others: a real estate broker or salesperson with an active license must carry professional liability (errors and omissions) insurance, which covers the licensee's professional mistakes rather than injuries at your property, and a day-care facility must keep public liability and fire insurance. Carrying your own landlord liability coverage is still wise: you remain liable for your own negligence, and a lease can't excuse it or make the tenant indemnify you for it (edu-exculpatory-clauses-mt). Your policy won't cover the tenant's belongings; the library's renter's insurance clause (tenants-property-insurance-ks-oh-ca) addresses that. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library.

title: Landlord's remedies: possession, rent and damages
bodyText:
After a lawful termination: once the lease has ended by the required notice (or by expiry), you have a claim for possession, for unpaid rent and for your actual damages for any breach of the lease, and you can bring them together in one action for possession. Possession, rent and damages can all be decided in that case; the damages hearing may follow, within 45 days after possession and rent are decided. If the tenant's breach was purposeful you may recover treble damages, except for an early move-out. A tenant who holds over after a lawful termination can owe up to 3 months' periodic rent or treble damages, whichever is greater, in the cases the holdover statute describes.

Before or without termination: you do not have to end the lease to be paid. You may sue for actual damages, or ask for an injunction, for any lease violation, and you may sue for rent while the tenant stays in possession; the tenant can then counterclaim, and the court may order rent paid into court. If the tenant abandons, you must make reasonable efforts to re-rent at a fair rental, and you recover rent only until a new tenancy starts or the term ends; ending a fixed term early without cause is capped at 1 month's rent in damages (or an agreed amount no higher). Every aggrieved party has a duty to mitigate. You may never retake possession yourself.

Which court: a possession case goes to district court or to a justice's, city or municipal court. A claim for money alone can go to small claims court if it is no more than $7,000 (small claims court cannot hear possession), to justice's court for contract claims up to $15,000, or to district court. The court may award the winner reasonable attorney fees and costs whatever the lease says.

Rent acceleration: no Montana statute lets a lease make all future rent due at once on default, and none bars it by name; given the mitigation duty and the early-termination damages cap, the library offers no acceleration clause. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: Lawn, Landscaping and Irrigation in Montana Rentals
bodyText: Lawn mowing, leaf raking, landscaping and keeping to an irrigation schedule are specified maintenance tasks. In Montana a landlord and tenant may agree that the tenant does specified repairs or maintenance tasks only in a separate writing signed by both, made in good faith and supported by adequate consideration, for work that isn't needed to meet building and housing codes, and without reducing your duties to other tenants. The library reads that rule as applying to every dwelling, including a single-family house, so it doesn't use its general Landscaping & Irrigation lease clause for Montana; use the separate Tenant Maintenance Agreement (maintenance-allocation-mt), which has a lawn, landscaping and irrigation option, including reporting leaks and watering problems. Without that agreement, keeping the grounds is part of your duty to keep the premises fit and habitable and the common areas clean and safe; the tenant must still use the property reasonably and not damage it. Weed rules stay with you as owner even if a tenant agrees to do the yard work: it is unlawful for any person to let noxious weeds spread or go to seed on the person's land, and a city may require owners to remove nuisance weeds and charge the cost against the property. Montana has no statute making tenants keep trees or plants clear of power lines. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library.

title: No late fee cap
bodyText: Montana has no limit on residential late fees: no cap, no percentage or dollar maximum, no required grace period and no notice step, and the mobile home lot act has none for park lots either. We found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library. The only Montana figure is for self-storage units, where a late fee of $20 or 20% of the monthly rent, whichever is greater, is treated as reasonable; it does not apply to homes or lots. What does limit you: a late fee must be agreed in the rental agreement, it then counts as rent, and Montana voids a damages amount fixed in advance unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix. Keep the fee near your real cost of late payment rather than setting it as a penalty. For park lots, nonpayment of rent or agreed late charges allows a 7-day termination notice. See the existing late-fee row (edu-late-fee-mt).

title: Working with law enforcement: no reporting duty
bodyText:
Working with law enforcement. Montana has no statute requiring a landlord to report crimes, drug activity or a drug lab at a rental to the police, to join a crime-free housing program, or to check or report to an offender registry. The reporting duty for a meth or fentanyl lab runs the other way: a law enforcement agency that learns a home was contaminated by a lab reports it to the state Department of Environmental Quality and the local health officer, and the property goes on the state's public list. Your own duty is to the next occupant: if you know the unit was a lab or was contaminated by meth or fentanyl use and it hasn't been remediated to state standards, you must tell each new occupant in writing before the lease is agreed (see the meth disclosure row); once the state confirms remediation and you give the documented notice, you are not liable to that occupant for claims based on meth in the home, and once the property is off the list you need not disclose the past contamination.

Calling the police for help: you or your agent may ask law enforcement to remove a person who can't produce authorization to occupy (never a tenant, who is removed only by court order), and to stand by while you change locks; if you knowingly give false information in that request, you must indemnify the agency for damages awarded against it. After you win a possession case, the sheriff executes the writ of assistance within 5 business days. If a court orders it in a criminal investigation, you must give law enforcement access and help to install a pen register or trap and trace device on a tenant's phone line, and you are immune from suit for that help except for gross negligence or willful or wanton misconduct. Montana has no general immunity for a landlord who reports a tenant's suspected crime. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No Lead-Safe Certificate for a Montana Rental
bodyText: Montana has no lead-safe or lead-free certificate for rental housing, no requirement to have a pre-1978 rental inspected or cleared for lead before letting it, no registry of older rentals and nothing to attach to a lease as a lead exhibit. Montana law mentions lead-based paint only in narrow places: a seller's disclosure statement on a sale must say whether the property has been tested or treated for lead-based paint, and that statement also applies if you give a tenant an option to purchase; a state brownfields fund may pay for lead paint abatement on eligible redevelopment sites; and a real estate licensee who breaks the federal lead disclosure rules commits unprofessional conduct. What does bind you is federal: for housing built before 1978, federal law requires you to disclose known lead-based paint and hazards and any reports, give the tenant the federal lead pamphlet, and include a lead warning and signed acknowledgments with the lease (see the library's lead-based-paint clause). A local government with self-government powers may not add a lead certification requirement for landlords beyond the state acts.

title: Montana Adds No Lead Notices of Its Own
bodyText:
Beyond the federal lead-based paint disclosure, Montana adds no lead notices of its own for rentals: no state lead form, pamphlet, certificate or packet to deliver with a lease, no notice to tenants of lead work in the building, and no notice when a water system tells you the property has a lead service line. The one Montana document that asks about lead is the seller's disclosure statement, which must say whether any part of the property has been tested or treated for lead-based paint (among other hazards).

It applies to sales and also to a lease with an option to purchase, so if you give a tenant a purchase option on a one-to-four-unit residence, give the seller disclosure statement before or when the option is signed, unless an exemption applies. For housing built before 1978 the federal disclosure, pamphlet and lease warning still apply (see the library's lead-based-paint clause). A local government with self-government powers may not add lead notice duties for landlords beyond the state acts.

title: No Lease Initialing Rule in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no rule that a tenant must initial any part of a lease, including a notice-to-end term, and no rule that a term is unenforceable because it was not initialed. We found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library; the only initialing rules in Montana law are outside landlord-tenant law (for example a solar sales contract's cancellation notice). What governs instead: either you or the tenant may end a month-to-month tenancy on at least 30 days' written notice (7 days for week-to-week), and a lease may not take away a right the landlord-tenant act gives, so a lease term requiring the tenant to give more notice than that is risky whether or not it is initialed. The library's clause (periodic-tenancy-notice-mt) keeps the tenant's notice at 30 days (7 for week-to-week). You may still ask the tenant to initial key terms as evidence that they were read, but Montana gives initials no special legal effect.

title: Recording a Montana Lease Is Optional
bodyText: Montana never requires you to record or register a residential lease. There is no lease registry, no state filing and no deadline, and no right of either party under the landlord-tenant or security deposit acts depends on recording. Recording is available: any instrument affecting the title to or possession of real property may be recorded with the county clerk and recorder of the county where the property is, once its signing is acknowledged before a notary (an abstract, often called a memorandum of lease, may be recorded instead). It matters only against strangers to the lease. An unrecorded lease stays valid between you and your tenant and against anyone who knows of it. But a lease for a term longer than one year that is not recorded is void against a later good-faith buyer or lender who pays value and records first; a lease of one year or less is not exposed to that rule. Whether a tenant's possession alone puts a buyer on notice is a question of case law that this library did not research, so if a lease runs longer than one year and the property may be sold or refinanced, record the lease or a memorandum of it, or make sure any buyer or lender gets a copy. Montana has no special rule for leases to relatives. A lease longer than one year must also be in writing (see edu-statute-of-frauds-mt). A local government with self-government powers may not add a lease-registration requirement for landlords, because it may not license landlords or regulate their dealings with tenants beyond the state acts.

title: Long Leases in Montana: Writing, Recording and Homesteads
bodyText: Montana sets no maximum length for a residential lease and needs no seal or special signing formality, with these limits. (1) A lease for longer than one year must be in writing and signed by the party to be bound; if an agent signs for that party, the agent's authority must also be in writing and signed (When a Montana Lease Must Be in Writing, edu-statute-of-frauds-mt). A written lease that only one side signed, given effect because the other accepted rent or possession, runs at most one year. (2) A lease for more than one year is an instrument creating an interest in real property: if it is not recorded with the county clerk, it is void against a later good-faith buyer or lender who records first. Record a long lease, or a memorandum of it, if the tenant's term must survive a sale or a new mortgage; leases of one year or less are exempt. (3) If the rental is a married owner's declared homestead, Montana law says the homestead cannot be conveyed or encumbered unless the instrument is signed and acknowledged by both spouses. No statute or case we found says whether a lease is such an instrument, so the cautious course is to have both spouses sign the lease and acknowledge it before a notary. (4) A lease of a town or city lot for longer than 75 years that reserves rent is invalid. Montana has no rule requiring a spouse's consent to lease other property, no community-property joinder rule for leases, and no cap on the length of an agricultural lease of private land (the term limits we found apply only to leases of state, county, city and other public property). This covers the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No Month-to-Month Parity Rule in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no rule that a month-to-month tenancy must be offered on terms no more burdensome than a fixed-term lease (or the reverse), and no cap on the difference in rent between the two. We found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library. So you may price and draft month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies differently, within the general limits: rules you adopt for the property must apply to all occupants in a fair manner; terms and prices may not discriminate on a protected basis under fair housing law; a month-to-month tenant's rent or terms change only on written notice at least 15 days before the end of a month (Rent Increases and Term Changes in Montana, edu-rent-increase-notice-mt); and you may not raise rent in retaliation for a protected complaint or union activity. Cities and counties cannot add a parity rule of their own, because Montana bars local regulation of landlords beyond the state landlord-tenant acts.

title: Type Size for Montana Leases
bodyText: Montana sets no minimum point size for a printed lease and no evidence or court rule that penalizes a lease printed in small type. We found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library; Montana's point-size rules are for insurance policies, retail installment and loan contracts, door-to-door and other consumer sales notices and similar documents, not leases. What does apply: Montana's Plain Language in Contracts Act requires a lease form you regularly use with tenants to be printed in type of readable size and in ink that contrasts with the paper, and to be divided into captioned sections (Montana's Plain Language in Contracts Act and Leases, edu-plain-language-contracts-act-mt). A tenant can recover $50 plus actual damages and costs for a noncompliant lease unless you made a good-faith attempt to comply. Keep the generated lease at an ordinary readable size; the cautious course is no smaller than the body text of an ordinary printed document.

title: Time limits to sue; a lease can't shorten them
bodyText:
Time limits to sue in Montana, and a lease can't shorten them. Montana has no special time limit for landlord-tenant or deposit claims; the general limits apply, counted from when the claim arises (when every element exists and the right to sue is complete) to the day the complaint is filed. A claim on a written lease, such as unpaid rent or damages for breach of a signed lease: 6 years (cut from 8 years for actions filed on or after October 1, 2025). A claim on an oral lease or an account: 5 years. A claim for injury to or waste of the property framed as damage rather than breach of the lease: 2 years. A claim under a statute that creates a liability or a penalty (for example the act's holdover or knowing-use penalties): 2 years, unless the statute sets its own period. Personal injury: 3 years. A tenant's suit over a withheld deposit can be filed no sooner than the written denial or the 30-day (or 10-day) refund period; which general period then applies (2 years as a statutory liability, or 6 years on a written lease) is a question only case law settles, so keep deposit records for at least 6 years. A written acknowledgment of the debt signed by the tenant, or any part payment, starts the period running again. Time while the person sued is out of the state and can't be served does not count.

A lease or other contract term that limits the time within which a party may enforce its rights, or bars a party from using the ordinary courts, is void in Montana (an arbitration agreement that the state arbitration act enforces is the one exception for the forum part). So don't add a clause such as "any claim must be brought within one year"; it won't bind the tenant, and a term waiving the tenant's rights under the landlord-tenant act is also unenforceable. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: Liquidated damages
bodyText:
Montana contract law voids any term that fixes in advance the amount of damages for a breach, to the extent it does so, unless the nature of the case would make the actual damage impracticable or extremely difficult to fix; only then may the parties agree an amount that is presumed to be the damage. The statute's text never uses the words "liquidated damages" (only its heading does), so look at any fixed charge triggered by a breach, whatever the lease calls it.

Montana's landlord-tenant act has one rule of its own: if either party ends a fixed-term lease early without cause, the other may recover damages up to 1 month's rent, or an amount agreed in the rental agreement that may not exceed 1 month's rent, and you are also entitled to rent until a new tenancy starts or the term ends, as long as you make reasonable efforts to re-rent.

Otherwise you recover your actual damages for a tenant's breach, trebled if the breach is purposeful, but never trebled for an early termination. We found no Montana statute or rule that expressly lets a landlord keep an agreed damages amount for a tenant's breach in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library.

In practice: keep any late fee near your real cost of late payment, don't use a premium holdover rate, use the library's early-termination option within its one-month cap, and remember that any fee or charge for cleaning and damages is presumed to be a security deposit, whatever it is called.

title: Lockout for unpaid rent
bodyText: Montana does not allow a lockout for unpaid rent, even if the lease says the tenant agrees to one, gives advance notice or offers a key on request. Except after abandonment or surrender, or as the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act itself permits, you may not take back the unit by changing locks, removing the tenant or belongings, or purposefully cutting off heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or other essential services, and the act permits no lockout for nonpayment. A lease clause allowing one would waive the tenant's rights under the act: it can't be enforced, and knowingly using a lease with it can cost you the tenant's actual damages plus up to 3 months' periodic rent. A tenant who is locked out may get back in or end the lease and recover up to the greater of 3 months' periodic rent or treble damages, plus the deposit and prepaid rent. The mobile home lot act has the same bar for park lots. After a 3-day notice for unpaid rent, use the court process; only the sheriff executes a writ of possession. The law-enforcement removal procedure for trespassers doesn't reach a tenant with a rental agreement. See the existing row on self-help eviction (edu-self-help-eviction-mt).

title: Shifting maintenance duties to the tenant
bodyText:
Montana lets you shift some maintenance to the tenant, within limits. Garbage receptacles and removal are your duty unless the rental agreement provides otherwise, so the lease itself can make the tenant responsible for them. You and the tenant may also agree in writing, in good faith and not to evade your obligations, that the tenant will take on garbage removal and the supply of running water, hot water and heat, and do specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodeling.

For specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling, Montana adds conditions: the agreement must be a separate writing signed by both of you and supported by adequate consideration (the statute doesn't say it must be a rent reduction, but something of real value must pass to the tenant), the work can't be work needed to bring the unit up to the building and housing codes, and the agreement can't reduce your duties to other tenants.

The library reads those conditions as applying to every specified task in every kind of dwelling, so for chores such as lawn care, snow removal or filter changes it offers the separate tenant maintenance agreement rather than a lease clause. A court can't find a lease unconscionable just because it states your duty to maintain the premises or the tenant's statutory duties.

title: No Meter Conservation Charge Rule in Montana
bodyText: No Montana statute, and no Public Service Commission rule among those searched, creates an on-bill or per-meter charge that repays energy-efficiency improvements and follows the premises to the next customer, or requires a landlord to tell a tenant or the next customer about one. Montana also has no statute on landlord-submetered water, such as a bar on meter surcharges or a required monthly meter statement. Three related programs work differently. Every customer of a utility or electric cooperative pays a universal system benefits charge, assessed at the meter, that funds conservation, renewable energy and low-income energy assistance; it is part of the ordinary bill, not a debt tied to your building. A regulated electric or gas utility may offer grants and subsidized loans for conservation work in dwellings, but no statute makes such a loan follow the meter. And a city or county may finance energy improvements to a multifamily building of five or more units under the Commercial Property-Assessed Capital Enhancements Act; the repayment is an assessment collected with the property tax that creates a lien running with the property, not a utility-bill charge, and the act sets no tenant rule. If you agree with a tenant to share any such cost, put the amount and its end date in the lease before signing. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws, the Constitution and the held Commission rules; tariffs and court decisions were not.

title: No Military or Airport Zone Disclosure in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no statute requiring a landlord to tell an applicant or tenant that a rental is near a military installation, in a military or airport noise or accident zone, or within any distance of Malmstrom Air Force Base or a missile site, and no statute giving a tenant a right to end a lease for that reason. What Montana has is land-use law. A city or county may designate a military affected area around military facilities (which include military airports, installations, missile sites and launch control centers, but reach no more than 1,200 feet from a launch control center or missile location) and adopt zones, height limits, noise contours and limits on residences and other uses there. Local governments must, and in some cases may, designate airport affected areas around airports, with maps filed with the county clerk and recorder; owners of lots in existing residential subdivisions there are notified, and once an area is designated no one may recover damages from the local government or airport for noise, fumes, vibration or light from normal airport operations. These rules bind owners and builders, not landlords as such. The cautious course: if a rental is in a designated military or airport affected area, or under a regular flight path, tell applicants in writing before they sign, and never answer a direct question misleadingly. Separately, foreign adversaries may not buy, lease or rent property with a direct line of sight to a military installation from a Title 35 entity (see edu-foreign-adversary-mt). Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws, the Constitution and the Montana rules held for this pass.

title: Minors as tenants and as eviction defendants
bodyText:
Age of majority: in Montana a minor is anyone under 18; there is no separate, higher age for signing a lease. A minor may make a contract like anyone else, but can usually disaffirm it (before turning 18 or within a reasonable time after) by giving back what was received. Two limits matter for a lease: a minor who is not under the care of a parent or guardian able to provide for them can't disaffirm a contract to pay the reasonable value of housing, which the statute treats as a necessity; and a minor granted limited emancipation by a court with the right to live independently, choose housing or enter contracts can't disaffirm contracts within that grant. Ask an emancipated minor for the court order and check what it covers.

Filing against a minor: no Montana statute bars an action for possession against a minor tenant, but the court rules treat minors differently. In a justice's or city court case the summons and complaint must be delivered to the minor and to the minor's guardian or guardian ad litem, and mail service with acknowledgment is not available for a minor; in district court a minor over 14 is served personally plus a copy left at home with an adult, and a minor under 14 through a guardian or parent. A minor defends through a guardian, conservator or similar fiduciary, or a guardian ad litem the court appoints. Name every adult occupant who signed the lease separately.

Screening: Montana's fair housing law lists age as a protected characteristic and defines it as years since birth, with no stated exception for minors; maturity or ability to handle responsibility may be considered without reference to age. Whether declining or conditioning a lease because an applicant is under 18 is lawful is not settled by statute, so apply the same objective criteria to every applicant and take advice before treating a minor applicant differently. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws, the court rules printed in the Code and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No nonrefundable deposits
bodyText:
Montana does not allow a nonrefundable security deposit, so there is no nonrefundable-deposit notice to give. Any deposit the lease requires the tenant to give you or keep in place is presumed to be a security deposit, and any fee or charge for cleaning and damage is presumed to be a security deposit no matter what it is called: a "cleaning fee", "pet fee", "move-out fee" or "nonrefundable deposit" is treated the same way. A security deposit may be kept only for the deductions the deposit law lists and must be accounted for in the written list at move-out, and any lease term contrary to the deposit law is invalid.

A charge that is neither a deposit nor for cleaning or damage is different: charges agreed in the lease count as rent. Montana has no rule requiring you to label such a charge nonrefundable, but say plainly in the lease what each one pays for. A property manager of four or more units who takes an application fee must refund it, less itemized costs of services actually performed, if the applicant does not become a tenant.

title: No separate nonrefundable notice
bodyText: Montana has no separate written notice for a nonrefundable deposit, because a nonrefundable deposit is not allowed: any deposit the lease requires, and any cleaning or damage fee however it is labelled, is presumed to be a refundable security deposit, and a lease term contrary to the deposit law is invalid. The only separate written document Montana's deposit law requires is the move-in statement of the property's present condition, signed by you or your agent, which you must give each tenant when you take a deposit.

title: Out-of-state owners: no agent statute; disclose who accepts service
bodyText:
Montana has no special rule for owners who live out of state. No statute requires a nonresident owner to name a Montana agent in each lease or bars the owner from suing until an agent is filed, and a tenant or manager does not withhold state income tax from rent paid to an out-of-state owner.

What does apply to every landlord: before the tenancy starts, you must give the tenant, in writing, the name and address of the person authorized to manage the property and of the owner or a person authorized to act for the owner to receive service of process, notices and demands, and keep that information current (the library's Management and Notices clause does this).

If you don't, whoever signed or manages for you becomes your agent for service of process and notices, and for performing the landlord's duties with the rent collected.

How a nonresident owner is served. Owning property in Montana subjects the owner to Montana courts for claims arising from it. A tenant can serve you personally (in Montana or, if you can't be found here, out of state in the same way), or serve an agent you appointed to receive service.

An LLC or corporation owner is served through an officer, manager, member of a member-managed LLC, managing agent or its registered agent; if none can be found in Montana, service can go through the Secretary of State, and in a case about the property itself a court can allow service by publication. An out-of-state LLC or corporation doing business here must register and keep a registered agent (see the row on court representation).

Reporting: if you hold the property through a partnership, LLC taxed as a partnership or S corporation that reports $1,000 or more of Montana-source income to a nonresident owner, the entity must file a composite return, file the owner's agreement to file and pay Montana tax, or remit tax for that owner. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the court rules printed in it, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set; federal tax reporting is outside this row.

title: Notice-service and eviction fees
bodyText: No Montana statute authorizes, caps or bans a fee charged to a tenant for preparing, posting or serving a notice, or for starting an eviction; we found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library. Montana notices can be given in hand, mailed with a certificate of mailing or by certified mail, or sent by e-mail to an address given in the lease (complete only on a read receipt or a reply that is not automatic), so serving one costs little. A flat notice fee charged because the tenant breached is damages fixed in advance, which Montana voids unless the actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix, and the cost of a notice can be fixed. You don't need a fee clause to recover real losses: the act's remedies are administered so that an aggrieved party recovers appropriate damages, and you may include a reasonable charge for your own labor. Once you sue, attorney fees, costs and necessary disbursements are for the court to award to the prevailing party, whatever the lease says. And any charge the lease makes payable to you counts as rent, so a notice fee would itself become rent due, to be demanded in the next nonpayment notice. The library doesn't offer a notice-service or eviction fee for Montana. A fee limited to your actual cost is not barred by any statute, but whether a court will enforce it is unsettled; a landlord who wants one should take advice before adding their own clause.

title: Termination notices can’t be waived
bodyText:
Default rule: a Montana tenancy ends only by the written notice the statute requires, delivered by a lawful method: 3 days to pay unpaid rent; 14 days for most other lease violations, with a right to cure where the violation can be remedied (3 days for an unauthorized pet, unauthorized occupants or verbal abuse); 5 days for a repeat of the same violation within 6 months, and 3 days for damage to the premises or dangerous activity, without a cure; 30 days to end a month-to-month tenancy and 7 days for week-to-week; and 30 days' written notice before a fixed term ends. Only after the tenancy has ended this way can you bring an action for possession, and you may never lock out or remove the tenant yourself.

Waiver: a lease can't waive or shorten any of these notices or the tenant's right to cure. Montana bars any rental agreement term in which a party agrees to waive or give up rights or remedies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and none of the notice provisions yields to the lease. A clause saying the tenant "waives notice to quit" or agrees to leave on less notice is unenforceable, and knowingly using it can cost you the tenant's actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent. Montana contract law also voids a term letting someone consent to a default judgment for the tenant. You may give more notice than the law requires, and you may agree a default extension period for the end of a fixed term. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No Montana Rule on Work During a Notice to Vacate
bodyText: Montana has no statute aimed at a pending notice to vacate: nothing specifically forbids alterations or work that make a unit uninhabitable while a notice to vacate or an eviction is pending, and nothing adds other terms to such a notice. We found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library. The general rules protect the tenant until the tenancy actually ends: you must keep the premises fit and habitable; you may not recover possession except through the court process, including by purposely cutting heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or other essential services, and a tenant ousted that way may recover possession or end the lease and recover up to 3 months' periodic rent or treble damages, whichever is greater; you may not retaliate against a tenant's protected complaint by decreasing services or bringing a possession action, except where code compliance requires alteration, remodeling or demolition that would effectively deprive the tenant of the unit; and you may enter only on 24 hours' notice at reasonable times and may not use entry to harass. So do not start work that makes the unit unlivable until the tenant has left or a court has ordered possession. What a Montana termination notice must say is in Notices for Lease Violations in Montana (edu-noncompliance-cure-mt).

title: Optional Lease Terms in Montana
bodyText: Montana lets a lease include any term the landlord-tenant act or other law does not prohibit, and several of the act's rules apply only "unless the rental agreement provides otherwise". These are the optional terms the library offers for Montana, each as a clause you may add (none is a default). Montana clauses: End of Term and Extension (lease-end-continuation-mt); E-mail Notices (electronic-notice-mt); Rules and Regulations (rules-mt); Tenant Maintenance Agreement (maintenance-allocation-mt); No Marijuana Cultivation (cannabis-cultivation-mt); Firearms (firearm-discharge-mt); No Dangerous or Criminal Activity (criminal-activity-mt); Landlord's Option to End the Lease After a Fire or Casualty (casualty-termination-mt); Damage Caused by Tenant (tenant-caused-damage-mt); Emergency and Death Contact (tenant-death-contact-mt); Mold Disclosure (mold-disclosure-mt); Residential Use Only (residential-use-only-mt); Early Termination (early-termination-mt). Shared clauses that carry a Montana statutory option: Notice of Extended Absence (extended-absence-notice-ks): notice of an extended absence over 7 days; Guest Policy (14-Day Limit) (guest-policy-day-limit): the guest period; Late Fee (late-fee): a late fee as agreed; Rent Payment (rent-payment): time and place of rent; Utilities Paid by Tenant (utilities-responsibility): garbage removal and utilities allocation. Added in the 2026 topic-gaps review, Montana clauses: Animal Care in Tenant's Absence (animal-care-access-mt); Tenant-Owned Appliances (appliances-excluded-mt); Carpet cleaning (carpet-cleaning-mt); Cold-Weather Precautions (cold-weather-precautions-mt); Shared-Area Lighting on Tenant's Electric Service (common-area-lighting-mt); Tenant-Installed EV Charging System (ev-charger-installation-mt); EV Charger in a Shared Parking Area (ev-charging-shared-area-mt); Hunting, Fishing and Trapping Reserved (hunting-rights-reserved-mt); Furnishings (furnishings-included-mt); Local government fees (government-fee-reimbursement-mt); Guaranty (guaranty-mt); Recorded Environmental Use Restriction (institutional-control-notice-mt); Trying to Resolve Disputes (informal-dispute-resolution-mt); Owner Occupancy Termination (owner-move-in-termination-mt); Entry for Regularly Scheduled Services (scheduled-services-entry-mt); Pool and Spa (pool-use-mt); Electronic Entry (smart-access-mt); Optional Parking Not Included in Rent (unbundled-parking-mt); Utility Allowance with Tenant-Paid Overage (utility-allowance-cap-mt); Shared Water, Sewer and Trash Charges (utility-apportionment-mt); Transfer of Utility Accounts to Tenant (utility-transfer-mt); Tenant Portal (Optional) (tenant-portal-mt); Waterbeds and Liquid-Filled Furniture (waterbed-mt); and shared clauses that apply in Montana as written: The Premises Is an Accessory Dwelling Unit (accessory-dwelling-unit-term-co); Rent Concessions (rent-concession-wi); Rent Paid in Installments (rent-installments-or); Television, Satellite and Internet Service (telecom-access-mn); No Admitting a Barred Person (barred-person-covenant-ne); Authorization for Utility Notices to Landlord (utility-shutoff-notice-authorization-co).
