Lawful options the library does not offer, each explained in its own row: a contract interest rate on unpaid amounts (edu-legal-interest-mt); a premium holdover rate (edu-holdover-rate-mt); a rent escalation in a fixed term (edu-rent-increase-notice-mt); rent escalation (gaps pass) (edu-rent-escalation-mt); a property-tax or insurance pass-through (edu-tax-escalation-mt); authority for a death contact to remove belongings (edu-tenant-death-mt); a collection fee (edu-no-collection-fee-rule-mt); a notice-service fee (edu-no-notice-service-fee-mt); a separate deposit-installment clause (edu-no-deposit-installments-mt); a designated repairer for tenant repairs (edu-no-designated-repairer-rule-mt); a separate fire-code clause (edu-fire-code-standard-mt); a cooling-equipment clause (edu-no-portable-cooling-rule-mt); a portable solar clause (edu-no-portable-solar-right-mt); a sex-offender registry sentence (edu-sex-offender-disclosure-mt); a smoke-drift acknowledgment (edu-no-smoke-drift-waiver-mt); a voluntary sprinkler statement (edu-no-sprinkler-disclosure-mt); a life-tenant status clause (edu-no-usufructuary-lessor-mt); texts as an extra copy of notices (edu-actual-notice-method-mt); a planned utility shutoff clause (edu-utility-interruption-submeter-mt); force-placed renter's insurance (edu-renters-insurance-rules-mt); and an option to purchase the property, below. You may add your own clause for any of these after taking advice. Terms Montana bars are listed in Lease Terms Montana Prohibits (edu-prohibited-terms-mt). Option to purchase: a lease with an option to purchase a home of one to four units (or an individually owned unit) is a contract under Montana's seller disclosure law, so as seller you must give the tenant a written disclosure statement of the adverse material facts you actually know, before or when the option is signed; the tenant may waive it in the offer, and if you deliver it late the tenant may rescind within 3 days unless you agreed otherwise in writing. Montana has no separate lease-option or rent-to-own statute for homes (no early-exercise, cure or option-payment rules). The library does not offer an option-to-purchase clause, because an option is a real estate sale contract that needs its own terms and the seller disclosure; you may add one after taking advice. This covers the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Shared-Meter Disclosure in Montana
bodyText: Montana has none of the three California lease disclosures grouped under this topic. First, no statute requires a landlord to tell a tenant about a former military ordnance or training site nearby. Former military training sites that may be contaminated with hazardous wastes or explosive ordnance count as military facilities under the state's military-area zoning law, so a local government may zone around them, but that creates no landlord duty. Second, no statute requires notice to applicants or tenants before you apply for a permit to demolish a rental. You end a month-to-month tenancy with at least 30 days' written notice (7 days for week-to-week) and a fixed-term lease at its end, and Montana has no just-cause rule; a demolition needed to comply with a building or housing code is one ground on which a possession action is not treated as retaliation. Third, no statute requires a disclosure that a tenant's gas or electric meter serves areas outside the unit. For electricity, most buildings started or rewired since 1981 must have individual meters, with narrow exceptions, and shared water, sewer or trash charges are a matter for the lease (see edu-utility-apportionment-mt and utility-apportionment-mt). The cautious course: tell applicants in writing about a planned demolition or a meter that serves other areas before they sign, and state any shared-meter charge in the lease. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws, the Constitution and the Montana rules held for this pass.

title: Elevators and Other Building Facilities in Montana
bodyText: Montana's landlord-tenant act requires you to keep in good and safe working order all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning systems and the other facilities and appliances, including elevators, that you supply or must supply (the library's Maintenance & Repairs clause, landlord-maintenance-mt), and the tenant must use them in a reasonable manner. Elevators and similar equipment carry their own state law. If your building has an elevator, escalator, dumbwaiter, platform lift or stairway chairlift, the owner or lessee of the equipment must register it with the Department of Labor and Industry, make sure it is inspected every year (every 2 years for a freight elevator) by the department or a licensed elevator inspector, and make sure the periodic tests the department requires are done by a licensed elevator contractor using a licensed elevator mechanic. Installation or alteration needs a permit and a licensed elevator contractor. Knowingly violating these rules is a misdemeanor and can be stopped by court order. The elevator law does not apply to private residences or farm and ranch operations; it does not say whether a rented single-family house counts as a private residence, so check with the department before relying on that exemption. Montana has no consumer-protection or product-safety statute putting a duty on landlords for other building facilities such as automatic garage door openers or gates. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set. The department's elevator rules (including any rule on posting the inspection certificate) and the building codes Montana adopts by reference are not in that set and were not read.

title: Owner Move-In in Montana
bodyText:
Montana has no statute that gives, requires or limits a landlord's right to end a tenancy so the owner or a family member can move in, and no minimum time the owner must then live there. Month-to-month or week-to-week: you may end the tenancy without a reason on at least 30 days' written notice (7 days for week-to-week); no move-in reason is needed (Ending a Month-to-Month or Week-to-Week Tenancy, periodic-tenancy-notice-mt).

Fixed term: Montana's act says that if either party ends a lease without cause before the end of the term, the other party is entitled to damages of up to one month's rent, or an amount agreed in the lease that may not exceed one month's rent. No statute or case we found says whether a landlord can recover possession mid-term without a lease term reserving the right, so the cautious course is to reserve it in the lease with the library's optional Owner Occupancy Termination clause (owner-move-in-termination-mt).

Ending a fixed term to move in is still a termination without cause, so your liability to the tenant for ending early is capped at one month's rent; the clause sets the agreed amount you will pay, more than nothing and not more than one month's rent.

Limits that still apply: use the right in good faith; the tenant owes rent only to the termination date and gets the deposit back under the deposit rules; a possession action brought within 6 months after a tenant's protected complaint is presumed retaliatory; and if the tenant does not leave you must go to court. The statutory holdover penalty (up to 3 months' periodic rent or treble damages) applies to a fixed term only where you ended it with cause, so it does not apply here.

This covers the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: Parking Rules and Towing Notice in Montana
bodyText:
Montana has no statute specific to parking rules at rentals (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library, including the tow truck laws and the Department of Justice tow truck rules).

There is no required parking section or heading in a lease, no rule that the lease state whether parking is provided or what it costs, no ban on adding or changing a parking charge mid-lease as such, no limit on the vehicle information you may ask for, no rule that a parking permit run with the lease, and no posted notice or waiting period before a vehicle at a rental is towed for expired registration. Montana's general rules statute governs parking rules.

A parking rule is enforceable against a tenant only if its purpose is the convenience, safety or welfare of the occupants, protecting your property from abusive use or fairly distributing facilities held out for tenants generally; it is reasonably related to that purpose; it applies to all occupants fairly; it is explicit enough to tell the tenant what to do; it is not meant to evade your obligations; and the tenant had notice of it when entering into the lease or when it was adopted.

Rules must be in writing and given to each tenant and to each new tenant on arrival. A rule adopted after the tenant signs that substantially modifies the tenant's bargain (for example, taking away a space or adding a charge) is not valid until 7 days after written notice in a week-to-week tenancy or 30 days after written notice in a month-to-month tenancy; the library's rules clause makes such a change binding during a fixed term only if the tenant agrees in writing. A parking charge agreed in the lease is rent under Montana's definition.

**Towing.** No Montana statute regulates a landlord's towing of a vehicle from private residential parking, requires signs before such a tow, or says who may authorize it; the tow truck laws govern tow trucks' equipment, insurance, inspection and the law-enforcement rotation, not tows from private lots.

A vehicle abandoned 5 days or more on private property may be taken into custody by the sheriff, city police or tribal law enforcement at the request of the owner or person in lawful possession or control of the property, and its last registered owner is presumed liable for the removal and storage costs. A city or county may by ordinance let a private parking service (parking offered to the general public for pay) impound vehicles, but never by booting. Check local ordinances before you tow.

The library's clauses are rules-mt, parking-vehicle-rules and assigned-parking-space; towing is also covered in edu-towing-mt.

title: Rights a Montana lease can’t waive
bodyText:
Montana's non-waiver rule covers the whole Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, not one part of it. A rental agreement may not provide that either party agrees to waive or give up rights or remedies under the act. Such a term is unenforceable, and a party who purposefully uses a lease containing terms it knows are prohibited owes the other side its actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent. The same rule applies to mobile home lot rentals, and the security deposit law has its own rule voiding any contrary lease term or tenant waiver.

Two things are not waivers. First, where the act itself lets the agreement decide (where and when rent is paid, the length of a periodic tenancy, garbage removal, the guest period, a default extension period, an agreed early-termination amount of no more than one month's rent), the lease can set the term. Second, after a dispute arises the parties may settle and give up a claim, although a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable settlement. Montana has no special rule for a home sold and leased back to the seller; the seller who stays on as a tenant is covered by the act like any other tenant, so the general rule applies to that lease. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No Scheduled-Services Entry Exception in Montana
bodyText:
Montana has no exception that lets you enter for regularly scheduled services, such as pest treatment or filter changes, without notice, even if the lease states the right conspicuously.

For every entry other than an emergency, you must give the tenant at least 24 hours' notice of your intent to enter (posting it conspicuously on the main entry door counts) and enter only at reasonable times, and a lease cannot shorten that notice or waive it, because Montana's entry notice rule has no exception for an agreement and the landlord-tenant act voids a lease term waiving a tenant's rights.

No statute or case we found says whether a schedule given at signing counts as notice for each later visit, so the cautious course is a separate notice before each visit.

What a lease can do is list the services the tenant agrees to, so that the tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry to supply them, and set a reasonable time window: the library's optional Entry for Regularly Scheduled Services clause (scheduled-services-entry-mt) does this and keeps the 24-hour notice for each visit (Landlord's Entry in Montana, edu-landlord-entry-mt).

This covers the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: Pest Control and Pesticide Notice in Montana
bodyText:
Montana has no statute requiring a landlord to notify tenants before pest control treatment of a unit or common area, or to give tenants a pesticide warning or disclosure. Three rules come close. First, your own entry to treat, or a pest control operator's entry on your behalf, needs at least 24 hours' notice and must be at a reasonable time, except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable.

Second, a city or county may adopt an ordinance requiring licensed commercial applicators to post a sign when they apply a pesticide, including, for an interior application, at each public access to the treated property; once posted, neither the applicator nor the property owner or manager may remove the sign until the pesticide is dry or the label's reentry interval has passed, whichever is later.

Spot treatments under 100 square feet and some products are exempt, and a local government may not require more than the state law allows. Third, for a building owned or leased by a public agency and open to the public, such as a dormitory, the building operator must post a notice at each access before an indoor pesticide treatment (baits, pastes and gels, disinfectants and retail home-use products excepted) and keep application records for 2 years.

Anyone in the business of applying pesticides for others must hold a state applicator's license. The cautious course: tell tenants in writing which pests will be treated, when, with what product, and any preparation or reentry instructions, and keep the posted signs up as required.

Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws, the Constitution and the Montana rules held for this pass.

title: No Pet and Eviction Fact Sheet in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no requirement to give a tenant a state fact sheet or any other written information about pets and eviction, whether or not you know the tenant has a dog or cat, and the state publishes no such form. We found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library. What governs pets instead: the lease sets which pets are allowed and any pet deposit or pet rent (the library's Pets clause, pet-policy-mt; Pet Deposits and Pet Rent in Montana, edu-pet-deposit-mt). If a tenant keeps an unauthorized pet, you may give a written noncompliance notice with a 3-day period instead of the usual 14 days; if the tenant removes the pet before the date in the notice, the lease does not end. An emotional support animal or a service animal requested by a tenant with a disability is not a pet and is handled as a reasonable accommodation (Service and Emotional Support Animals in Montana, edu-assistance-animals-mt).

title: Montana's Plain Language in Contracts Act and Leases
bodyText: Montana's Plain Language in Contracts Act applies to a lease form you prepare in advance and give a tenant to sign, if you regularly rent out property and the tenant is an individual renting a home for personal, family or household use. The lease must be written in plain language, which the Act defines as: clear and coherent, using words with common and everyday meanings; divided into sections with captions; printed in type of readable size; and in ink that contrasts with the paper. Wording a statute, rule, court decision or government agency requires, and a legal description of the property, are not violations. If the lease does not comply, a tenant who signed it may recover $50 plus actual damages and court costs. You are not liable if you made a good-faith attempt to comply, a tenant cannot sue after the tenant's obligations under the lease are scheduled to end or if a lawyer represented the tenant at signing, a class action is capped at $10,000 plus actual damages, and noncompliance does not void the lease or excuse the tenant from paying rent or performing. The tenant cannot waive these rights. The Act does not cover a contract where the value of the property leased exceeds $50,000, or "a transfer of real estate". It does not say how a lease's value is measured or whether a lease counts as a transfer of real estate, so the cautious course is to treat every residential lease as covered. Montana's Act has no readability score, no required statement listing the tenant's waivers, and no Attorney General preapproval process. Separately, at the end of a tenancy you must give the tenant a plain and understandable notice of the rules for property left behind (edu-abandoned-property-notice-mt). This covers the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No Montana Rule on Political Canvassing at Rentals
bodyText: Montana has no statute that requires you to let candidates, campaign workers, petition circulators or voter-registration workers into an apartment building or other rental property to reach tenants' doors, or that forbids you to (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library). Access by outsiders to common areas is your decision as owner under general trespass law: a person may be told to leave and, if the person stays or returns, may be trespassing. But a tenant may invite a candidate or campaigner as the tenant's own guest, and a person with a tenant's verified permission is authorized to be there, so do not try to stop tenants from inviting someone in. Political signs are covered separately in edu-political-signs-mt: Montana's sign statute stops homeowners' associations and other private entities from banning campaign and ballot-issue signs on property whose owner authorizes them (they may still limit size, location and timing), which protects your choice as owner rather than giving a tenant a sign right against you, so set any sign rules in the lease. Montana's Constitution says no person, firm or corporation shall discriminate against anyone in the exercise of civil or political rights because of political or religious ideas; how far that reaches a private landlord is not settled. Cautious course: if you limit soliciting or canvassing in common areas, put the rule in writing, give it to every tenant, and apply it the same way to every candidate, campaign and cause; do not treat tenants differently because of their political views.

title: Pools and Hot Tubs at Montana Rentals
bodyText:
Montana has no statute or state rule that puts a pool fence, barrier, alarm or lease safety-notice duty on a residential landlord as such (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library). Two other laws reach pools at rentals.

**Public pool law.** Montana regulates every "public swimming pool", which includes spas and hot tubs, unless it is on private property and used only by the owner, the owner's family or their invited guests (the exception also covers common-area pools of owner-occupied condominiums).

A pool or spa at an apartment complex or other multi-unit rental that tenants may use is therefore a public pool: you need an annual license from the Department of Public Health and Human Services, must operate it in a sanitary and safe manner, keep the records the department requires, and follow the department's pool rules.

A privately owned public pool needs no lifeguard only if a sign saying "No lifeguard is on duty" (or words of substantially the same meaning) is prominently displayed and one person per shift who is currently certified in CPR is on the premises and accessible to the pool. Operating without meeting the law is a misdemeanor and a public nuisance. A private home rented to guests by the day or week that offers a spa must post the same no-lifeguard sign.

**Single-family rental.** Whether a pool or hot tub at a single rented house is a public pool is not settled. The exception names only the owner, the owner's family and their invited guests, not a tenant, so a literal reading could bring a tenant-used pool under the license law; the opposing reading is that a pool rented with a private home is still a private pool.

Cautious course: before a tenant uses a pool or hot tub at a single-family rental, ask the local health department or the Department of Public Health and Human Services whether it needs a license.

**Construction and upkeep.** The state building code adopts the International Swimming Pool and Spa Code (with chapters 7 through 10 deleted) for pool and spa construction; its text, including any barrier provisions, was not read for this library. A pool you supply is part of the premises: keep it and its gates, fences, covers and equipment in good and safe working order and keep the pool area safe. A lease can't excuse you from liability for your own negligence. The library's optional pool rules clause is pool-use-mt. If the pool belongs to a condominium or other association, the association, not you, holds any license.

title: No Cooling-Device Rule in Montana
bodyText: Montana gives tenants no right to install a portable or window air conditioner, evaporative cooler or other cooling device, and no statute limits a lease term that restricts them or requires a lease to mention them. Montana also does not require landlords to provide cooling: the heat duty runs only from October 1 to May 1. If you supply air conditioning or other cooling equipment, you must keep it in good and safe working order, and the tenant must use it reasonably. So you may allow, condition or refuse a tenant's cooling unit. The library's No Alterations clause already requires your written consent for installations, and the Use of Property clause bars fastening things to the property without consent; both defer to any right the law gives the tenant. One such right does exist: a tenant with a disability may ask to make a reasonable modification at the tenant's own expense, or for a reasonable accommodation, where it is necessary for full use of the home, and you may, where reasonable, require the tenant to restore the interior afterward. A separate cooling-equipment clause is lawful in Montana (other states' versions list the landlord's equipment and set mounting and electrical rules); the library does not offer a Montana one because the two shared clauses already cover consent, and you may add your own after taking advice. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws, the Constitution and the Montana rules held for this pass.

title: No Tenant Solar-Device Right in Montana
bodyText: Montana gives tenants no right to install a solar panel, plug-in or balcony solar device, or battery system, and no statute voids or limits a lease term or a homeowners' association covenant that restricts one. The state's solar easement law only says how a written easement for a solar device's sun exposure is created and recorded; it gives a tenant nothing. Neither local governments nor the state building code may require buildings to be built with solar panels or solar wiring or batteries, which also gives tenants no right. A tenant-installed system that operates in parallel with the utility and is meant to offset the tenant's own use is a net metering system, which must include, at the customer-generator's expense, all equipment needed to meet the electrical, safety and interconnection requirements, and the utility's interconnection rules apply. So you may allow, condition or refuse a tenant's solar device. The library's No Alterations clause already requires your written consent for installations, and the Use of Property clause bars fastening things to the property without consent; both defer to any right the law gives the tenant, and a tenant with a disability may still ask for a reasonable modification. A separate solar-device clause is lawful (other states' versions add equipment, electrician and utility-approval terms); the library does not offer a Montana one because the shared clauses cover consent, and you may add your own after taking advice. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws, the Constitution and the Montana rules held for this pass.

title: Unit-Count Thresholds in Montana Law
bodyText: Montana's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies the same way to a landlord with one unit or a thousand: it has no small-landlord exemption and no duty that grows with the size of your portfolio, and Montana has no limit on investors buying single-family homes (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library). A handful of other laws turn on unit counts. Property managers. A person who leases no more than four residential units is exempt from the property manager license (as are owners and relatives managing family property, among others). A property manager of four or more dwelling units who charges an application fee must refund it, less itemized out-of-pocket costs, if the applicant does not become a tenant (edu-application-fee-mt). Fair housing. Montana's Human Rights Act does not apply to renting no more than three sleeping rooms in a single-family home the owner lives in, and its age and familial-status rules do not apply where the owner lives in one unit of a building for no more than two families. Both exemptions need both parts (owner residence and the size limit). Montana has no exemption based on how many houses you own: federal law exempts some owners of three or fewer single-family houses and owner-occupied buildings of up to four units, but those owners remain covered by Montana law. New buildings of four or more units must meet accessibility design rules (all units if there is an elevator, otherwise ground-floor units). For blind, deaf and service-animal access, renting out a single room in a family home is excluded. Construction liens. A contractor or supplier must ordinarily give the owner notice of the right to claim a lien within 20 days after first furnishing work (45 days on some lender-financed jobs), or the lien is limited. That notice is not required for work on a dwelling for five or more families or on an improvement that is partly or wholly commercial, so the owner of a larger building can face a lien without advance warning; keep track of subcontractors and suppliers and get lien releases before paying. Buildings. The state building code may not require fire sprinklers in a single-family home or a building of no more than two units; the energy code is enforced by the state for buildings of five or more units; and low-pressure heating boilers in apartments of six or fewer families are exempt from state boiler inspections.

title: No possession bond for landlords
bodyText:
No possession bond: Montana has no statute giving a landlord a bond for possession at the end of a term, and a lease or bond can't do it by contract either: a term letting anyone confess judgment against the tenant, or act as the tenant's agent to confess judgment or consent to a default, is void, and a confession-of-judgment term in a rental agreement is also a barred term that can cost you a penalty if used knowingly. Recover possession through an action for possession after a lawful termination.

Bonds and undertakings that do exist on the tenant's side: (1) the hearing deadline in a possession case can be extended past the statutory limit if you and the tenant agree, and no undertaking is needed for that; (2) a tenant who appeals a justice's, city or municipal court judgment for possession can stop the writ only by filing a written undertaking, with two or more sureties, promising not to commit waste and to pay the value of use and occupation (up to a sum the court fixes), or a cash deposit; you can waive it in writing, and the district court must waive it for a tenant found indigent; (3) in a nonpayment case the court may order rent paid into court while a counterclaim is decided.

The older forcible-entry and unlawful-detainer chapter's continuance undertaking (the defendant who asks for a continuance must secure damages and rent) applies only to occupancies outside the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws, the court rules printed in the Code and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: Private Wells at Montana Rentals
bodyText: Montana has no statute or state rule requiring a landlord to test a private well that serves a rental, to give a tenant test results, or to notify a tenant about well water quality (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library; the Department of Environmental Quality's drinking water rules were not in that set). Size matters, though. A water system that has at least 15 service connections, or that regularly serves at least 25 people daily for 60 or more days a year, is a public water supply system, whether it draws from a community well or another source. A well serving an apartment complex, a mobile home park or a group of rentals that large makes you a supplier of water regulated by the Department of Environmental Quality: plans must be approved before the system is built or changed, the water must meet maximum contaminant levels, and the department's monitoring, reporting and public notice rules apply, including notice to all users when the system violates the rules. For a smaller well, your landlord-tenant duties govern: supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times, keep the plumbing and water system you supply in good and safe working order, and keep the unit fit and habitable. Cautious course: have the well water tested by a certified laboratory before each new tenancy and periodically, keep the results, fix any contamination, and tell the tenant promptly if you learn the water is unsafe to drink.

title: What a Montana Tenant May Not Do
bodyText: Montana law itself lists what a tenant may not do, and the library's Montana lease already carries each item as a lease term. (1) Damage: a tenant may not destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises or permit anyone to do so; the statute has no intent or negligence requirement. You may end the lease on 3 days' written notice specifying the damage (Tenant Maintenance & Cleanliness, tenant-maintenance; Damage Caused by Tenant, tenant-caused-damage-mt). (2) Dangerous activity: a tenant may not engage in, or knowingly allow, activity that creates a reasonable potential of damage to the premises or injury to neighbors, such as drug manufacture, a clandestine lab or gang activity; 3 days' written notice (No Dangerous or Criminal Activity, criminal-activity-mt). (3) Disturbance: a tenant must behave, and make guests behave, so as not to disturb neighbors' peaceful enjoyment (No Disturbance or Nuisance, no-disturbance). (4) Entry and locks: a tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry to inspect, repair, supply services or show the unit, and may not remove, replace or add a lock without your written permission and must give you a key; for a refusal you may give a 24-hour notice to correct and then a 3-day notice to terminate (Landlord's Entry, landlords-access-mt). (5) Use: the tenant must use the unit only as a dwelling unless you agree otherwise, follow your valid written rules, and use each room and the facilities reasonably (Residential Use Only, residential-use-only-mt; Rules and Regulations, rules-mt). Other violations follow the 14-day notice to cure (Notices for Lease Violations in Montana, edu-noncompliance-cure-mt). You may also recover actual damages for any violation, and treble damages if it was purposeful (except for leaving early). Montana's Tenant's Statutory Duties row (edu-tenant-statutory-duties-mt) lists the tenant's affirmative duties.

title: Promises to repair
bodyText: Montana has no statute or rule requiring a landlord's promise to clean, repair or improve the unit to be in writing, to carry a completion date, or to be made before the lease is signed; we found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library. Montana's consumer protection act has no list of specific practices such as a "false promise". It bans unfair or deceptive acts or practices in trade or commerce in general terms, and trade and commerce include offering and distributing real property, so a repair promise made to get a tenant to sign and never meant to be kept could be challenged under it; real estate licensees who manage rentals can also be disciplined for false promises. A promise written into the rental agreement binds you like any other term: you must deliver possession in compliance with the rental agreement, and the tenant may recover actual damages and get an injunction for your failure to comply with it. Cautious course: write every promised repair or improvement, with a completion date, into the lease or a signed addendum, and don't make oral promises, which the lease's entire-agreement clause may leave out but which can still feed a deception claim.

title: No Chemical Exposure Warning Rule in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no counterpart to California's Proposition 65: no statute requires a landlord, or any business, to post or give a warning that a building or product exposes people to chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm. Montana's hazardous chemical information act applies to employers and their workplaces (chemical lists, safety data sheets and labels for employees, and emergency planning information), not to tenants. The contamination rules that do reach rentals are the meth and fentanyl notice and known mold (see edu-hazardous-contamination-disclosure-mt), and federal lead-based paint disclosure applies to housing built before 1978. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws, the Constitution and the Montana rules held for this pass.

title: No Property-Tax Share of Rent Statement in Montana
bodyText: Montana does not require you to tell a tenant what share of the rent goes to property taxes, whether yearly, when rent changes or on request, and the Department of Revenue has no power under the statutes we found to make you certify the rent you received. We found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library. Montana's renter property tax relief works without a landlord statement: under the elderly homeowner and renter credit, a renter aged 62 or older with gross household income under $45,000 who lived in Montana at least 9 months of the year and rented for at least 6 months may claim a credit based on a "rent-equivalent tax" that the law fixes at 15% of the gross rent actually paid, reduced on a sliding scale by household income. The renter must file a receipt showing the gross rent paid with the claim, and supplies any further information the department asks for. No credit is allowed for a dwelling that is not subject to Montana property taxes (except county or city housing authority housing) or for rent paid through a public rent subsidy, and the department may adjust the rent if you and the tenant did not deal at arm's length. Montana has no landlord-specific rent-receipt rule, but its general law entitles a tenant who pays rent to a written receipt on request (Mont. Code Ann. § 28-1-1111), and a tenant who may qualify will need proof of the rent paid, so the cautious course is to give a written statement of the total rent received for the year when an older tenant asks. This covers the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: Asking About Protected Characteristics in Montana
bodyText: Montana bars asking about a protected characteristic only when the question is asked to discriminate. It is unlawful to inquire into the sex, marital status, race, creed, religion, age, familial status, physical or mental disability, color or national origin of a person seeking to rent for the purpose of discriminating on any of those grounds. Montana has no broader ban on asking about, or keeping records of, protected characteristics in housing, and no rule on what a rental application may contain (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library). Two narrower rules apply. When a tenant asks to keep an emotional support animal, you may not request information that discloses the diagnosis or severity of the tenant's disability or any medical records about it, although the tenant may volunteer them. And any notice, statement or advertisement that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination on a protected ground is itself unlawful, so an application question that signals a preference can be a violation even if you never act on it. Federal fair housing rules separately restrict asking applicants whether they have a disability. Cautious course: ask only what your written screening criteria and the lease need, and ask it of everyone (for example, the names of all occupants, including children, to apply the occupancy limit; age only to confirm an adult signer or to run qualifying housing for older persons); ask about disability only in response to a request for an accommodation, and then only what Montana's support-animal statute and federal law allow; and keep anything you learn out of your decision. The Act's narrow exemptions (such as renting no more than three sleeping rooms in the home you live in) are covered in edu-children-occupancy-mt and edu-fair-housing-mt.

title: No Montana Statute Voiding a Lease for Unlawful Use
bodyText: No Montana statute makes a lease void, voidable or automatically ended because the tenant uses the premises for a prohibited purpose, such as gambling, prostitution, drug activity or a nuisance. We found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library. What governs instead: unless otherwise agreed, the tenant must occupy the unit only as a dwelling, and the library's Residential Use Only clause (residential-use-only-mt) bars any illegal use; activity that creates a reasonable potential of damage to the premises or injury to neighbors (including drug manufacture, clandestine labs and gang activity) lets you end the lease on 3 days' written notice (No Dangerous or Criminal Activity, criminal-activity-mt); other lease violations follow the 14-day notice (Notices for Lease Violations in Montana, edu-noncompliance-cure-mt). Two rules reach you as owner. It is the crime of sex trafficking to knowingly lease or let a place you control be regularly used for prostitution, or to fail to make a reasonable effort to stop that use by ejecting the tenant, notifying law enforcement or other lawful means. And premises found to be a public nuisance (including a place where people gather to engage in unlawful conduct) or an alcohol nuisance can be closed by court order for up to a year, with any reopening on a bond; the possessor who permits the nuisance can be enjoined (Nuisance and Disturbance in Montana Rentals, edu-nuisance-mt). So if you learn of such a use, act through the lease's termination notices and the courts, and notify law enforcement where prostitution is involved. This covers the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No Recycling Notice Rule in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no statute requiring a landlord to tell tenants where and how to recycle, or to provide recycling service at a rental. You must, unless the rental agreement provides otherwise, provide and maintain appropriate receptacles for garbage, rubbish and other waste and arrange for its removal, and the tenant must dispose of waste in a clean and safe manner; recycling is not separately required. Local governments may not regulate or tax bags, cups, bottles and similar containers, but that limit does not reach curbside recycling programs or designated residential recycling locations, so a city or hauler program may apply to your property; check locally. If you offer recycling, the lease rules (rules-mt) are the place to say what goes where. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws, the Constitution and the Montana rules held for this pass.

title: No right to redeem after notice or judgment
bodyText:
Before termination: a tenant who gets a 3-day nonpayment notice saves the tenancy by paying the rent due within the 3 days. If you accept full payment of the rent due afterwards, you waive the nonpayment as a ground for termination; accepting a partial payment waives nothing.

After the notice period or a judgment: Montana gives a residential tenant no right to redeem the tenancy by paying the arrears late, whether before the hearing, after judgment or before the writ is executed. Once the 3 days pass without payment you may terminate, and if you win possession the court issues the writs immediately. You are free to accept the money and let the tenant stay, but you don't have to; if you take full payment of the rent due, treat the nonpayment as waived. In the case itself the tenant can counterclaim for amounts owed under the lease or the Act, and if no rent remains due after the counterclaim is applied, judgment for possession goes to the tenant; the court may also order rent paid into court.

Occupancies outside the Act: the older unlawful-detainer chapter, which applies only to occupancies the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act excludes, still lets a tenant (or a subtenant or mortgagee of the term) pay the rent found due, with interest, damages and costs, within 5 days after a nonpayment judgment on an unexpired lease and be restored to the tenancy. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No Montana Religious Display Rule
bodyText: Montana gives tenants no statutory right to display religious or cultural items (for example a mezuzah on the doorframe, a wreath, a prayer flag or a holiday display) and has no statute limiting a landlord's display rules as such (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library). Montana's sign statute protects only political campaign and ballot-issue signs, and only an owner's choice (edu-political-signs-mt). Two rules shape any limit you set. First, Montana's Human Rights Act bars discrimination in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental because of creed, religion or national origin, so a rule that allows some displays but not those of a particular faith or culture, or is enforced that way, is risky; federal fair housing law is to the same effect. Second, any rule must apply to all occupants in a fair manner, must be in writing and given to every tenant, and a new rule that substantially changes a tenant's bargain mid-lease needs 7 or 30 days' written notice (and, under the library's rules clause, the tenant's agreement during a fixed term). Montana's Constitution also bars any person, firm or corporation from discriminating in the exercise of civil or political rights because of culture or religious ideas; how far that reaches a private landlord is not settled. Cautious course: keep display rules content-neutral (size, placement, safety, no damage to doors or walls, no blocking exits or hallways), allow small items on the tenant's own door or doorframe, apply the rules the same way to every faith and culture, and treat a small mounting hole as ordinary wear rather than damage.

title: No demand needed before rent is late
bodyText:
Default rule: Montana does not require you to ask for rent, or send a reminder, before rent is late. Rent is payable without demand or notice on the date and at the place the lease sets (or, if the lease is silent, at your address or by electronic transfer to the account you designate, at the start of each month).

Before you can end the tenancy for unpaid rent, though, you must give the tenant the 3-day written notice of nonpayment and of your intention to terminate if the rent is not paid within that time; that notice is the only notice the statute requires, and the tenancy ends only if the tenant does not pay within the 3 days.

For the few occupancies the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act does not cover (for example employee housing conditional on employment, or primarily agricultural occupancy), the older unlawful-detainer chapter applies instead, and its 3-day notice must require payment and state the amount due. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: Rent escalation clauses
bodyText: A Montana lease may lawfully provide for rent changes during a fixed term, such as a schedule of stated increases, an index adjustment, or a right to raise rent on notice: the landlord-tenant act lets the parties agree terms including rent. Montana sets no cap, frequency limit or notice period for such a change; we found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library, and no state or local rent control applies. The library doesn't offer a rent-escalation clause for Montana, for three reasons. Montana has no exception from its retaliation rule for increases under a lease clause: you may not raise rent to retaliate for a tenant's code complaint, written repair complaint or union activity, a complaint within 6 months before an increase is presumed to be the reason, and the penalty is up to the greater of 3 months' periodic rent or treble damages. A clause letting you set a new rent on notice may be challenged as indefinite or unconscionable, and no Montana statute or rule settles it. And a month-to-month tenancy already lets you change rent by written notice served at least 15 days before the end of a month. A fixed term's rent otherwise can't change unless the lease provides for it. A landlord who wants an escalation clause can add their own after taking advice; the library offers no rent-escalation or tax and insurance pass-through clause for Montana (see edu-tax-escalation-mt). See edu-rent-increase-notice-mt.

title: Rent not free of the duty to maintain
bodyText: A Montana rental agreement, or any document related to it, may not let you collect rent free of your duty to maintain the premises; the mobile home lot act has the same rule. Montana's version names only the rental agreement and documents related to it: unlike the uniform act, it doesn't list assignments, conveyances, trust deeds or security instruments, and we found no other Montana provision that does in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library. Two related rules still apply. A lease can't make the tenant waive rights or remedies under the act, including the repair remedies. And if you or the person who signs leases for you don't disclose in writing who manages the premises and who receives notices and demands for the owner, the person who signed for you becomes an agent for performing the landlord's obligations under the act and the lease, and must spend or make available for that purpose all rent collected from the premises; that duty also binds any successor landlord, owner or manager. Accepting rent is a separate question: accepting full payment of the rent due waives only a claimed breach for nonpayment of rent, and accepting part of the rent waives nothing.

title: Rent reporting to credit bureaus
bodyText: Montana has no rent-reporting law: no rule that a landlord must offer to report on-time rent to credit bureaus, no rule that a landlord must warn a tenant before reporting late rent, no state rent-reporting program, and no rule for or against requiring a tenant to enroll in one. We found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library. If you choose to report rent payments, Montana's consumer reporting law makes anyone who gives a credit bureau false information, or gives information with malice or a willful intent to injure the tenant, liable to be sued, so report only accurate, current information and correct errors promptly. Federal credit-reporting law also places accuracy and dispute duties on anyone who furnishes information to a credit bureau. Any charge for a reporting service you agree with the tenant is part of the rent under Montana's act, so put it in the rental agreement.

title: Renter's Insurance Requirements in Montana
bodyText:
Montana has no statute or rule on a landlord requiring renter's insurance: none lets the tenant choose the carrier, sets a deadline for proof of coverage, governs force-placed coverage or an administrative fee, or requires a written statement that you do not insure the tenant's belongings or a flood notice before signing.

Requiring renter's insurance is a lawful lease term, and the library's Tenant's Property & Renter's Insurance clause (tenants-property-insurance-ks-oh-ca) states that your insurance does not cover the tenant's property and requires the tenant to carry property and liability coverage and show proof on request. Three terms to avoid.

(1) A waiver of subrogation, in which the tenant (or the tenant's insurer) gives up claims against you for losses your own negligence causes: Montana bars any lease term by which a party agrees to the exculpation or limitation of liability for the other party's negligence, so treat it as barred, whether one-sided or mutual. Such a term is unenforceable, and knowingly using it can cost you the tenant's actual damages plus up to 3 months' periodic rent.

(2) Requiring the tenant to name you as an additional insured on the tenant's liability policy: no Montana statute or case we found decides whether that is a forbidden shift of liability for your own negligence onto the tenant, so the cautious course is not to require it. Asking to be listed as an interested party who is notified if the policy is cancelled is a safer alternative.

(3) Buying coverage for the tenant and charging for it if the tenant does not show proof: no statute authorizes or limits it, and arranging a policy for a tenant for money can amount to selling insurance, which needs an insurance producer license. The library does not offer a force-placed coverage clause for these reasons; you may add your own after taking advice.

This covers the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No repair-cost termination right
bodyText: Montana has no statute that lets you, or the tenant, end a lease because repairs would cost too much compared with the rent or the property's value, and none that excuses a repair on cost grounds; we found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library. Your duty to comply with health and safety codes and to keep the premises fit and habitable runs for the whole tenancy, and a lease can't waive it. The only cost figures in the act limit the tenant: a tenant may repair and deduct only repairs that cost no more than 1 month's rent, and a breach that would cost less than 1 month's rent to fix is a claim for damages. If complying with the building or housing code would require alteration, remodeling or demolition that effectively deprives the tenant of the unit, the anti-retaliation rule doesn't stop you from bringing a possession action, but you still need a lawful way to end the tenancy: 30 days' written notice for a month-to-month tenancy (7 days for week-to-week), and during a fixed term only a right the lease gives you, such as the library's optional casualty-termination clause after a fire or casualty.

title: No Repair Escrow or Small-Landlord Exemption in Montana
bodyText: Some states let a landlord with only a few units, or an owner who lives on site, opt out of a tenant's rent-escrow or repair remedies by giving a notice. Montana has nothing to opt out of and no way to opt out. It has no rent-escrow program: a tenant cannot deposit rent with a court, a city or an escrow agent to force repairs. Rent goes into court only inside a case you bring, for possession for nonpayment or for rent while the tenant is in possession, where the court may order the tenant to pay accrued and accruing rent into court while it decides the tenant's counterclaim. Montana's repair remedies (ending the lease after written notice and 14 days to fix, 3 working days in an emergency; repair-and-deduct up to one month's rent; damages and an injunction; essential-services remedies) apply to every tenancy the act covers, however few units you own and whether or not you live there. Don't put a small-landlord or owner-occupant exemption statement in the lease: a term by which the tenant gives up rights or remedies under the act is unenforceable, and knowingly using one can cost you the tenant's actual damages plus up to 3 months' periodic rent. The only lawful way to move repair work to a tenant is a good-faith agreement for specified tasks, in a separate signed writing for adequate consideration, that does not cover basic code compliance (the library's Tenant Maintenance Agreement). Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library.

title: Repair notices and lease reporting terms
bodyText: Montana's tenant remedies use two kinds of notice. Ending the lease because you failed to maintain the premises needs a written notice specifying the problem, and the essential-services remedies need written notice specifying the breach and a reasonable chance for you to correct it. Repair-and-deduct needs only that the tenant has given you notice and you haven't made the repair within a reasonable time, and under the act a person has notice of a fact they actually know about, as well as one delivered by hand, mailed with a certificate of mailing or by certified mail, delivered at your place of business through which the lease was made, or sent to an e-mail address given in the lease (complete once a read receipt or a reply that is not automatic comes back). So a lease term saying a repair request counts only if it is in writing, or only through one portal, can't cut off a remedy that the statute grants on notice you actually have: a term waiving the tenant's rights or remedies under the act is unenforceable, and knowingly using one lets the tenant recover actual damages plus up to 3 months' periodic rent. In the other direction, if your lease invites tenants to report problems by phone, say that a call is a repair report and that written notice is still needed to end the lease, so the clause can't be read as giving up your right to the written notices the act requires; a call still gives you actual notice for repair-and-deduct. No Montana statute requires the lease to state a repair-request address, e-mail or portal, but you must disclose in writing the name and address of the manager and of the owner or the owner's agent for receiving notices and demands. Cautious course: ask for written repair requests (the library's maintenance clause does), take emergencies by phone as well, and treat any problem you actually know about as reported.

title: Required Disclosures for Montana Rentals
bodyText:
What a Montana landlord must disclose or hand over. This is the index; each item has its own row.

**AT OR BEFORE SIGNING.** (1) Manager and owner: in writing, at or before the tenancy begins, the name and address of the person authorized to manage the property and of the owner or the person authorized to accept legal papers, notices and demands for the owner, kept current; if you don't, whoever signs or manages for you becomes your agent for those purposes (Management and Notices clause, landlord-disclosure-mt).

(2) Condition statement, if you take a security deposit: a separate written statement of the unit's present condition, signed by you or your agent, saying if it has never been rented; and, if the tenant asks in writing, a copy of the damage and cleaning list given to the previous tenant. Without it you generally can't charge the deposit for damage or cleaning (edu-condition-statement-mt, existing-condition-mt).

(3) Rules: any rules must be in writing and given to each tenant on arrival; a rule binds the tenant only if the tenant had notice of it when signing or when it was adopted (rules-mt). (4) Mold: if you know of mold in the building, or know it has been tested, disclose it before or when the lease is signed and give any test results and evidence of treatment; the optional statutory mold statement, signed by the tenant, adds protection from liability (mold-disclosure-mt).

(5) Meth or fentanyl: if you know the property was a meth or fentanyl lab or was contaminated by use and it has not been cleaned to state standards by a certified contractor, written notice before the tenant agrees to the lease (edu-meth-disclosure-mt). (6) Lead paint (federal), for housing built before 1978: the Lead Warning Statement, your disclosure of known lead-based paint or hazards, a list of records given, the EPA pamphlet and signed acknowledgments, before the tenant is obligated (lead-based-paint).

(7) Condominium units: the lease must state the land description, property name, the declaration's recording information, the unit designation, its intended use and its share of the common elements (condominium-unit-lease-contents-mt).

(8) Lease with an option to buy a home of one to four units, or an individually owned unit: the seller disclosure statement of known adverse material facts, at or before signing; if it comes later the tenant-buyer may rescind within 3 days, unless the tenant-buyer waived it in the contract (see the option to purchase entry in edu-optional-lease-terms-mt).

(9) E-mail notices: you may not require an e-mail address; if you want to give notices by e-mail, the lease must contain a provision letting the tenant choose to receive them (electronic-notice-mt). (10) If a real estate broker or salesperson manages the property: disclosure to tenants of the licensee's contractual relationship with the owner, and of licensee status when first seeking information from a tenant.

(11) Federal programs: a housing choice voucher lease needs the HUD tenancy addendum (edu-voucher-tenancy-addendum); a denial based on a screening report needs the federal adverse action notice (edu-fcra-adverse-action-notice).

**DURING THE TENANCY.** A new rule that substantially changes the deal takes effect only after 7 days' (week to week) or 30 days' (month to month) written notice (rules-mt); a written decision on an emotional support animal request (edu-assistance-animals-mt); updated manager and owner information, and notice of a sale or change of manager (edu-sale-management-change-mt). Notices that end a tenancy or start a deadline are listed in edu-written-notice-required-mt.

**AT THE END.** A plain-language notification of how you will handle property left behind (edu-abandoned-property-notice-mt); written notice of cleaning still needed, with 24 hours to do it, before deducting cleaning charges (not needed if the tenant left without notice; the 24 hours do not apply if the lease was ended in a possession case and you have a claim pending in court); and within 30 days (10 if nothing is owed and the tenant shows no unpaid utilities) a written list of rent due and damage and cleaning charges with any refund, unless the lease was ended in a possession case and you have a claim pending in court (security-deposit-return-mt).

**NOT REQUIRED IN MONTANA.** No state tenant-rights statement or state form, no notice of whether the unit is covered by a rent or just-cause law (Montana has neither), and no radon, flood, bed bug, asbestos, foreclosure, sex-offender, utility-billing or licensee-status-on-the-first-page disclosure, and no sale-leaseback warning (see each item's own row). Every lease form you use must also meet Montana's plain-language rule (edu-plain-language-contracts-act-mt).

Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library.

title: Required fees
bodyText:
Montana doesn't require a lease to list its required fees or their purposes, to state charges for partial payment, to show rent and mandatory fees as one Total Monthly Payment, or to give a set notice period before adding a fee. It doesn't cap a markup on a service a third party bills you for, and it doesn't bar a fee for maintaining common areas (the mobile home lot act expressly contemplates common area maintenance fees set in the rental agreement).

We found none of these rules in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library.

What applies instead: a charge counts as rent only if it is agreed in the rental agreement; any fee for cleaning or damage, whatever it is called, is presumed to be a security deposit; no fee may be based on how rent is paid, except to recoup an electronic bank fee you incur; and accepting a partial payment doesn't waive your rights.

To add a fee mid-tenancy, get the tenant's written agreement during a fixed term; in a month-to-month tenancy you may change the terms by written notice served at least 15 days before the end of a month, taking effect at the end of that month. The library's optional fee list (fees-and-charges-mt) lets you set out every fee in the lease.

When you list fees, don't list a fee or charge for cleaning or damage, refundable or not: it is part of the security deposit. Don't list a fee based on how rent is paid, except one that only recoups an electronic bank fee you incur for an electronic payment. And don't list attorney fees, court, eviction, notice or collection costs, or any fixed charge for breaking the lease other than the late fee and returned-payment charge in their own clauses.

title: No State Rights and Responsibilities Guide in Montana
bodyText: Montana publishes no official landlord-tenant rights and responsibilities guide that you must give a tenant, before signing, at renewal or at any other time, and there is no acknowledgment to collect for one. The documents Montana law does make you hand over at the start of a tenancy are specific: the written name and address of the manager and of the owner or the owner's agent for notices (see landlord-disclosure-mt), the separate written move-in condition statement if you take a security deposit (see edu-condition-statement-mt), a written meth or fentanyl contamination notice where the property is affected (see edu-meth-disclosure-mt), a disclosure of any mold you know is present and of any mold testing, with the results (see mold-disclosure-mt), and the federal lead-based paint disclosure and pamphlet for housing built before 1978 (see lead-based-paint). A local government with self-government powers may not add a guide-delivery duty, because it may not regulate landlords' dealings with tenants beyond the state acts. Any guide a state office or court posts online is information only, not a document you are required to deliver.

title: No Code-Variance Notice to Tenants in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no state sanitary or housing code for rental dwellings that comes with a variance you must give to tenants, and nothing requires you to attach any code variance, exception or waiver to a lease or show it to a tenant. Variances do exist in nearby areas. The state building code may be varied by the Department of Labor and Industry after a public hearing where strict compliance would cause undue hardship, but no variance may adversely affect provisions for health, safety and security; local building codes must have their own appeal procedure. Local health board sewage rules must use variance standards identical to the state environmental department's, with appeal to that department. A public water system may get a temporary variance to use bottled water for a nitrate problem, and then the system owner, not you as landlord unless you own the system, must post warnings and give annual notices to users. A building-code or sewage variance is a matter between you and the building or health authority; your duty to the tenant stays the same: keep the unit fit and habitable and comply with the building and housing codes that apply to it. Do not ask a tenant to sign anything waiving those duties, which Montana law forbids in a rental agreement. A local government with self-government powers may not add a variance-disclosure duty for landlords beyond the state acts.

title: Seasonal Rentals in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no seasonal-tenancy statute. A lease of a home for a season (a summer cabin, a ski-season condo, a harvest-season house) is an ordinary tenancy under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, with the same deposit, repair, entry and notice rules as any other lease. Two points catch seasonal landlords. First, a written lease does not simply end on its end date: unless the lease sets its own extension period, the tenancy continues month to month if neither side gives the other 30 days' written notice before the original end date. To end a seasonal lease on schedule, give written notice at least 30 days before the end date. Second, if either side ends the lease early without cause, the other side's damages are capped at one month's rent or a lower agreed amount. If the tenant is the one who leaves early, you may also collect rent until a new tenancy starts or the term ends, but you must make reasonable efforts to re-rent. Stays that are not tenancies: the act does not govern transient occupancy in a hotel or motel. A home, condo or room offered to transient guests by the night or week is lodging, not a lease: a whole home rented to transient guests on a daily or weekly basis is a tourist home that needs an annual state health license, and stays of less than 30 days are subject to Montana's lodging facility use and sales taxes. Cities and counties may regulate short-term rentals, which state law defines as a dwelling offered for a fee for 30 days or less; check local rules. The line between a short vacation stay and a tenancy is not drawn by statute; if a guest is living in the home as a residence, or the stay runs a month or longer, treat it as a tenancy under the act and use a lease. Housing for seasonal workers is covered in the library's employee housing row, and rural rentals that include hunting, fishing or farming privileges in the hunting rights row. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library.

title: Deposit rights can’t be waived
bodyText:
Default rule: Montana's security deposit law governs any deposit a tenant must provide or keep in effect, and any fee or charge for cleaning or damage, however it is labelled. You may deduct only unpaid rent, late charges, utilities, penalties due under lease terms and other money owed, damage the tenant caused, and actual cleaning costs (cleaning only after written notice and 24 hours for the tenant to do it). Within 30 days after the tenancy ends you must give the tenant a written list of charges with the balance (10 days if nothing is owed), or lose the right to deduct for damage and cleaning. You must give a separate signed condition statement at the start if you take a deposit.

Waiver: none of this can be changed by the lease. Any lease term contrary to the deposit law is invalid, and any attempted waiver of it by the tenant is invalid, whether oral or written. That covers, for example, a nonrefundable cleaning fee, a fixed cleaning charge, a longer refund period, or a tenant's agreement to give up the itemized list. Whether the act's knowing-use penalty (actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent) also applies to a deposit term is unsettled, so treat it as if it does. The same rules apply to mobile home lot rentals.

title: No deposit-standards disclosure rule
bodyText:
Montana does not require you to post or disclose the standards you use to set deposit amounts, even if different tenants pay different deposits, and it sets no limit on the amount. Two limits still apply. First, fair housing: you may not set a different deposit or other term for a tenant because of sex, marital status, race, creed, religion, color, age, familial status, physical or mental disability or national origin. Second, if a licensed real estate broker collects deposits for you, the Board of Realty Regulation's trust-account rules govern how the broker holds them. Money the broker receives on behalf of others must go into a trust account, normally within three business days; the account must be liquid, readily accessible, insured in a Montana financial institution, identified as a trust account and reconciled every month it has activity; the money may not be kept in a sweep account or put at risk; the broker must keep complete running records and keep trust-account records for eight years; and failing to account for trust money or violating Montana's deposit law is unprofessional conduct.

Those rules apply to brokers handling other people's money as licensees, not to an owner holding deposits on its own rental. Brokers may act as property managers; Montana also licenses property managers separately, and any Board rule written for those licensees is outside the library's research set, so a licensed property manager should follow the same trust-account practice and check the Board's current rules. Montana's deposit statute itself has no separate-account requirement.

title: Senior Housing Staff and Age Limits in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no work-card, work-permit or licensing requirement for people who work at 55-and-older or other senior apartments, and no background-check rule for their staff. Two related rules apply only in narrower settings. An assisted living facility, a licensed health care facility, must run a background check on everyone who accepts a job there and may not employ a person found guilty of an offense involving abuse, neglect, exploitation, mistreatment or misappropriation of property, or with a licensing-board or nurse-aide-registry finding of that kind. And anyone who runs or works at a roominghouse, retirement home or complex, nursing home, group home, adult foster care home, adult day-care center or assisted living facility must report suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation of a vulnerable adult; a senior housing operator should train staff on that duty. A senior community that offers meals or a central kitchen, personal care or supervision may also need a state health care facility license; check with the state health department before opening one. Age-restricted housing itself: Montana forbids housing discrimination because of age and familial status, and lifts those two rules only for housing for older persons: housing under a state or federal program designed and operated to assist elderly persons, housing intended for and solely occupied by people 62 or older, or housing intended and operated for occupancy by at least one person 55 or older per unit under the federal 55-plus standard as Montana adopted it on March 31, 1996 (the current federal standard requires at least 80% of occupied units to have a resident 55 or older, published policies showing that intent, and age verification; build to those three). An age limit outside those categories is unlawful in Montana even where federal law, which does not protect age as such, would allow it. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library, including the Human Rights Bureau's housing rules.

title: Penalties for Denying a Service Animal in Montana
bodyText:
Montana's service-animal statute gives a person with a disability who has a service animal (a dog or miniature horse individually trained to assist a person with a disability, not an emotional support animal) full and equal access to all housing, and says the person may not be required to pay extra for the animal but is liable for any damage it does. Blind, visually impaired and deaf persons likewise have full and equal access to any housing offered for rent. So a no-pets rule, pet deposit or pet rent cannot be applied to a service animal.

**Penalties.** The criminal penalty in the service-animal law (a misdemeanor for denying or interfering with admittance to or enjoyment of public places and accommodations) is written for public accommodations such as hotels, motels, trailer parks and campgrounds, not for rental housing as such; it does not mention the housing-access sections (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library).

Housing denial is punished instead under Montana's Human Rights Act: refusing a service or assistance animal that a person with a disability needs is a refusal of a reasonable accommodation, and anyone who willfully engages in an unlawful discriminatory practice is guilty of a misdemeanor (a fine up to $500, up to 6 months in jail, or both).

The Department of Labor and Industry may also impose civil penalties of up to $10,000 (up to $25,000 for a repeat violator within 5 years), and a court may award damages, attorney fees and, for a repeat violator, punitive damages. Using force or threats to interfere with a person's housing because of disability is a separate crime. If you rent spaces in a trailer park or run a campground, the public-accommodation penalty may reach you directly.

Since 2025 it is also a misdemeanor to keep interfering with a service animal after being warned, or to let your own dog negligently interfere with one.

**Your rights.** Unless federal law says otherwise, you may deny an emotional support animal that poses a direct threat that another accommodation cannot reduce or eliminate; a service animal's handler is liable for damage it causes. Montana's misrepresentation statute (penalties for passing off an animal as a service animal) applies at public accommodations, not to rental housing (edu-service-animal-misrepresentation-mt). The library's rules are in edu-assistance-animals-mt and assistance-animal-accommodation.

title: Sex Offender Registry Information and Montana Rentals
bodyText: Montana has no statute requiring a landlord to tell tenants or applicants about registered sexual or violent offenders living nearby or in the building, to put a registry notice in the lease, or to check the registry before renting (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library). What the law does say: the name and address of a registered sexual or violent offender are public, and the Department of Justice and local registration agencies publish further details (photograph, offenses and, for higher-risk offenders, more) by internet and other means. A private entity, like a state or local agency, is not liable in negligence (only for gross negligence or willful or wanton misconduct) for a good-faith decision to release or not release information under the registry law; whether that protects a landlord who passes on registry information to tenants is not settled, so if you share it, share only what the public registry shows, accurately, and do not single out or harass the person. If a real estate broker or salesperson handles the rental, the licensee's responsibility is limited to disclosing that registry information may be maintained and by whom, and any actual knowledge the licensee has of registry information that pertains to the property. A registered offender must report a change of residence (including to an apartment) within 3 business days, and a high-risk sexual offender may not establish a residence near schools and similar places or where a minor lives; those duties are the offender's, not yours (edu-no-sex-offender-rule-mt). A lease sentence telling tenants where to find the registry is lawful and you may add one after taking advice; the library does not offer it as a clause because Montana requires none and notice value alone is not a reason for a lease term. Any screening criteria you use must be written and applied the same way to everyone.

title: No Single-Family Occupancy Notice in Montana
bodyText: Montana requires no special notice because a rental is a single-family home. There is no presumption that a tenant lacks lawful occupancy unless the lease is notarized or signed by a licensed property manager, so there is nothing of that kind to disclose, and Montana has no rule about placing a disclosure at the top of the first page or printing it in a larger font. A Montana lease is valid without notarization; notarizing matters only if you want to record the lease with the county (see edu-lease-registration-mt). What Montana does have is a fast removal route for people with no right to be there: a person who cannot produce authorization to occupy, such as a written rental agreement or verified permission from you or from a tenant for a guest, may be removed by law enforcement at your request, and you must indemnify the officers if you knowingly give them false information. So give every tenant a signed copy of the lease, which is the simplest proof of their right to occupy, and never use that route against a real tenant, who can be removed only through the court eviction process (see edu-unauthorized-occupant-mt and edu-self-help-eviction-mt).

title: No Shoreline Access Disclosure in Montana
