bodyText: Montana has no statute requiring a landlord to tell a tenant about public access to a shoreline, stream or lake, a public access easement, or lakeshore building limits. Three rules matter if a rental fronts water. First, under the stream access law the public may use surface waters capable of recreational use, whoever owns the bed, but that gives the public no right to enter or cross private land to reach the water, and it excludes some uses (such as permanent docks or moorings, and camping or seasonal objects within sight of, or within 500 yards of, an occupied dwelling) unless the landowner agrees. Second, a landowner, the landowner's agent or the landowner's tenant owes people using the water, or a bridge or county road right-of-way to reach it, no duty except to avoid willful or wanton misconduct. Third, on a lake of at least 160 acres, any work that alters the lake or the lakeshore (the high-water perimeter plus 20 feet inland), such as a dock, wharf, fill or breakwater, needs a local permit, and unpermitted work may have to be undone. If tenants may use a dock or shore, the lease should say what they may and may not do, and that they need your consent for any work on the shore or in the water. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws, the Constitution and the Montana rules held for this pass.

title: Showing notice can’t be shortened
bodyText:
Default rule: the tenant may not unreasonably refuse to let you in to show the unit to prospective tenants or buyers, mortgagees, workers or contractors, but except in an emergency (or where notice is impracticable) you must give at least 24 hours' notice of your intent to enter and enter only at reasonable times. Posting the notice conspicuously on the main entry door counts. If the tenant refuses lawful access, you may give a 24-hour notice to correct and then a 3-day notice to terminate, or ask a court to order access.

Waiver: a Montana lease can't shorten or waive the 24-hour notice for showings, whether in the lease or in a separate signed addendum. The statute has no "unless otherwise agreed" and no waiver form, and Montana bars any rental agreement term waiving the tenant's rights under the act; using one knowingly can cost you the tenant's damages plus up to three months' periodic rent.

If a tenant chooses to let you in sooner for a particular showing, that is the tenant's consent at the time, but don't ask for it in advance in the lease, and don't treat a refusal of a short-notice showing as a refusal of access. Plan end-of-lease showings around the 24-hour notice. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No rent protection during a government shutdown
bodyText:
No shutdown protection: Montana has no statute giving federal, state or other government workers extra time to pay rent, or protection from eviction, during a government shutdown or furlough. The ordinary rules apply: rent is due without demand on the due date, and if it is unpaid you may give the 3-day written notice of nonpayment and of your intention to terminate. A court has no statutory power to stay an eviction for a shutdown.

Related protections that may apply: a Montana National Guard member on active duty, or a dependent, can ask the court to stay a nonpayment case about their primary residence for up to 3 months or adjust the payments; and on a property with a federally backed mortgage or in a covered federal housing program, federal law requires 30 days' notice to vacate. Local governments can't add an eviction or rent-deferral rule of their own; state law bars them from regulating landlords' dealings with tenants beyond the state landlord-tenant and deposit acts. You may of course agree a written payment plan with an affected tenant; accepting a partial payment does not waive your rights. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: Renting in Single-Family Zones in Montana
bodyText: No Montana statute limits renting out a home in a single-family zone, caps how many homes in a neighborhood may be rented, or makes your right to rent depend on living on the lot. Montana has no state lot-split or two-unit program with an owner-occupancy affidavit, and no statewide minimum rental term. State law points the other way: a city of 5,000 or more must allow a duplex wherever it allows a single-family home and may not zone duplexes more strictly, and a city or zoning county must allow an accessory dwelling unit and may not require that the owner live in the house or the ADU (see edu-accessory-dwelling-unit-mt). Zoning still regulates how land and buildings are used for residence, and both cities and counties may regulate short-term rentals (30 days or less), so a local ban, permit or cap on short-term rentals in a residential zone is allowed. Whether a local zoning rule may go further and limit ordinary long-term rentals, or require owner occupancy of a rented house, is not settled by any statute: a local government with self-government powers may not regulate landlords' dealings with tenants beyond the state landlord-tenant act, but zoning laws bind those governments too, and no court decision was researched for this library. Treat any such local rule as possibly enforceable, check your city or county code before buying or converting a home to rent, and take advice if a rule appears to stop you renting. A city or county that has come under the Montana Land Use Planning Act is, by that Act's words, not bound by the duplex and ADU protections in the older zoning chapter, so check its own code. Building a new building for lease or rent on a tract with no zoning can require local review.

title: Smart Locks and Electronic Entry in Montana
bodyText:
Montana has no statute on smart locks, keypad or app-based entry, entry logs or biometric entry in rentals, and no statute letting a domestic violence survivor make a landlord or other account manager cut another person off a connected device. The ordinary rules apply to an electronic system as they do to keys. Using the system to enter is entry: you need at least 24 hours' notice except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable, and may enter only at reasonable times.

Disabling a tenant's code or credential to keep the tenant out is an unlawful exclusion, for which the tenant may recover up to 3 months' periodic rent or treble damages, whichever is greater. A system you supply is equipment you must keep in good working order. A tenant may not remove, replace or add a lock without your written permission and must give you a key, so a tenant-installed smart lock needs your permission and your access.

Montana's Consumer Data Privacy Act covers only businesses that control or process the personal data of at least 25,000 Montana consumers (not counting data used only to complete a payment), or at least 15,000 if more than 25% of gross revenue comes from selling personal data, so most landlords are outside it, though a large manager or the lock vendor may be inside it.

Where it applies, fingerprint, face or other biometric data used to identify a person, and precise location data, are sensitive data that may be processed only with the person's consent. The cautious course: tell tenants in writing what the system records and who can see it, offer a code, card or key instead of any biometric or app-only credential, and use entry records only to run and secure the property. The library's optional Electronic Entry clause (smart-access-mt) sets these terms.

Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws, the Constitution and the Montana rules held for this pass.

title: No Smoke-Drift Waiver in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no statute that lets a lease have the tenant acknowledge that tobacco smoke may drift in from other units and give up a nuisance claim, and no statute or state rule on secondhand smoke drifting between rental units (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library). The library does not offer a smoke-drift waiver. A Montana lease may not make a tenant waive rights or remedies under the landlord-tenant act or excuse you from liability for your own negligence, and a contract meant to exempt anyone from responsibility for a violation of law is against public policy, so a waiver would likely fail at least in part, and knowingly using a prohibited term can cost you up to 3 months' rent in addition to damages. A plain acknowledgment that smoking is allowed in other units, with no waiver, is lawful, but the library doesn't offer one either: it has no legal effect in Montana, and the library's default is a smoke-free property (smoking-policy-mt). You may add your own after taking advice. Montana's Clean Indoor Air Act bans smoking, including marijuana and electronic smoking devices, in enclosed public places, which include any indoor area that serves as a place of work; a private residence is exempt unless it is used as a licensed day-care home, adult foster care home or health care facility. A rental office or staff room is therefore smoke-free by law, and if the office is open to the public you must post the required no-smoking sign at its public entrances. Whether an enclosed common hallway where staff work is covered is not settled; cautious course: ban smoking in all enclosed common areas by lease, as smoking-policy-mt does. A lease signed after January 1, 2021 may ban smoking marijuana but may not bar a tenant from lawfully possessing marijuana or consuming it by other means (edu-cannabis-mt). A tenant must also not disturb neighbors' peaceful enjoyment of the premises.

title: Snow and Ice Removal in Montana Rentals
bodyText: Clearing snow and ice from walks, steps, driveways and parking is a specified maintenance task. In Montana a landlord and tenant may agree that the tenant does specified repairs or maintenance tasks only in a separate writing signed by both, made in good faith and supported by adequate consideration, for work that isn't needed to meet building and housing codes, and without reducing your duties to other tenants. The library reads that rule as applying to every dwelling, including a single-family house, so it doesn't use its general Snow Removal lease clause for Montana; use the separate Tenant Maintenance Agreement (maintenance-allocation-mt), whose snow and ice option covers walkways, driveways, porches and entrances that only the tenant uses. Shared walks, stairs and parking are common areas you must keep clean and safe, and that duty can't be handed to one tenant in a way that reduces your duties to the others. Cities may require the owners of adjoining premises to keep sidewalks free from snow, and may charge the cost of removing snow and ice from sidewalks against the abutting property; an agreement with your tenant doesn't change your duty to the city, so check the local ordinance (local codes weren't read). Montana's landlord-tenant act has no snow rule of its own; for comparison, a mobile home park landlord must arrange snow plowing to keep park roads passable. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library.

title: Benefits: no eviction defense, but exempt from collection
bodyText:
Not a defense to eviction: Montana has no rule that a late Social Security, public assistance or housing-assistance payment excuses unpaid rent, delays a possession case or requires a continuance or reinstatement. A tenant who relies on benefits gets the same 3-day nonpayment notice and the same possession case as any other tenant (Montana National Guard members on active duty and their dependents can ask for a stay or payment adjustment). Receiving Social Security is not itself a defense either.

Collecting a money judgment: benefits a tenant has received or is entitled to receive under federal Social Security or local public assistance laws are exempt from execution under Montana law, as are veterans' and disability benefits, except for child support or spousal maintenance debts; proceeds of exempt property that is sold, or that is lost, damaged or destroyed and for which the tenant has been compensated, stay exempt for 6 months if traceable, such as in a bank account. Federal law separately protects Social Security benefits from execution, levy, attachment, garnishment or other legal process. So you can win possession and a judgment for rent, but you can't collect that judgment from the tenant's Social Security money; look to non-exempt property or wages, or to the security deposit as the deposit law allows. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No special-district statement in a Montana lease
bodyText:
**Special districts.** Montana does not require a lease to say that a rental sits in a special district, a special or rural improvement district, a business improvement district, a water and sewer district or any other assessment district, and there is no statement for the tenant to sign. District assessments are levied on the property and are your cost as owner; if you want the tenant to pay any part of one, the lease must say so as part of the rent or charges.

What role a tenant has: a petition to create a general special district may be signed by 40% of the registered voters or by the owners of 40% of the property in the proposed district, so a tenant who is a registered voter there counts like any other resident voter; the right to protest the district's program or assessments belongs to the owners of property liable to be assessed, so the protest is yours, not your tenant's.

This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure Rule in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no law requiring you to tell a tenant, in the lease or anywhere else, whether the building has a fire sprinkler system or when it was last maintained or inspected, and no state grant, loan or tax credit for adding sprinklers to a rental was found (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state building and fire code rules held for this library). A voluntary sprinkler statement in the lease is lawful, but the library does not offer one: no Montana law calls for it and it gives you no protection the lease lacks without it. You may add your own after taking advice. If a tenant asks, answer accurately; a false statement about a safety system can create liability. When sprinklers are required, and your duty to keep an installed system working, are covered in edu-fire-sprinkler-duty-mt.

title: Montana money limits at a glance
bodyText: Montana sets few dollar limits on a residential lease. There is no cap on the security deposit, the late fee, the application fee, or pet, key, move-in or cleaning charges, and no state or local rent control (we found no cap in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library). The limits that do exist: a returned-payment service charge of no more than $30, and only after a written demand (returned-payments-mt); no fee based on how rent is paid, except to recoup an electronic bank fee you incur (edu-payment-method-fee-mt); early-termination damages of no more than 1 month's rent, or an agreed amount not over 1 month's rent, plus rent until re-rented or the term ends (early-termination-mt); interest of 10% a year unless a written agreement sets another rate, and no agreed rate above the greater of 15% or 6 points over the prime rate (edu-legal-interest-mt); and, for a property manager of four or more units, a refund of the application fee to an applicant who doesn't sign, keeping only itemized costs actually spent (edu-application-fee-mt). Any fee for cleaning or damage, whatever you call it, is presumed to be a security deposit, so handle and refund it under the deposit rules (edu-deposit-rules-mt). A lease can't change the statutory penalties: up to 3 months' periodic rent for knowingly using a prohibited lease term, the greater of 3 months' periodic rent or treble damages for a lockout or utility shutoff, and attorney fees set by the court. And Montana voids a damages amount fixed in advance unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix, so keep every agreed charge near your real cost.

title: When a tenant may end a lease early
bodyText:
Tenant rights to end a lease early under Montana law:
- Your breach of the habitability duties: after written notice, the tenant may give written notice that the lease will end on a date at least 30 days later if you don't fix a health-and-safety problem within 14 days; a repair made before that date keeps the lease from ending, but fix it within the 14 days to be safe; in an emergency, if you don't fix it within 3 working days the tenant may terminate; a repeat within 6 months allows 14 days' notice. Not for a condition the tenant's household or guests caused.
- Fire or casualty that substantially impairs enjoyment of the unit: the tenant may vacate at once and give written notice within 14 days, unless the tenant's household or guests caused it purposefully or negligently.
- Failure to deliver possession at the start: the tenant may terminate on 5 days' written notice and get back prepaid rent and the deposit.
- Unlawful lockout or purposeful cutoff of heat, water, electricity, gas or other essential services, and unlawful or harassing entry: the tenant may terminate (plus money remedies).
- Montana National Guard members on active duty ordered to a permanent duty station more than 60 miles away: termination 45 days after written notice with a copy of the orders, with no early termination fee or damages.

Federal servicemember law adds a right for any servicemember who signed a lease and then entered military service, or who received permanent-change-of-station orders or deployment orders for at least 90 days after signing (and for the spouse or dependents after a servicemember's death in service, or after a catastrophic injury or illness).

Notice is written, with a copy of the orders; for a monthly lease, termination takes effect 30 days after the next rent due date following delivery; you may charge no early termination fee, must prorate rent and refund rent paid in advance within 30 days, and may not hold the deposit for rent accruing after termination.

What Montana does not have: no early-termination right for domestic violence, no termination right for a landlord's fraudulent misrepresentation written into the landlord-tenant act (general contract law on rescission for fraud applies), and no required lease statement of these rights. Ending a fixed term early without cause is not barred; damages are capped at 1 month's rent (or an agreed lower or equal amount), plus rent until re-letting under the mitigation rules.

This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No Radiator Cover Rule in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no statute or state rule requiring you to cover steam radiators, to install covers when a tenant asks, or to tell tenants about radiator covers in the lease or in a posted notice (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library). Your general duties still apply: keep the heating system and the radiators you supply in good and safe working order, keep the premises fit and habitable, and keep common areas safe. A building's steam boiler may also need state inspections and a licensed operator unless it is a low-pressure boiler in a house or an apartment building of six or fewer families (see edu-heating-mt). Cautious course: where a radiator gets hot enough to burn and a young child, an elderly person or a person with a disability lives in the unit, consider fitting a cover or guard, and respond promptly to a tenant's request. A cover must not block the heat the unit needs.

title: No Stove or Refrigerator Requirement in Montana
bodyText:
Montana has no statute or state rule requiring you to supply a stove, range or refrigerator in a rental, and none setting terms for a tenant who brings their own (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library). What matters is what you supply. You must keep in good and safe working order every appliance you supply or are required to supply, so list the appliances that come with the unit in the lease (the library's Appliances & Equipment Included clause does this) and maintain them; the tenant must use them in a reasonable manner and may not damage them. An appliance the tenant owns is the tenant's to maintain unless you agree otherwise. For units completed after July 1, 1977 you must also keep up the building code requirements that applied when the unit was built; what the model codes require in a kitchen was not read for this library. Rooming houses (rented sleeping rooms without their own cooking facilities) are regulated as public accommodations under a separate law, and a renter whose room lacks its own toilet, bath or shower, refrigerator, stove or kitchen sink shared with other occupants is a roomer under the landlord-tenant act.

Don't list an appliance you leave at the property for the tenant to use as one the tenant owns. Because you must maintain every appliance you supply, either list it in the Appliances & Equipment Included clause and maintain it, or remove it before the tenant moves in.

title: Student Housing in Montana
bodyText: Montana's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act does not govern housing provided by the Montana university system or by any other college or postsecondary school: residence halls, dormitories and campus apartments, including housing the school provides to faculty and staff. That housing runs on the school's own housing contract and policies instead. For the university system the Board of Regents rents its housing at rates it sets and has full control and management of it; a community college's trustees have the same powers. Montana's security deposit law does not apply to that housing, and a dispute over possession goes under the general unlawful detainer statutes rather than the act. The exclusion does not reach a private landlord who rents to students. A house, apartment or purpose-built student building that you own and lease directly to students is covered by the act and the deposit law in full, whether or not you market it to students or sit next to a campus. Housing a school leases from you and then provides to its students is the hard case: the safer view is that the school's arrangement with the students is excluded, but your lease with the school is a commercial contract and any lease you sign directly with a student is covered. The exclusion also fails if an arrangement is set up to avoid the act. Montana has no other student-housing rule: no student-tenant termination or hearing procedure, no rule for leases that end when a student leaves school, and no limit on requiring a parent to guarantee a student's lease; use the library's ordinary clauses. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library.

title: Voucher Program Inspections in Montana
bodyText: No Montana statute or rule addresses a housing assistance program's inspection: a tenant who refuses one, or a landlord who refuses to rent because the program requires one. Montana's fair housing statute has no source-of-income protection, so turning down a voucher because of the program's inspection and contract is not barred by statute, though whether the Montana Constitution's ban on discrimination based on social origin or condition reaches that choice is unsettled; take advice before refusing vouchers outright. Montana has no state rental inspection program. Inside an occupied unit, Montana's access rule covers you and your agent: the tenant may not unreasonably refuse you entry to inspect or repair, you must give at least 24 hours' notice (unless an emergency or impracticable) and enter at reasonable times, and if the tenant refuses lawful access you may give a 24-hour notice to correct, then a 3-day notice to terminate, or seek a court order, plus damages. A housing agency inspector enters under the federal program's own rules, which make allowing the agency's inspections part of the family's obligations (federal rule not read for this note). For a voucher unit, if the tenant blocks an inspection, tell the agency in writing right away so the missed inspection isn't treated as your failure, offer to give your own 24-hour notice and attend with the inspector, and fix any deficiency the agency finds within its deadline: 24 hours for a life-threatening one and 30 calendar days otherwise, unless the agency extends it.

title: Voucher Rent When a Unit Fails Inspection in Montana
bodyText: No Montana statute or rule prorates or abates rent between a subsidized tenant and a housing agency when a unit is unfit. The Montana Housing Act's supervision powers reach sponsors of housing developments financed by the Board of Housing, not an ordinary landlord. For a Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8) tenancy, federal rules govern the agency's share. You must maintain the unit to the federal Housing Quality Standards and, after notice, correct a life-threatening deficiency within 24 hours and any other within 30 calendar days or an extension the agency approves. Once the agency notifies you in writing of a deficiency it may withhold its payments, and must pay them back if you fix the unit within the cure period. If you don't, it must abate its payment, including amounts it withheld, and tell you and the family that the payment contract will end if the unit still fails after 60 days (or a longer period it sets). The family owes only its own share: you may not demand more from the tenant or collect the abated or withheld amount from the tenant, and the agency's failure to pay is not grounds to end the tenancy. If the agency finds the tenant, a household member or a guest caused the deficiency (beyond ordinary use), it may waive your duty to fix it, and then it may not withhold or abate; the family can be held responsible for unpaid tenant-paid utilities, appliances it must supply, or damage beyond ordinary wear. Montana's own remedies still run to the tenant: written notice that the lease ends in 30 days unless you fix a health-and-safety problem in 14 (three working days in an emergency), repair and deduct up to one month's rent, damages, and the essential-services remedies. None of them says how a reduction is split between the tenant's share and the agency's payment. Fix deficiencies within the agency's deadlines, keep repair records, and tell the agency at once if the tenant caused the problem.

title: Late fees in subsidized tenancies
bodyText: Montana has no special late-fee rule for subsidized tenancies, and no late-fee limit of any kind. We found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library. Federal rules still matter. Under a Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8) contract, the housing agency's failure to pay its share is not the tenant's lease violation, and the family is not responsible for the agency's share. So if your lease has a late fee, charge it only when the tenant's own share is late, measure it on that share, and never charge the tenant because the agency paid late. Other subsidy programs and your agency contract may limit late fees further; check them before charging one. Montana's general late-fee guidance also applies (edu-late-fee-mt, edu-voucher-tenancy-addendum).

title: Repair Orders, but No Receivership, for Montana Rentals
bodyText: Montana has no receivership remedy for substandard rental housing: no statute lets a city, county or the state ask a court to put a receiver in charge of a neglected rental building, and no statute lets a city foreclose code-violation liens against rental property in rem with notice to occupants. The general receivership statute covers creditors, mortgagees, co-owners and judgments, not code enforcement. What Montana does have are repair-or-demolish orders. The state fire prevention and investigation section or your local fire chief may declare a building that is especially liable to fire, for example from disrepair, age, dilapidation or defective wiring, chimneys, gas or heating, to be a public nuisance and order the hazard removed or the building repaired or torn down. A repair-or-demolish order is filed in district court and must be served on you and, if the building is occupied, on the tenant; you or the tenant may contest it within 20 days. If you do not comply, the authority may do the work, its allowed costs become a lien on the land, and the land may be sold if the lien is not paid within 3 months; failing to comply is also a misdemeanor fine for each day. Local health officers may order unsanitary conditions corrected and recover their costs, and cities and towns may condemn and demolish hazardous structures under their own codes. Your tenant's own remedies for disrepair are in the landlord-tenant act (see edu-tenant-repair-remedies-mt).

title: Passing on tax and insurance increases
bodyText: Montana has no statute on passing property tax or insurance increases to a residential tenant. It doesn't require a lease clause to state the tenant's exact share or to refund a share of any abatement, and it doesn't limit how you collect the share. We found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library. So a tenant owes a share of a tax or insurance increase only if the lease says so; during a fixed term you can't add it later without the tenant's agreement, and in a month-to-month tenancy you may change the terms by written notice served at least 15 days before the end of a month. An agreed share counts as rent and may be deducted from the deposit if unpaid. Two Montana cautions. First, since tax year 2026 a long-term rental (rented for periods of 28 days or more for at least 7 months of the year to tenants who live there) can get a much lower property tax rate, but only if you apply between December 1 and March 1 and reapply when the Department of Revenue asks; don't pass on an increase that comes from not claiming it. Second, Montana bars raising rent to retaliate for a tenant's protected complaint and presumes retaliation for 6 months after one, with no exception for escalation clauses, so keep the bill and the calculation. A pass-through clause is lawful in Montana, but the library does not offer one: it treats a tax or insurance pass-through as a rent escalation in a fixed term, which it declines because the share is hard to verify and the retaliation presumption has no exception for it. If you want one, add your own clause after taking advice, and build in the two cautions above.

title: Cable, Satellite and Internet Access in Montana Rentals
bodyText:
No Montana statute gives a cable, satellite, internet or telephone provider a right of access to a rental or apartment building, gives a tenant a right to choose a provider, bars charging different rent to subscribers, or regulates exclusive provider deals in apartments. Local self-government units may not regulate landlords' dealings with tenants beyond the state landlord-tenant acts.

Federal law does reach leases: the Federal Communications Commission's over-the-air reception devices rule prohibits any lease provision that impairs a tenant's installation, maintenance or use of a satellite dish or similar antenna one meter or less across, or a TV broadcast antenna, on property within the tenant's exclusive use or control, such as a private balcony or patio.

A restriction impairs if it unreasonably delays or prevents installation, maintenance or use, unreasonably increases the cost, or prevents an acceptable signal, and any fee must be reasonable. So you may require consent before a tenant or installer drills into walls, roofs or common areas, but do not ban or hold up a small dish placed on the tenant's own balcony or patio.

The library's optional Television, Satellite and Internet Service clause and the No Alterations clause both yield to these rights. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws, the Constitution and the held Montana rules; the federal rule's excerpt was read, the rest of it and FCC rulings were not.

title: Tenancies at Will in Montana
bodyText: Montana law treats a tenancy at will as different from a periodic tenancy. A residential rental the Landlord and Tenant Act governs is never left open-ended: unless the agreement says otherwise it is week to week for a roomer who pays weekly and month to month in every other case, and either side ends it by written notice at least 7 days (week to week) or 30 days (month to month) before the date in the notice. A fixed-term lease that runs out without either side giving 30 days' written notice also continues month to month, unless the lease sets a different extension period. The general one-month tenancy-at-will notice does not apply to tenancies the act governs. Don't call a residential tenancy "at will" or write it as ending at any time without notice; use a month-to-month term (the library's Ending a Month-to-Month or Week-to-Week Tenancy clause). Tenancies at will still matter in two places. First, arrangements outside the act (for example an employee whose housing depends on the job, or a rural rental with hunting or farming privileges): a tenancy at will, however created, ends only by your written notice to leave within a period of not less than one month, served as the unlawful detainer statute provides, and only after that period can you sue for possession. Second, after a trustee's sale under a deed of trust: the buyer is entitled to possession on the 10th day after the sale, and anyone still in possession under an interest that came after the trust deed, usually including a tenant, is treated as a tenant at will. No Montana statute says whether such a tenant also gets the act's notice periods, so the cautious course for a buyer is written notice of at least one full month and not less than 30 days, and a court action rather than self-help; federal law can require more (see the federal row on tenants after foreclosure). A tenancy at will does not need to be in writing. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library.

title: Tenant bankruptcy: no Montana rule; federal stay applies
bodyText:
No Montana rule: Montana has no statute on what happens to an eviction, a writ of possession or a lease when a tenant files for bankruptcy. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act only says that bankruptcy law, like other general law, supplements it. Federal bankruptcy law governs.

Federal law in outline: filing a bankruptcy petition generally triggers an automatic stay that stops acts to obtain possession of the debtor's property, which can include continuing an eviction. Federal law makes two exceptions for a residential tenant: (1) where you obtained a judgment for possession before the petition was filed, the eviction may continue, but the tenant can keep the stay for 30 days by certifying, with the petition, that state law would let the tenant cure the whole money default after the judgment and by depositing the next 30 days' rent with the bankruptcy clerk (Montana's landlord-tenant act gives no right to cure after a judgment for possession, see edu-no-redemption-mt; you may object, and the court must hear the objection within 10 days); and (2) an eviction based on endangering the property or illegal use of controlled substances, if you file with the bankruptcy court and serve on the tenant a certification under penalty of perjury that such an eviction has been filed, or that the tenant endangered the property or used or allowed controlled substances in the prior 30 days, and the exception takes effect 15 days after you file and serve the certification unless the tenant objects (the court then hears it within 10 days). In a chapter 7 case, a residential lease the trustee does not assume or reject within 60 days after the order for relief (or a longer time the court sets) is deemed rejected; in chapter 11, 12 or 13 the decision can wait until a plan is confirmed.

Cautious course: when you learn a tenant has filed, stop eviction steps, collection of pre-filing rent and deposit deductions for pre-filing debts until you have checked the stay with a bankruptcy lawyer or obtained relief from the bankruptcy court; keep a copy of any pre-filing possession judgment. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: Tenant Information and Privacy in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no landlord-tenant statute making tenant or applicant information confidential, requiring a tenant's consent before you share it, or limiting what you may tell a reference caller, a lender, a buyer or a debt collector. General laws still apply. (1) Emotional support animal requests: you may not ask for information that discloses the diagnosis or severity of a tenant's disability or for medical records; treat anything a tenant volunteers as confidential. (2) Data security: if you own or license computerized data with a person's name plus a Social Security number, driver's license or state or tribal ID number, a financial account or card number with its access code, medical record information or a taxpayer ID, and that data is acquired by an unauthorized person, you must notify each affected Montana resident without unreasonable delay and send a copy of the notice to the attorney general's consumer protection office; a vendor holding the data for you must tell you at once. You must also take reasonable steps to destroy records containing such information once you no longer need them (shredding, erasing or making it unreadable). (3) Montana's Consumer Data Privacy Act covers only businesses that control or process the personal data of at least 25,000 Montana residents (not counting data used only to complete a payment), or 15,000 if more than 25% of gross revenue comes from selling personal data. Most landlords are below that; a large manager, a screening company or a portal vendor may be above it. A covered business must limit what it collects to what is reasonably necessary for the purposes it discloses, keep it reasonably secure, give a privacy notice, honor requests to access, correct and delete data, and get consent before processing sensitive data such as health, immigration status or precise location. Public housing authorities and colleges are outside it. (4) Montana's Constitution protects individual privacy; how far it reaches a private landlord is a case-law question. The cautious course: share tenant information only as needed to run the tenancy, collect a law, or answer a lawful request, and get the tenant's written consent before giving anything beyond dates of tenancy and payment history to a third party. Victims of abuse and federally assisted housing have their own rules (see the domestic violence confidentiality row). Screening reports are governed by federal law. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library.

title: Housing an Employee in Montana
bodyText: Montana's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act does not govern an employee's occupancy when the right to live there is conditional on the employee's work in and about the premises, such as a resident manager, caretaker or maintenance worker housed on the property as part of the job, unless the arrangement was set up to avoid the act. The exclusion is narrow. An employee who rents on ordinary terms, an employee housed by you who works somewhere else, and a tenant who does chores for a rent credit are all ordinary tenants under the act; a tenant's repair or upkeep tasks still need the separate signed agreement the act requires (the library's Tenant Maintenance Agreement). When the exclusion applies, the written employment and housing terms and general contract and property law govern instead: the security deposit law does not apply; if no term is fixed, the hiring renews for the rent period (up to a month) unless a party gives notice that long before it ends; if you fail to make repairs you ought to make after notice, the occupant may repair and deduct up to a month's rent or move out; and possession is recovered through an unlawful detainer action, not the act's eviction procedure. An occupancy at will needs at least one month's written notice before you can sue, and you may not turn the occupant out by force or threats. Pay: if housing counts toward wages, only its reasonable cost counts, only if you customarily furnish it, and never more than 40% of the total wage. Housing two or more employees or families living separately on one parcel can be a work camp that needs a state health license (shelter for farm or ranch workers is excepted). Montana has no rule requiring an employee-housing disclosure or an offer of a lease when the job ends. The library does not offer an employee-occupancy clause: making occupancy conditional on employment is lawful, but it takes the arrangement out of the act this lease is written for, so it belongs in a separate employee housing agreement. You can add your own after taking advice; state the job, the charge for the housing, and how long the employee has to leave after the job ends. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library.

title: Insurance Claims Between Landlord and Tenant in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no statute on insurance claims between landlords and tenants. In particular, no statute bars you or your insurer from recovering from a tenant for an accidental fire or other loss the tenant caused, no statute makes a tenant an implied co-insured under your policy, and no statute authorizes a mutual waiver of insured losses. What does apply: a tenant may not destroy, damage or impair the premises or let anyone else do so, and a tenant (with family and guests) who caused a fire or casualty purposefully or negligently loses the right to end the lease or pay reduced rent because of it. The library's optional Damage Caused by Tenant clause sets out recovery for that damage. Whether your property insurer, after paying you, can sue a negligent tenant (subrogation) is decided by case law, not statute, and was not researched; expect the insurer to try, and expect the tenant's renter's liability coverage to be what pays. Lease terms to avoid: a Montana lease may not have either party excuse, limit or indemnify the other party's liability for that party's negligence or purposeful misconduct. A waiver of subrogation, whether one-sided or mutual, gives up claims for losses the other side's negligence caused, so the library does not offer one and treats it as barred; a consent or initials box does not cure it. Such a term is unenforceable, and knowingly using one can cost you the tenant's actual damages plus up to 3 months' periodic rent. You may require renter's insurance with property and liability coverage (the library's Tenant's Property & Renter's Insurance clause), and you may recover from the tenant the actual cost of damage the tenant caused, including your deductible as part of that actual loss, and the security deposit may be applied to damage from the tenant's accidental as well as willful acts; don't set a flat damage or deductible fee, which Montana treats as a security deposit. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025 (including the insurance code), the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library.

title: Tenant Portals in Montana
bodyText:
Montana has no statute on tenant portals. The ordinary rules decide what a portal can do. Payment: the lease may name how and where rent is paid, including an online portal, and Montana does not require you to accept cash. But you may not charge an extra fee based on how rent is paid, except to recoup an electronic bank fee you incur for an electronic payment, and that fee may not exceed your actual cost; a convenience fee the portal adds is safest treated as your fee.

And a lease may not require the tenant to provide an e-mail address as a condition of renting. Most portals need an e-mail login, so don't make the portal the only way to pay: name at least one method that needs no portal account or e-mail address, such as a check or money order delivered to your address.

Signatures and documents: electronic signatures and records work only between parties who have each agreed to deal electronically, and a tenant who agreed can refuse to sign or receive later documents electronically; that right can't be waived in the lease. A record you send must let the tenant print or save it, or it can't be enforced against the tenant. Notices: a message posted in a portal is not one of the act's notice methods.

A notice counts if the tenant actually knows of it, if it is delivered in hand or mailed with a certificate of mailing or by certified mail, or if it is sent to an e-mail address the tenant chose to give in the lease (complete only on a read receipt or a reply that isn't automatic). Give required notices those ways and use the portal for copies.

Data: a portal holds applicants' and tenants' personal and bank data, so Montana's breach-notice and record-destruction rules apply to you and your vendor, and a large manager or vendor may be covered by the Consumer Data Privacy Act. The library's optional Tenant Portal clause sets these terms. A term requiring an e-mail address is prohibited, and knowingly using it can cost you the tenant's actual damages plus up to 3 months' periodic rent; a term waiving the tenant's right to stop dealing electronically is void.

Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library.

title: Tenant Records and Data Security in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no statute requiring a landlord to keep a rent ledger, give a tenant a statement of account or copies of the tenant's own file, include a ledger in a notice for unpaid rent, or charge a set amount for copies (no landlord-specific rent-receipt rule, but Montana's general law entitles anyone who pays money to a written receipt from the person paid, and the payer may demand a proper signature on it; see edu-confirmed-absences-outside-title-mt). A 3-day notice for unpaid rent need only give written notice of the nonpayment and that the lease will end if the rent is not paid within 3 days. The records Montana does require: within 30 days after a tenancy ends, a written list of any rent due and damage and cleaning charges, sent with any refund (10 days if nothing is owed and the tenant shows no unpaid utilities; the list rule does not apply if the lease was ended in a possession case and you have a claim pending in court); and, if you take a deposit, a separate signed written statement of the unit's condition at move-in; if the new tenant asks in writing, you must also give a copy of the list of damage and cleaning charges you gave the previous tenant, so keep each departing tenant's list at least until the next tenancy starts. How long to keep records: no statute sets a period for an owner. Keep the lease, payment records, the condition statement and deposit records for at least 6 years after the tenancy ends, the longest time a claim on a written lease can be brought. A licensed real estate broker or salesperson must keep leases and trust account records for 8 years; a licensed property manager should follow the same period. Security of applicant and tenant data: Montana has no general rule requiring a landlord to have a written information security program. But if you own or license computerized data with a person's name plus a Social Security number, driver's license or ID number, a financial account or card number with its access code, medical information or a taxpayer ID, and it is acquired by an unauthorized person, you must notify each affected Montana resident without unreasonable delay and send a copy to the attorney general's consumer protection office. Destroy records containing that information once you no longer need them, by shredding, erasing or making them unreadable. Large businesses covered by Montana's Consumer Data Privacy Act (generally those holding data on 25,000 or more Montana residents) must also keep data reasonably secure and honor a person's requests to see, correct, delete or get a copy of it; others have no such duty. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library.

title: No Required Statement of Tenant Rights in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no required statement of tenant rights. No state agency writes one, no statute makes you attach a summary of the law to the lease or have the tenant sign or initial an acknowledgment of one, and nothing bars you from suing or evicting until you have handed one over. The written statements you must give are narrower: the name and address of the manager and of the owner or the owner's agent (see landlord-disclosure-mt), the separate move-in condition statement when you take a security deposit (see edu-condition-statement-mt), the meth or fentanyl contamination notice where it applies (see edu-meth-disclosure-mt), the disclosure of known mold and mold testing (see mold-disclosure-mt), the federal lead-based paint disclosure for housing built before 1978 (see lead-based-paint), and, when a tenancy ends, a plain and understandable notice of how you will handle property left behind (see edu-abandoned-property-notice-mt). A local government with self-government powers may not add a tenant-rights statement requirement, because it may not regulate landlords' dealings with tenants beyond the state acts.

title: Changing Lease Terms by Notice in Montana
bodyText: In a Montana month-to-month tenancy you may change the rent or any other term of the lease, including a fee the lease already provides, by written notice served on the tenant at least 15 days before the end of a rental month; the change takes effect at the end of that month if the tenant stays on. Montana sets no longer notice for raising a fee than for raising rent, and you do not have to end the tenancy and offer a new one to change a term. A new or changed rule about the tenant's use and occupancy that substantially changes the tenant's bargain is different: it is not valid until 30 days after written notice in a month-to-month tenancy (7 days in a week-to-week tenancy). Because the two notice periods overlap, the cautious course for any change is written notice at least 30 days ahead, timed to take effect at the start of a rental month. The change-of-terms statute covers month-to-month leases only: in a week-to-week tenancy, change a term other than a rule by the tenant's written agreement, or end the tenancy on 7 days' written notice and offer new terms. During a fixed term you cannot change a term on your own unless the lease itself provides for the change. A changed fee must still be lawful (no fee for the way rent is paid except to recoup an electronic bank fee; a cleaning or damage fee is a security deposit), and a change may not be made in retaliation for a tenant's protected complaint or organizing. Rent increases in particular: Rent Increases and Term Changes in Montana (edu-rent-increase-notice-mt); rules: rules-mt. This covers the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No Exemption Notice Needed in Montana
bodyText: Some states require a lease statement telling a tenant that a property is exempt from a rent cap, a just-cause eviction rule or a tenant's right to buy. Montana has none of those laws, so there is nothing to be exempt from and no exemption notice, filing or statement to give: Montana has no state rent cap and bars local governments with self-government powers from controlling rent on private residential property (No Local Rent Control in Montana, edu-rent-control-mt); a periodic tenancy can be ended by the required written notice without a reason (No Just-Cause Eviction Rule in Montana, edu-for-cause-eviction-mt); and tenants have no right to buy when you sell (No Tenant Purchase Right on Sale in Montana, edu-no-tpa-notice-mt). Do not copy another state's exemption notice into a Montana lease; it would recite laws that do not apply here. Montana's exclusions from its landlord-tenant act (for example, an employee whose housing depends on the job, or transient hotel stays) and from its fair housing law apply by their own terms and need no notice to the tenant. We found no exemption-notice rule in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library.

title: No Tenant Purchase Right on Sale in Montana
bodyText: Montana gives a residential tenant no right of first refusal, no right of first offer and no opportunity or option to buy the property when you sell it, and requires no notice to tenants that you intend to sell or have listed the property. We found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library. No purchase-right notice belongs in your lease. What Montana does attach to a sale: once you sell in good faith to a bona fide buyer and give the tenant written notice of the sale, you are relieved of liability for later events except for the tenant's deposit and prepaid rent, and the buyer steps into your rights (Selling or Changing Managers of a Montana Rental, edu-sale-management-change-mt; deposits on sale, edu-deposit-on-sale-mt). Montana also has no condominium-conversion purchase right (edu-no-conversion-notice-mt). Mobile home lots, if you rent them: residents still have no right to buy the park, but you may not prohibit resident association or tenant meetings about the park's future, including a sale or change of use; before changing the park to another use you must give each mobile home owner and tenant 15 days' written notice before asking the local government for permits, then 6 months' written notice of termination describing the change, and you must warn prospective residents during that period. Montana instead encourages a sale to residents through its income tax: capital gain from selling a mobile home park to a qualifying tenants' or residents' association, a nonprofit buying on its behalf, or a county or municipal housing authority is excluded from Montana taxable income.

title: No Sunset on Montana Tenant Protections
bodyText: No Montana tenant-protection law is on a repeal or expiry clock. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, the security-deposit law, the mobile home lot act, the general landlord-tenant chapter, the eviction chapter and the fair housing law carry no sunset or termination date, so nothing you build into a lease today stops applying on a set date. The one dated change in Montana landlord-tenant law runs the other way: until January 1, 2031, a temporary covid-19 law limits a landlord's liability on a tenant's habitability or common-area claim for injury or death from covid-19 exposure to gross negligence, willful and wanton misconduct or intentional tort, and the landlord's maintenance-duty statute is printed in a temporary version made subject to it. From January 2, 2031 that limit lapses and the maintenance duties apply without it; the duties themselves do not change. Risk of change comes from ordinary amendment instead: the Legislature meets in odd-numbered years and amended the act in 2025 (for example, the payment-method fee rule and the deposit-refund exception). This covers the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No Lease Translation Duty in Montana
bodyText: Montana does not require you to give a tenant a lease, notice or disclosure in any language other than English, or a translation, even if you advertise or negotiate the lease in another language, and it prescribes no lease text that must be translated. We found no such rule in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library; Montana's other-language rules are for telephone sales notices, insurance policies, powers of attorney, court proceedings and government records. English is the official language of state and local government, but that rule does not govern private leases. What does apply is Montana's Plain Language in Contracts Act: a lease form you regularly use must be written clearly and coherently in words with common and everyday meanings, divided into captioned sections, in readable type (Montana's Plain Language in Contracts Act and Leases, edu-plain-language-contracts-act-mt; type size, edu-lease-type-size-mt). If a tenant reads English poorly, a translated copy or an interpreter at signing is a sensible courtesy that no Montana statute requires.

title: Trespass Notices at Montana Rentals
bodyText:
Montana's criminal trespass law applies to rental property, and Montana's landlord-tenant act adds its own trespasser rule; Montana has no separate statute on landlord no-trespass notices (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library).

**Criminal trespass.** A person commits criminal trespass by knowingly entering or remaining unlawfully in an occupied structure or on the premises of another (a fine up to $500, up to 6 months in jail, or both). A person enters or remains unlawfully when not licensed, invited or otherwise privileged to be there.

Privilege to be on land comes from the explicit permission of the landowner or another authorized person, or from the landowner's failure to post notice denying entry, and the landowner or other authorized person may revoke it at any time by telling the person directly. Montana's posting method (written notice, or orange paint, at each outer gate and normal point of access) is written for private land generally; a written no-trespass notice handed to the person is the surer course at a rental.

Each separately secured unit in a building is its own occupied structure, so a tenant's unit is the tenant's to admit people to.

**Rentals.** Under the landlord-tenant act, a person who enters or remains on the premises after you ask the person to leave, without your written permission to remain, is an unauthorized person or trespasser, and law enforcement may remove immediately a person who cannot produce authorization; you or your agent may ask them to, and providing false information makes you liable to indemnify them.

But authorization includes a tenant's written or verbal permission for the tenant's own guest (verbal permission must be verified by the tenant), so you cannot use trespass law alone to keep out a person a tenant invites. To cover that case, use a lease term binding the tenant not to admit a person you have barred in writing (the library's optional barred-person-covenant-ne).

Never use trespass to remove a tenant, who may be removed only through the court process (edu-unauthorized-occupant-mt, edu-self-help-eviction-mt). Bar people for conduct, in writing, and apply bans evenly, because fair housing law applies to the terms and privileges of a tenancy.

title: No Truth-in-Renting Law in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no truth-in-renting law. No state agency prepares a statement of tenants' and landlords' rights that you must give tenants or post, and no statute requires you to deliver or acknowledge one (No Required Tenant Rights Statement in Montana, edu-no-tenant-rights-statement-mt, lists the specific written disclosures Montana does require). We found no such law in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library; the only "truth in" laws in the Montana Code are references to the federal Truth in Lending Act in credit statutes. The protections a truth-in-renting law gives elsewhere come from other Montana rules: a lease may not contain the terms Montana's landlord-tenant act prohibits, such as a waiver of the tenant's rights under the act, and knowingly using such a term can cost you actual damages plus up to 3 months' periodic rent (edu-prohibited-terms-mt, edu-knowing-use-penalty-mt); and a lease form you regularly use must be in plain language (Montana's Plain Language in Contracts Act and Leases, edu-plain-language-contracts-act-mt).

title: No Montana Unbundled Parking Rule
bodyText:
Montana has no law requiring or forbidding you to rent parking separately from the dwelling, no rule on how a separate parking charge must be shown, and no cap on a parking charge (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules held for this library). Whether parking comes with the unit or is an optional extra is your choice. Two points apply.

A parking charge you agree on in the lease is part of the "rent" under Montana's definition, so an unpaid parking charge can be included in a notice for unpaid rent; state the amount in the lease and do not raise it during a fixed term unless the lease allows it.

And zoning: since October 1, 2026, city zoning under the general zoning statute may not require more than one parking space for each residential dwelling unit (or more than half a space for each unit under 1,200 square feet), or any minimum for certain buildings such as deed-restricted affordable housing, so newer buildings may have fewer spaces than units; you remain free to provide more. Local governments zoning under the Montana Land Use Planning Act are under the same one-space limit.

If you offer parking as an option, the library's optional clause is unbundled-parking-mt; if parking comes with the unit, use assigned-parking-space.

title: Leasing as a life tenant: no usufruct in Montana
bodyText:
Leasing when you don't own the property outright. Montana has no civil-law usufruct; the word appears in Montana law only in water compacts. The nearest Montana interest is a life estate (for example a parent who deeded the house to the children but kept it for life). The owner of a life estate may use the land as a fee owner would, but may not injure the inheritance, must keep buildings and fences repaired from ordinary waste, and must pay the taxes and annual charges; committing waste can cost treble damages. A grant by the owner of an estate for life or for years that tries to transfer more than that owner holds does not forfeit the owner's own estate, but passes only what the owner could lawfully transfer. Read together, a lease from a life tenant generally lasts no longer than the life estate, and the remainder owners take the property free of it unless they agreed to the lease; no Montana statute says so directly or says what the tenant is owed when it happens.

What to do: before you sign as (or rent from) a life tenant, check the deed; if the lease may run past the life estate, have the remainder owners sign the lease, or keep the term short. The owner disclosure every lease must carry should name the person entitled to receive notices and service for the owner. A status clause for life tenants would be lawful, but the library does not offer one: Montana sets no rule it could track, and binding the remainder owners needs their own signatures fitted to the deed, so add your own clause after taking advice. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: No Montana Cap on Rebilled Utilities or Utility Allowances
bodyText:
No Montana statute, and no Public Service Commission rule among those searched, caps what you may charge a tenant for a utility bill you pass on, bars a markup or billing fee, requires master-metered electricity to be included only in a fixed rent, or regulates a utility allowance with a tenant-paid overage. So a lease may say you pay a utility up to a set amount and the tenant pays the excess. The excess counts as rent when the lease makes it payable to you, and unpaid utilities may be deducted from the deposit.

The allowance limits what you pay, not the service: if the lease makes you responsible for water or heat you must still supply it, and you may never shut off or reduce a service because the tenant hasn't paid. Charge only what the provider actually billed for the unit, with no markup or fee, and show the bill.

Montana defines a regulated utility broadly and whether reselling electricity or gas to tenants makes a landlord one is unsettled, so use an allowance for electricity or gas only where the utility's own meter serves the unit alone. The library's optional Utility Allowance clause follows this course. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws, the Constitution and the held Commission rules; Commission orders, tariffs and court decisions were not.

title: Splitting Utility Bills Among Tenants in Montana
bodyText:
Montana lets the lease decide who pays for utilities, including a tenant's share of a bill that covers more than one unit. No Montana statute makes unenforceable a term that has the tenant pay for a utility that isn't separately metered to the unit, and no Public Service Commission rule among those searched governs how a landlord prices or splits gas, electricity or water among tenants.

Garbage removal is your duty unless the rental agreement provides otherwise, and a tenant may agree in a good-faith writing to take on your duty to supply water, hot water and heat. Any utility charge the lease makes payable to you counts as rent, and unpaid utilities may be deducted from the deposit.

Electricity is different in practice: a building started or rewired since early 1981 must, with narrow exceptions, be metered by the utility unit by unit, and whether billing tenants for electricity or gas makes you a regulated utility is unsettled. The library's optional Shared Water, Sewer and Trash Charges clause therefore covers water, sewer, storm water and trash only, at the provider's actual charge with no markup or fee, with a copy of the bill. Never shut off or reduce service to collect a share.

Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws, the Constitution and the held Commission rules; Commission orders, tariffs, court decisions and city utility rules were not.

If you figure the tenant's share from a submeter, use one that serves only the unit and is suitable and maintained for commercial measurement under Montana's weights and measures law.

title: Utility deposits held by a landlord
bodyText:
A deposit you take from a tenant to cover utility charges is a security deposit in Montana. Any deposit the lease requires the tenant to give you is presumed to be a security deposit, and the deposit law lets you deduct unpaid utilities from it. So hold it, account for it and return it with the rest of the deposit: within 30 days with the written list, or within 10 days if nothing is owed and the tenant shows that no utilities are unpaid. Montana has no separate landlord utility-deposit rule. Utility charges the lease makes payable to you also count as rent under Montana's definition of rent.

A deposit a utility company takes from a tenant is between the tenant and the utility. For utilities regulated by the Public Service Commission, the Commission's rules say when a deposit may be required and cap it at one-sixth of estimated annual billings, require 6% yearly interest, and require the deposit plus interest to be refunded (normally by check mailed within 30 days) after 12 months of prompt payment or when service ends, less any amount owed. Those rules bind the utility, not you, and do not apply to a deposit you collect yourself. If you supply heat, power or water to others through your own system rather than passing on a utility's bill, take advice on whether utility regulation reaches you.

title: No Utility Disclosure Attachment Required in Montana
bodyText: No Montana statute, and no Public Service Commission rule among those searched, requires a residential lease to carry a utility disclosure or attachment, such as average utility costs, a billing history, how shared utilities are split, or a statement that water or power is available. Montana's seller disclosure statement, which covers utility connections, applies to sales of one-to-four-unit homes and to a lease with an option to purchase, not to an ordinary lease. One related rule helps a prospective tenant: a Commission-regulated electric or gas utility must provide a property's average annual energy use, in dollars and based on the past 12 months at current rates, to the owner or the owner's representative or to a person involved in a real estate transaction on the property, which includes leasing; it may not disclose personal information. A prospective tenant can therefore ask the utility. What to do: state in the lease which utilities the tenant pays and, for any utility you bill, how the charge is figured; a separate attachment is optional. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws, the Constitution and the held Commission rules; utility tariffs and court decisions were not.

title: Copies of Utility Shutoff Notices to a Landlord in Montana
bodyText:
Montana's Public Service Commission rules require each gas and electric utility the Commission regulates to offer a voluntary third-party notification system. If the customer names a third person to receive termination notices, the utility must send that person a duplicate of each notice, and the third person is not liable for the account unless they agreed to guarantee it. The utility's statement of its termination policy, given to every new customer, must explain how to designate a third party.

So a tenant who holds the account can name you to receive copies of shutoff notices; the designation is made by the tenant with the utility. The rule does not cover electric cooperatives or city utilities, which may or may not offer such a service, and the Commission's water-utility rules have no third-party rule. If the account is in your name instead, the utility must notify your tenants before shutting off for your nonpayment (see the landlord-account note).

The library's optional Authorization for Utility Notices to Landlord clause has the tenant authorize you as a notice contact and sign the utility's form; it makes you responsible for none of the tenant's charges and cannot oblige a provider to act. No Montana statute addresses this. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws, the Constitution and the held Commission rules; utility tariffs were not.

title: No Utility Shutoffs by a Billing Landlord in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no statute, and no Public Service Commission rule among those searched, setting a procedure for a landlord who submeters or bills electricity (or any utility) to interrupt or disconnect a tenant's service for nonpayment. The Commission's notice, winter and medical protections bind the utility, not you. What governs you is the landlord-tenant act. You may not take possession by purposefully interrupting heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or other essential services. A tenant whose services you purposefully interrupt or diminish may recover possession or end the lease, and recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus the deposit and prepaid rent if the lease ends. You may not retaliate by decreasing services after a protected complaint. And if the lease or the act makes you responsible for a service and you purposefully or negligently fail to supply it, the tenant may, after written notice and a reasonable chance to fix it, buy the service and deduct the cost from rent, recover damages for the loss in rental value, or move to substitute housing and owe no rent for that time. So treat an unpaid submetered or billed utility charge as unpaid rent or a lease breach, and use written notice and the court process; never cut off or reduce the service to collect it. No Montana statute addresses short planned shutoffs for repairs, and the act's remedy for a purposeful interruption has no stated repair exception, so the library does not offer a clause permitting planned interruptions; keep any repair shutoff short, give notice, restore service promptly, and take advice before adding such a clause yourself. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws, the Constitution and the held Commission rules; Commission orders and court decisions were not.

title: Utility Accounts in the Landlord's Name in Montana
bodyText: If the gas or electric account for an occupied rental is in your name, the Public Service Commission's rules protect your tenants if you fall behind. Before any shutoff a regulated utility must find out whether the residence is occupied by a tenant. As a landlord customer you get a first notice at least 30 days before the proposed shutoff date. The utility must also give written notice to each unit reasonably likely to be occupied by an affected tenant, no earlier than five business days after notifying you and at least 15 days before the shutoff, and not until any dispute you raise about the amount is resolved. The tenant notice states the average and the largest monthly bill for the past 12 months and that tenants may have rights under Commission procedures and Montana law. Before a nonpayment shutoff that would affect tenants, the utility must notify the Commission in writing, and the Commission may look at what tenants have paid toward the bill, vacancies, rent withholding, your recent payments, weather, illness, ages and other housing. A utility may not shut off a customer because someone else failed to pay. No Montana statute lets tenants seek a receiver for unpaid utilities or pay the utility and deduct it by name, but the landlord-tenant act does: if the lease or the act makes you responsible for heat, water, electricity or gas and you purposefully or negligently fail to supply it, the tenant may, after written notice and a reasonable chance to correct, buy the service and deduct the cost from rent, recover damages, or move to substitute housing and owe no rent for that time. You may never let service lapse, close an account or ask for a shutoff to force a tenant out or to collect money. For water from a Commission-regulated water utility, the owner is liable unless the renter applies in the renter's own name; unpaid city water and sewer charges can be levied against the property. A utility is liable for direct damages if it discontinues service in breach of a continuous service agreement; the code doesn't define that term, so check any such agreement you have with the utility. Electric cooperatives and city utilities follow their own rules. Pay landlord-held accounts on time and tell the utility which units are occupied.

title: Utility Shutoff Protections in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no statute on utility shutoffs for nonpayment. The Public Service Commission's rules govern the gas and electric utilities it regulates. From November 1 to April 1, no shutoff may take place without the Commission's specific prior approval. During that period, and on any day when it is freezing at 8 a.m. or the Weather Service forecasts a snowstorm or freezing temperatures for the next 24 hours, residential service may not be shut off if the customer shows inability to pay (or to pay except in installments), or that the customer or a household member is 62 or older or handicapped. Service may not be shut off where a licensed health care professional certifies that losing it would aggravate a medical condition threatening a permanent resident's health, subject to payment-arrangement conditions. A shutoff needs written notice (normally a second notice at least 10 days before the date), an attempt to reach the customer in person or by phone, and may happen only between 8 a.m. and noon, and not on a day, or the day before a day, when the utility can't reconnect. Water utilities the Commission regulates must give similar notices and may not disconnect on a Friday, weekend or the day before a holiday. We found no rule barring shutoffs during a declared storm or other emergency beyond these weather limits, and winter does not simply extend the notice period. Electric cooperatives and city water and sewer systems are not regulated by the Commission and follow their own policies. These rules bind the utility. They give you no right to shut off a tenant's service, which you may never do to collect rent or force a move-out. If the account for a rental is in your name, see the separate rules for landlord accounts. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws, the Constitution and the held Commission rules; Commission orders and tariffs were not.

title: No Montana Rule on Transferring Utilities to the Tenant
bodyText:
No Montana statute, and no Public Service Commission rule among those searched, sets a deadline for a tenant to put utilities in the tenant's own name, lets you cut off landlord-name service the tenant did not transfer, or lets a court in a protective-order case order a utility account transferred.

A lease may require the transfer and repayment of what the provider billed you in the meantime (the library's optional Transfer of Utility Accounts clause); that repayment counts as rent when the lease makes it payable to you. Do not close your account or ask a utility to disconnect service to make the tenant transfer or pay.

A tenant whose heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or other essential service you purposefully interrupt may recover possession or end the lease and recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater. A disconnection you request is not a utility shutoff under the Commission's rules, so none of the tenant notices or winter protections would apply.

For water from a Commission-regulated water utility, a renter applies in the renter's own name and is then liable; until then the owner is. Use written notice and the court process for unpaid amounts. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws, the Constitution and the held Commission rules; utility tariffs and court decisions were not.
