title: No Landlord Incentive for Renting to Veterans in Montana
bodyText: Montana offers a private landlord no tax credit, payment, grant, deposit guarantee, damage fund or other incentive for renting to a veteran or a servicemember, and no Montana law requires, regulates or bars a veterans' rent discount or preference in private housing. We found none in the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the selected Administrative Rules of Montana searched for this library. Montana's veterans' housing help goes to veterans themselves: the Montana Board of Housing's veterans' home loan mortgage program helps veterans buy a home, the board may develop housing programs for veterans who cannot get conventional financing, and the disabled veteran property tax program reduces the tax on a qualified veteran's own home. Montana's veteran tax credits and preferences are for employers hiring veteran apprentices or giving a veteran hiring preference, not for landlords. Veteran or military status is not a protected class under Montana's fair housing law, but the protected classes (such as disability and age) still apply to veteran applicants like anyone else. If you choose to give veterans a rent concession, record it in the lease with the library's rent concession clause. A Montana National Guard member on active duty ordered to a new permanent station more than 60 miles away may end a lease early (Montana National Guard Members: Lease Rights, edu-servicemember-mt).

title: No Water Heater Temperature Rule in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no statute or state rule requiring you to set, limit or check a water heater's temperature, at the start of each tenancy or at any other time, or to install anti-scald valves (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state building, fire and energy code rules held for this library). Your duties are general: supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times, unless the unit's hot water comes from an installation in the tenant's exclusive control; keep the plumbing and any water heater you supply in good and safe working order; and, for units completed after July 1, 1977, comply with the codes that applied when the unit was built. How a water heater is installed is governed by the plumbing code the Department of Labor and Industry adopts (Montana uses the Uniform Plumbing Code), and a central hot water supply boiler in a building of more than six families also falls under the state boiler inspection law (see edu-heating-mt). What the plumbing code says about water heater temperatures or mixing valves was not read for this library. Cautious course: at each turnover, check that the water heater works and is set within the manufacturer's recommended safe range so the hot water can't scald, and tell the tenant whether they may adjust it.

title: Waterbeds and Waterbed Deposits in Montana
bodyText:
Montana has no statute on waterbeds or other liquid-filled furniture. You may refuse one, or allow one on conditions such as a proper frame and liner, an approved location and the tenant carrying insurance that covers water damage; the library's optional Waterbeds and Liquid-Filled Furniture clause (waterbed-mt) sets those terms.

If you want extra money to cover the risk, treat it as part of the security deposit: in Montana any fee or charge for cleaning or damage, however you name it, is presumed to be a security deposit, and any deposit the lease requires the tenant to keep up is presumed to be one too.

So a waterbed deposit must be accounted for and returned under the same rules as the rest of the deposit, including the itemized list and refund within 30 days of the tenancy ending (10 days if there is nothing to deduct and the tenant shows no unpaid utilities; the list rule does not apply if the lease was ended in a possession case and you have a claim pending in court), and it may be applied only to damage, unpaid rent and the other listed items. Do not label it non-refundable.

Montana sets no cap on the total deposit. A requirement that the tenant carry insurance is not a deposit and is lawful, but it does not shift to the tenant damage caused by your own negligence. Searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the 2025 session laws, the Constitution and the Montana rules held for this pass.

title: No Window Guard Rule in Montana
bodyText: Montana has no statute or state rule requiring you to install window guards or window stops for children, to give a window-guard notice in the lease, or to use any particular release mechanism on security bars (searched: the Montana Code Annotated 2025, the Montana Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state building and fire code rules held for this library). Window safety comes through the building code and your general duties. The state building code adopts the 2024 International Building and Residential Codes, and Montana's version requires emergency escape and rescue openings in all sleeping rooms of residential buildings that have no automatic sprinkler system (the state code reaches residential buildings with fewer than five units only where your city, town or county applies it); for units completed after July 1, 1977 you must keep up the code requirements that applied when the unit was built, and you must keep the premises fit, habitable and safe. What the model codes say about window sill heights, window opening control devices or bars over escape windows was not read for this library. Cautious course: never put bars, grilles or screens that can't be opened from the inside without a key, tool or special knowledge on a bedroom window that serves as an escape opening; where children will live on an upper floor, consider window stops or guards that limit the opening but release from the inside for escape; and repair broken latches, screens and sashes promptly. Ask your local building official what applied when your building was built.

title: Which notices must be in writing
bodyText:
Which notices must be in writing in Montana. The landlord-tenant act requires a written notice for every notice that ends a tenancy or starts a cure or termination clock, and a spoken notice does not meet a written-notice requirement.

Landlord's notices that must be written: the 3-day notice to pay rent; the noncompliance notice (14 days, or 3 days for an unauthorized pet, unauthorized occupants or verbal abuse; 5 days for a repeat within 6 months); the 3-day notices for damaging the premises or for conduct that creates a reasonable potential of damage or injury; the 30-day notice ending a month-to-month tenancy (7 days for week-to-week) and the 30-day notice that keeps a fixed-term lease from rolling into month-to-month; the 14-day notice before you repair, replace or clean to fix a tenant's health-and-safety breach of the tenant's duties (or sooner in an emergency); a new rule that substantially changes the deal (7 or 30 days); a month-to-month rent or term change (15 days before the month ends); the notice of a sale or management change that ends your liability; the abandoned-property notice; the written notice before deducting cleaning charges (if the tenant left without notice, you may skip it, or leave it in the unit and tell the tenant by e-mail, phone or text); and the move-out list of deposit deductions.

Your owner and manager disclosure must be in writing too. Tenant's notices that must be written: notice of a habitability breach (14 days to fix, 30 to terminate) or of an emergency; notice that essential services failed; a 5-day termination when you fail to deliver possession; and notice within 14 days of intent to end the lease after fire or casualty. Consent to a guest staying longer than allowed, and to a transfer or sublet, must also be written.

Not required in writing: the 24-hour notice of entry (posting it on the main entry door also counts). How a written notice is delivered (in hand, certificate of mailing or certified mail, the landlord's place of business, or e-mail only where the tenant elected it in the lease) is in the How to Give Notice row. This covers the Montana Code Annotated, the Constitution, the 2025 session laws and the state rules in the library's research set.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Montana follows a version of the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' that is harder on the person who cashes the check (Mont. Code Ann. § 30-3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, in good faith gives you a check or other instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement that it is offered in full satisfaction, and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. Writing 'under protest' when you endorse it does not save the balance (Mont. Code Ann. § 30-1-207(2)). Unlike most states, Montana gives you no right to undo the settlement by repaying the check within 90 days. The only way out is for an organization (for example an LLC) that, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement naming a person, office or place for communications about disputed debts, and the check did not go there; even that does not work if an agent of yours responsible for the disputed debt knew the check was offered in full satisfaction, or received the check and any writing with it. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it uncashed.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Montana's landlord-tenant act imposes a duty of good faith: every duty under the chapter, and every act that must be done before using a right or remedy under it, carries an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-109). That binds you and the tenant alike. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
